The issue went onto the middle of the table beside the fieldbook and the use log on the seventh and **stayed there for the rest of the batch.** Tova Reed's arithmetic: *two shillings a season would be nothing; two shillings is a subscription.* The first money this holding put into a market in a month went the wrong way, and Lissa Vale proposed it and said so in the book | Ch 60 |
| **The refused sum, restated** | **forty-one lines, forty-one shillings, two pounds and a shilling.** Nine hundred smallholders; one in twenty buying a printed line is forty-five sales a line | Ch 60 |
| **Dunmar Fitch's entry that carries the movement** | *the refusal was entered on the twenty-eighth of last month, the sum not received, a shilling a line for every line that names a variety, **the number of houses the refusal reached is one.*** And the sentence that turned the chapter: **a refusal is a thing this body can only do in a room with people in it; the room the index goes to is eleven miles long in every direction and there is no way to hold it; refusal is a place, and the place is this yard, and outside this yard it is weather** | Ch 60 |
| **The trade article** | **a quarterly of the professional body, the same body Pike's Volume 01 circular went out in, the same roll that carries Renner's license and nine other men's in this district. Under a plain heading, a description of a result: a wetted lot of seed laid against a living bead cut from grafted stock reports the ground it was grown on in four seconds without a clerk, with figures for a lot of one variety, weight and water and time and number of trials. NO NAME, NO LICENSE NUMBER, NO YARD, NO DISTRICT, NO HOLDER.** **Every figure is accurate and was checked against this holding's own trials of the thirtieth of last month and no fault was found, which is itself a finding** | Ch 61 |
| **Renner's four things, and the fourth** | *I did not write it. I cannot stop it. It is technically correct. And a technically correct description of a device that makes a seed lie is the most dangerous thing anybody has ever printed about this holding.* Plus the structural sentence, which is the volume's argument and is **not** an act by an office: **what is printed in a quarterly of a professional body is not a raid, it is the trade; it goes where the trade goes, it costs what the trade charges, and every act of it is correct and timely and structural, and if it ruins a seed house in this fen that is a cost and not a crime.** Four licensed men in Tarrow including Renner, and the body examines on a working and not on a paper | Ch 61 |
| **Renner's own undertaking** | **he will not build another bead this season, not for sale and not for hire; he has told his foreman and he will tell his nine men on the Friday; and if somebody offers him money for a collar by the middle of next month he will come up the fen road and say so in writing, because he would rather be the man who says it than the man who is found out.** He also reports, and gives up, his own finding: the article could not have come from this fen's book (which does not describe the method) and could not have come from the woman with the list of eleven holdings, and it came from somebody who sat where he sat | Ch 61 |
| **Corvin Slee's second visit and what the fen did with it** | **he came to the gate on the tenth, would not come past the posts, walked four miles, said the district has written for the low quarter's own survey, and offered Marek a copy of it in his coat.** **Marek refused the copy as well as the walk.** His reason, which is the reason the chapter exists: *a copy in this building is a copy this building can be asked for, and then it is a person's to lose, and an office in Fennmere is a better keeper than a person and I have got no argument against an office at all this season.* Slee's answer: *then what are you protecting.* Marek's: **their right to be the only ones who have it.** The copy sat unopened on the middle of the table and was entered as received and unopened with a line under it saying the sheet is not of this holding and is not in this holding's book | Ch 62 |
| **The district clerk at the gatepost** | **not an officer; a clerk sent out to look at a thing and write down what he saw; he asked Marek to walk the line of the standing iron as this holding finds it, to set beside the district's; Marek refused in front of him and gave a reason that was entered.** Marek's reason: **a holding that is owed a survey cannot also be the body that goes and collects it, because the collecting is the part that makes it theirs.** The clerk wrote the refusal in the district's book, read nothing back, and told Marek it could be read against the holding later by a man in an office who had never stood at a gatepost, and Marek said that was correct and wanted it entered anyway | Ch 62 |
| **The cost of the refusal, entered by Dunmar Fitch on his own initiative** | **the low quarter keeps its own map; this holding keeps its hands off it; and that costs this holding the only leverage it has in the district on the one ground where forty-one houses are still drinking off a bed it killed. A later room will want to know whether we knew that at the time. We did** | Ch 62 |

| **Kellan Rusk's three figures, entered and checked** | **his own side draw, never above three hundred in a day for six years, from his own log, open to any member of the cooperative at any hour without notice, with the page numbers; the head as the log claims it, eleven hundred a day; the ground as the ground took it, seven hundred and twenty, this holding's own figure, entered before the reading, read back by him from this holding's own page. Eighty a day unaccounted for, eighty a day for six years, one hundred and seventy-five thousand two hundred.** The district's monthly return was produced, read front and back, and **matches the first figure with no fault in it**, which means any body that asks may now get at it. | **Kellan's line, entered verbatim** | **you have built a book that anybody can read and you have put everything in it that is true about you, and a book like that is not evidence. It is an invitation.** | Ch 63 |

The officer's stated reason, given unasked: there is a clause in the charter with a condition in it that neither the district nor this holding can test, and a node with an untestable condition in it is a node she has to defend at every renewal, and a number she can check is worth more to this holding than any objection she could raise.** It costs the fen nothing and gives it the only thing it has wanted since the twenty-first of last month | Ch 68 |
| **The district file, and what the officer did with the figure** | **she cannot act on it: it is in the book of a body that is not her holder, given by a man who is not her licensee, about water drawn through a bed her district maintains; she has no power to make it an account and no power to send a demand on it and will not pretend otherwise. What she has is a file, and the file is the only place in this district where the draw of a private charter can be recorded without anybody's consent. She entered eighty a day for six years on the strength of a licensed man's own disclosure, and it will be read the next time anything in this district comes up for a renewal or a variation or an objection.** **This is the open book working in the fen's favour for the first time, and it is entered as a fact about a form and not about anybody's character, and the fen did not want it** | Ch 68 |

The officer's ruling: **a person who discloses a breach of his own condition can still be believed about the thing that is not the breach** — the same rule that held for a sealed envelope in this district once before. **Nobody rescued him, nobody forgave him, nobody apologized to him, and Lissa Vale did not look away from him, which was the most anybody gave him** | Ch 68 |
| **Coll Renner's form** | **form RW/3. One page. A box for the licensed engineer, with his name and district already filled in in his own hand. The buyer would not buy a doubtful line and would take forty bags at a time when it was established, and would rather hear from the seed house than from the index. **The line is the March's, the March's holding is the trust's, the trust is a named party to a charter condition, and the cost of the refusal is a lost sale of forty-five bags at the trust's price** | Ch 65 |
| **Tova Reed's eighth line, and the lateness** | **the seventh line against the trust's interest becomes the eighth, and it is the first line she has ever entered that says she was wrong about a thing and not about a number. It is a buyer doing arithmetic, and I was wrong about the cost.** The number of bags that were not sold was written in pencil and struck out, and Dunmar Fitch made her initial the striking. Entered above it: **four days of lateness on a notice this holding was never served with, entered in her own hand and not softened.** It goes on the Thursday post of the **twenty-second** | Ch 65 |

She is not going to go to Cray to warn them, because a steward who warns people about the size of their own rights is a steward who has decided the rights are too big.** Entered by Anneke Roos as an opinion and not as a minute, and Dunmar Fitch did not ask to see it | Ch 66 |

| **The stranger of the twenty-first to the twenty-third** | **a woman of about forty, of a seed house in a town two hundred miles from here with no fen in it, and the house of the buyer who wrote to Cray. | **The answer to the fieldbook's book** | **asked on the twenty-third, on her way out, by the only stranger in six weeks who had asked it: is there a use log for the fieldbook. Lissa Vale said no. | **Being readable is a position** | *a woman came two hundred miles to buy an answer about a bean and we handed her a season's water. Being readable is a position and not a virtue. No one asked us to be a good citizen. We are not thanked for it and cannot be.* | Ch 67 |

Nobody in that room said the word.** Tova Reed did not touch her case. Marek did not look at the sheet, which has lain on the middle of the table since the twenty-ninth of last month under a reader's own marginal line in her own hand | Ch 68 |

## The section-nine margin notes: the ninth, the tenth and the eleventh, and the counting

**The chain is now eleven and the counting has been checked twice.** Six at the end of Volume 01 → **seven** in Ch 50 (the twenty-third) → **eight** in Ch 58 (the first) → **nine** in Ch 62 (the tenth) → **ten** in Ch 66 (the twentieth) → **eleven** in Ch 68 (the twenty-fourth). All three new notes are signed by nobody but Marek and are read back before they are initialled.

1. **The ninth, Ch 62, the tenth.** Asked on the tenth in front of the district's own man to walk another body's survey and refused for standing and not for right; a copy of that survey offered and not taken; the low quarter keeping its own map at its own cost and this holding keeping its hands off it; the report of the animal of the nineteenth standing in three places with nothing under it; the cost entered, that the fen loses its only leverage where forty-one houses drink off a bed it killed. Closes with the sentence.
2. **The tenth, Ch 66, the twentieth.** The whole of the book read aloud once in daylight on the nineteenth to five households and two strangers, the standing log and the use log and the annex and the beat and the leak and the shortfall and the nine earlier notes and the certified copy and the copy to Cray all in one hearing; the sentence that a readable book is worth what a reader will do about it; the vote that every entry be read aloud by a person and not a room. Closes with the sentence.
3. **The eleventh, Ch 68, the twenty-fourth.** The district officer, the figure, the breach, the district file, the order for the load test, and the map. Closes with the sentence, **and the sentence is on it because the note carries the map question and the map question is an argument** — which is the reason the eighth did not carry it and the reason the tenth does, and Dunmar Fitch writes both of those reasons under the tenth note so that a chain cannot be seen to drop a link.

**The closing sentence, *This is worth nothing against a cut*, stands on nine of the eleven notes and is off the sixth and the eighth — that is, at the moment Chapter 68's note is written, it has been on the last three in a row, and the two that lack it are the only two that lack it.** That is the whole of the pattern and it is stated on the page twice in this batch: **the two notes without it are the two that were records and not arguments, and both of them say so underneath in the engineer's own hand.** The count was verified against Chapter 67's conversation, where a reader of the book works it out for herself from the page. **A later writer may not add a note that carries the sentence without saying whether it is a record or an argument, and may not remove one.**

## The Volume 02 Batch 0002 review pass

**An independent review ran after Chapters 60–68 were drafted and every finding was applied in the prose. The findings are `reviews/volume-02-batch-0002.findings.md` — twenty-two, seven blocking, plus four found while applying them — and this is the state-side record of what a later writer has to know, not a transcript of the prose work.**

**The batch was not restarted. No scene was replaced. No planned plot was changed.** Three things follow from that and are the whole of what changed at the state level:

1. **The batch is days 65–84, the fifth through the twenty-fourth. Day 85 is unused and belongs to Chapters 69–76.** The prompt's ordinal column was off by one against its own weekday column; the weekday column is right, because day 61 is locked as the first and a Thursday, and the chapters were dated from it. The one figure that settles it is Ch 68's own arithmetic: *twenty-three days from the first to the twenty-fourth*, *eleven days since the request was minuted*, *thirty-five days* to the expiry are all true only if the twenty-fourth is day 84.
2. **Kellan Rusk is licensed on the Tarrow water record under a monitored charter, and is not on the rootwright roll.** The three-name rootwright roll is Coll Renner's. The batch had blurred the two, and the blur was load-bearing, because the one Fieldbook panel requires a licensed man. **The two rolls are now distinguished on the page and a later writer may not merge them back.**
3. **The use log is six lines from Chapter 63 and is read as six in Ch 63, Ch 66 and Ch 67.** The table is above. **Line six records only the contact and the hour, so the panel remains quoted in no document after the fix.**

**The dating pass, in one line: sixteen uses of *two months back* were applied to days 31–60, which are *last month*, and all sixteen are corrected. Three uses survive and all three are genuine October.** One instruction in the review to change an eleventh from *two months back* to *last month* was **wrong** — the eleventh follows the tenth in the same month, and that month is October — and was not applied.

**The arithmetic pass, in one line:** the lateness figures now run four on the eighteenth, six on the twentieth, **eight** on the twenty-second, and each is stated on the day it is true; **Cray is nine hundred miles by the March road and a hundred and eleven further by the ordinary cart, and the distance from the seventh to the fourteenth is seven days; the sale was forty-five bags and not forty; the index is a hundred and forty copies of two hundred pages and not a hundred and forty sheets; the three acres went sour three weeks ago and not two months; the price list at eighteen pounds is four levies of four pounds five and not a year's raise; and the purchase of the index is paid for before it arrives, in a hand to a carter on the Friday, not on the Thursday post after it has already been on the table.**

**Prose repaired without changing the plot:** two set-pieces that read as beat lists are broken into paragraphs; Kellan's bench speech is whole in Ch 63 and compressed in Ch 68, where he points at the fen's own hand instead; the buyer is a woman throughout; the collie is out of the public reading; the man of about fifty's non-vote is entered; two of Chapter 60's staging paragraphs and one of Chapter 65's were cut for repetition; the stray double blank line and four *hand flat* gestures are gone; and Chapter 65, which had entered the same line twice in one scene and re-narrated the post's arrival after playing it out, now does each once.

**Known and accepted, and not to be re-attempted: the staging.** Eight of nine chapters sit at the seed-house table. The review proposed moving two of the batch's central set-pieces out of it; **both were declined at the fix pass, because both are long unbroken dialogue and moving either one costs more than it buys, and the residue is recorded here as a weakness rather than fixed silently.** A later writer should vary the staging deliberately and should not assume the batch modelled it.

**Length after the pass: 9 chapters, 2,507–3,100 words, 25,388 total.** Two chapters went over the ceiling when the fixes landed and were trimmed back into it by cutting restatement, not by cutting a scene. **Chapters 60 and 63 are the two nearest a ceiling and a later writer should trim rather than pad.**

## The Fieldbook panel: one spent, in Chapter 63, and the allowance

**Spent, once, in Chapter 63, on the twelfth, at the eleventh hour, at the well house, on the head of the node.** **Kellan Rusk is a licensed man on the Tarrow water record, under a monitored charter. He is not on the rootwright roll and never was: that roll has three names and Coll Renner's license is on it. The two rolls are now distinguished on the page in Ch 63 and a later writer may not blur them back together.** He tested the contact with a plain wire gauge and wrote the reading of the test down before he let the instrument near anything. **Lissa Vale wrote the use-log line first, on the page, and read it back, and Marek initialled it after her.** The instrument came out of the case Lissa Vale had carried down from the seed house that morning; it has been on Marek's mother's table since the twenty-first of last month, and **it is in the instrument and not in a person**, and it is set as a block quotation of three plain lines in the volume's own house format:

> This is the mouth.
>
> There is more than one source and it will not say which.
>
> A node does not keep a list.

**It is spent on a thing the instrument can read.** It is not spent on the seed line, on the bead, on the hand in the register, on the market, or on a page: the instrument reads a node and Chapter 59 has established on the page that it cannot read paper, and this batch did not reopen that.

**It cost something and the cost is on the page.** Eleven seconds he cannot account for, as with the four on the cut face; the four inches on his forearm hot and staying hot; his hand from the wrist down no use for the rest of that day and most of the next; Kellan Rusk holding the case down the well house steps because Marek could not get the latch with two fingers. **And the third line refused the fen the answer it wanted, in the same three lines, which is the cost that matters: the eighty a day is a figure about a mouth, and nothing will name the sources, and the fen's own book cannot hold it.**

**Nothing in this batch quotes the three lines in a document, and the use-log line records only that the instrument was laid on the head at a stated hour with a licensed man present.** Lissa Vale wrote nothing else, and gave the reason in one sentence, and it is the same rule Dunmar Fitch applied on the third of last month to a different set of lines: *there is nothing in it that a man with a rule can check, and a line in a book that cannot be checked is a line somebody can use.* The reading went into the book as **a contact and not as a finding**.

**The Volume 02 allowance is now zero for Batch 0002, and one panel per batch is available to Batches 0003, 0004 and 0005.**

## Stage and contact accounting after Volume 02 Batch 0002

- **Marek is Stage 2, Grafthand, and this batch does not move him.** The stage is one small graft old. He can make a small reliable graft between living tissue and a limited local branch and he can keep two or three active links; a fourth fails. **He still cannot draw, has no bead, no anchor work, no bridge above a local conduit, no seedheart, no caretaker link and no reading of the deep archive, and the touchroot sense is unchanged and still unreliable and still worth nothing in front of anybody except a licensed engineer standing next to him.** No number in this batch may be used to move him.
- **The rootmark is present and unchanged: four inches along the inside of the left forearm, branching twice, permanent, recorded in this holding's book by Coll Renner under his own hand with the hour and the witnesses.** In this batch it is hot after a contact and the hand is useless for two days in four, and **nobody in this yard wrote the word *became* and nobody may.**
- **Contacts: four behind him, unchanged in kind and cost, plus one contact made in Chapter 63 and entered as a contact and not as a finding.** **The Ch 63 contact is not a fifth contact in the Volume 01 sense and may not be counted as one.** It was eleven seconds at a node, with a licensed man, with the contact tested and the use-log line written and read back first, it cost the mark and two days of the hand, and it produced three lines that cannot be checked and cannot be entered.
- **No draw and no return by rootlight in this batch, and the panel's third line is the reason the volume does not need one: a node does not keep a list.**

## New locks from the drafted Volume 02 Batch 0002

- **A refusal is a place, and the place is this yard.** The batch's governing fact. It is entered in the book with the number of houses the refusal reached, which is one, and it may not be softened by any later chapter into anything about markets being wrong.
- **Nobody may call the index's doubt an attack, and the proposal and the refusal are both on the page with Marek's name against the proposal.** A true thing that costs this holding money is not a crime, and a category that is true cannot be caught at anything. This is the same rule that governs the Crown-held column and the legend, and it now governs a private printer as well.
- **A body that is owed a survey may not also be the body that goes and collects it, and may not hold a copy of one either.** The low quarter's map stays in the low quarter's hands and the fen's copy of it stays unopened on the fen's own table. The cost is entered, and the fen has lost the only leverage it had in the district on the one ground where forty-one houses are still drinking off a bed it killed, **and it knew that when it did it.**
- **The open book cannot be repealed, and a body cannot consent to the removal of its own record.** The vote of the twentieth is not a repeal and is not a softening: it is a body that cannot unwrite a page and will not stop writing. **A later batch may not have this body vote the book shut, and may not have the district waive the condition.**
- **Every entry is read aloud before it is initialled, and the reader is a person.** A person is anybody who comes. **This rule is now in force and every subsequent entry in the volume obeys it on the page, and a chapter that enters something without showing the reading is a chapter that has broken it.**
- **Being readable is a position and not a virtue, and the holding is not thanked for it and cannot be.** No one has asked it to be a good citizen. This must not be converted into a compliment in a later chapter.
- **There is no use log for the fieldbook, there never has been, and there is not going to be.** A stranger asked and Lissa Vale said no in one word. **A later chapter may not supply one, may not have anybody propose one, and may not have anybody thank anybody for the absence.**
- **The instrument reads a node and not a book, and the third line of the Ch 63 panel is in force: a node does not keep a list.** The fen cannot manufacture provenance out of the ground. This is the rule Movement 3 will work against, and a later batch may not quietly suspend it.
- **The district is not a villain and did not act in this batch.** Every Crown act is correct, timely and structural: a quarterly article is the trade and not a raid, a return is a document and is produced before a figure is heard, a file is the only place a private draw can be recorded without consent, a load test is ordered because a node with an untestable condition is hard to defend, and the map is wanted because a nine-year-old sheet carries a mark this holding can now name. **A later writer may not let the two be confused, and may not let a district officer lie, obstruct, or act corruptly.**
- **The figure of eighty a day is in the district file and will be read at the next renewal, a variation, or an objection.** The invitation works both ways. This is not a rescue and the fen did not want it.
- **The open book's cost is now paid three ways and no chapter may say it was free: a lost sale of forty-five bags entered in Tova Reed's own hand as the first line she has ever entered that says she was wrong about a thing and not about a number; the fen's only leverage in the district; and the second condition of clause three taken out of the building in a stranger's notebook.**
- **Kellan Rusk's breach stands disclosed in his own words, beside the figure and not below it.** He is not rescued, not forgiven and not thanked. His monitored charter is not renewed, reduced or resolved by this batch. **The word *became* and the word *redeemed* are both prohibited for him in this volume.**
- **Nothing romantic has happened and nothing may lean that way.** Tova Reed put two sheets of yard paper in her own book and did not give them back and said the compost and not the other thing. **That is the whole of it and it is institutional, and no later chapter may make it anything else.**
- **Lissa Vale is not forgiven and is not thanked.** She proposed the two shillings and said so in the book; she read the whole of the use log to a stranger herself and gave the reason out loud; she wrote the use-log line before the instrument; she refused to enter the panel; she wrote a rule in October and told a stranger it was hers to keep; and she answered *no*, in one word, to the only question nobody had asked in six weeks. **Her refusal of the fourth of last month is hers, is not Sera Quill's, is not her own fourth, and is not numbered.**
- **Nia is not in this batch.** Not in a room, not in a letter, not by report, and nobody may say she decided not to deliver the letter. **The letter is in the open drawer of the seed-house table, sealed.** The absence is a working absence: the monthly report, the mill figures, the reading aloud, the rule about the reader being a person and the answer to a stranger all got done by other people in three weeks, and the fen has not once written down why.
- **Sera Quill is not in this batch, is not asked about Brinewake, and nobody has asked about her fourth refusal.** It is unnumbered and it may not be numbered. **The next monthly examination, at which the load test is to be performed with a licensed engineer present, is the one at which the volume's first licensed witness will have to be somebody else**, and no chapter may have her simply arrive.
- **Sera Quill, the fieldbook, the C/4, the register, the long line, the bypass, the Thornwild settlement, the word *seat*, Marda Vole, Dunmar's *none known*, the sealed envelope, and the works schedule behind the certified page are all untouched by this batch and none of them may be undone by it.** The bypass is unbuilt, unfunded, and Ivo Tarrant's four men do not come back. The register's log is still not produced and the applicant is not entitled to it. **No second demand for the register may be sent and none was.**
- **The leak is still a leak and is still not mended: five-eighths of an inch, twice measured, two rules, at the seventh hour, pump on, into the housing and not into the pit, the pit four feet of iron water and not up a quarter of an inch.** One sixteenth in thirteen days and still no rate written. **It cannot be mended under load and the panel did not diagnose it and nothing in this batch made it a mystery.** The beat is logged ten times and undiagnosed. The 399 hundredweight shortfall is carried forward and not discharged and is seventy-nine pounds sixteen at four shillings. The compost line is still nothing put in, none available, last put in twenty-one hundredweight and a quarter on the fourteenth by levy. The bed is at three and a half degrees. The graft is being fed about a twentieth of what it was designed to be fed and the starve is still not visible from the top of the field.

## Proposed canon changes recorded, not silently applied — Volume 02 Batch 0002

Batch 0002 added eight things by drafting. All are local detail, mechanisms, forms, prices, places or people, and none changes a world rule:

1. **The Ashcombe index as a purchased object** — two hundred pages, two shillings, a subscription rather than a purchase, and a copy on the middle of the fen's own table beside the fieldbook and the use log. **A body that buys its enemy's printer and puts it in the room with its own record is a new posture and it is now established.**
2. **The trade article and the professional quarterly** — the body is the same body Pike's circular went out in, the article carries no name and no license number and is technically accurate, and the defence anybody has is a book. **A market in methods, and the first appearance of a Crown-facing trade that is not a raid.**
3. **Form RW/3, the schedule of works** — one page, a box for the licensed engineer, a box for the four conditions, a blank line at the foot for the order of the work. **A new form class, and the shape of the method as a thing a foreman can carry to a holding he has never seen.** The order of the work is refused and the compost is the reason.
4. **Renner's price list and route** — day work at four shillings, a yard at a pound a month, a copper collar at two shillings, a crew of four for a season at eighteen pounds, eleven farms on the fen road. **A price list is a new document class in the volume and it is the first material anybody has put on that table in a season.**
5. **The C/4's date as the fen's own computation** — the fen is not the addressee, is not entitled to a copy of the notice, does not know when it was served, and enters the fourteenth as a computation and not as a fact. **A clock the holding cannot check, and a standing lateness that runs from the fourteenth of this month.**
6. **The vote of the twentieth** — every entry read aloud before it is initialled, the reader is a person, a person is anybody who comes, and the fact of who voted and who only heard is entered. **A new standing practice inside an existing charter condition, adopted by the body and not by the district.**
7. **The stranger of the twenty-first to the twenty-third** — a seed buyer with a pencil, a town two hundred miles off with no fen in it, and the disclosure that she is going to write to a printer. **A seed house outside the district is now a party to this holding's record without ever having been one, and the mechanism is the annex's fourth term.**
8. **Hilary Skeath, of the district water office for the Tarrow district**, about thirty-five, who gives her name once at a gate and is entered in the book by the clerk, and who orders the full-draw load test and says the district will want the map next. **A named district water officer for the winter.** She is **not** a member of the cooperative, and **no new named member of the cooperative was created in this batch**: the crew is still Ilsa Kern, Jonas Byre, Anneke Roos, Gael Senn, Lissa Vale and Dunmar Fitch, plus the man of about fifty and the man of about seventy, who are held by function and may not be given names without recording it.

None of the eight changes a world rule, a power rule, a relationship lock, or the ending. **The ending is untouched: Chancellor Iona Vey remains the final antagonist, the Rootway is not a mind, and the volume's question — who altered the maps and the seed records enough to make a bridge between this fen and the dry Salt March legal, and who was paid for the alteration — is still unanswered and has gained one line, not one answer.** The ninth lock is the district's statement that it will want the map next, and nobody in that room said the word.

Off the press on the fourteenth and carried up the fen road on a hand barrow.** Last page: Coll Renner's two hundred words on what a bead reads and does not read and what one part in eleven means; under them Tova Reed's two sentences, one of which is that a lot of one part in eleven is a sale the law allows and the trade has agreed to and that no office in this district will call it fraud, and that is a notice and not an opinion; under those, his name and his license number. Lissa Vale read all two hundred pages out in the yard on the fourteenth. One copy sold in the yard at a shilling, one to the buyer's house | Ch 74, Ch 75, Ch 76 |

Two men, not one, and he has said two because there were two. He refused in writing on the ninth, kept a copy, dated and signed, and sent the letter back by the hand that brought it, and came up the fen road on the tenth, five days before the fifteenth he had promised in a yard on the eighth, and gave the fen the offer before he said anything else** | Ch 75 |
| **Why he refused, and the fen's own rule** | **a man who makes a bead on a Sunday is a man whose beads have no record, and a bead with no record is worth whatever the man selling it says it is worth** — and the rule he quotes back at them is the fen's own, made in the spring, that no work on this node is done between dusk and dawn without a licensed engineer standing in it, because a thing done at night is a thing nobody can check. *I am not going to be the first man in this district to sell a night, and if I did there would not be a book in this fen afterwards that could do one thing about it, and I would have taken twelve pounds for it, and the book would have been right* | Ch 75 |
| **The name he did not give** | **one of the two men buys on the Ashcombe index and Renner knows his name and would not say it in a book, and the reason is entered in his own words: if I say his name in your book, then your book is a thing somebody can take off me.** The clerk entered that a man declined to name a buyer and gave his reason, the body accepted it, and **Anneke Roos initialled as an opinion, faster than any in a season, a standing of this holding: a man may decline to name a buyer in a book this body keeps; the clerk enters that he declined and why; the body does not ask again and does not enter the name if it is told one. The clerk added that nobody in the yard is to go and find it out and come back with it** | Ch 75 |
| **How many collars exist** | **four made by Renner in eleven years — two given away, one sold, one lost, and the one lost is the one in this yard — and a fifth man in this district who has one and whom Renner has not asked and does not intend to ask, entered on the page so that nobody can say afterward that it was not.** Four remain in the Fennmere yard and he is not selling them | Ch 75 |
| **Form RW/3, paid** | **Renner filled in his own copy on the sixth and sent it to a holding on the Marrowfield road that cannot afford a cooperative, with the line at the foot written out in his own hand and his name on it as the licensed man, and told the fen there is no compost in that holding and wrote that down too — and told the fen first, on the tenth, because the fen refused it and he did not have to.** This is the form coming back filled in by another hand, half a season early | Ch 75 |
| **The district's answer of four lines** | **written to the district on the eleventh about the offer and answered on the Thursday cart: a licensed man's private arrangement with a purchaser is not a matter for the district; the district examines a man on a working and not on a paper; there is no form; a person may write to the Assembly and the Assembly will examine him and will not tell the person what it found.** No copy in Cray and cannot be. **A form for the water, a form for the seed, a form for a form, and not one form for a man being offered twelve pounds to cut a collar on a Sunday, and that is not because anybody is hiding anything** | Ch 75 |
| **The two walks** | **Jonas Byre went to two of the eleven holdings on Renner's price list on the eleventh with the offer and the refusal in his coat. The first heard him out, thanked him, asked what his standing was, was told he is a member of a cooperative eleven miles off and his license is not a license for anything, and shut the door. The second did not open the door, had heard about the collar, wanted to know what it cost, and is thinking about it.** Both entered with the hour at the well house door | Ch 75 |

A one-page covering letter over a man Tova Reed named once, and nine sheets, produced late, in full, with a schedule of four things the trust cannot produce and the reason in each case.** One of the four is a column | Ch 76 |

There is no column for cuttings, none for a line dispersed to ground and not returned from, none for a steward. The answer says so in one line: the trust cannot produce a record of cuttings dispatched, there being no column for it, and no such record was made, and this is not an omission from the answer but the absence of the thing itself** | Ch 76 |

The trust cannot move a crate north or south until the season turns, and has asked in the same line whether this holding would hold the trust's seed for one season. The holding would, cannot pay carriage, and was not asked to** | Ch 76 |
| **The trust's sentence, which is the volume's answer said by a body nine hundred miles off** | *A line kept in one book is a line that can be got at. A line kept in eleven grounds and no book is a line that can be sold. The trust has not been paid for the cuttings and does not know that they were paid for and has now entered that it does not know, and the trust's position is that this is a fault in the trust and not in any holder, and that a fault of that kind cannot be corrected by paying anybody, and can only be corrected by saying it out loud in a book that anybody may read. The trust understands that the trust has said so in one* | Ch 76 |
| **The cutting list is now in two books in two countries** | **Tova Reed wrote the eleven names to the trust on the ninth of next month, three days after telling the fen, and they went with the copy of the fen's book because the annex's fourth term sends a copy of everything to Cray. The eleventh name is this holding, which is a party to a charter condition. One list, two hands, no private copy anywhere — and it is the first time in eleven years that has been true of anything she has done, and it also means the fen can now be asked for it** | Ch 76 |

It went on the Thursday cart with the printing, with a second sheet of a page and a half, answered inside four days.** The second sheet names the ninth legend mark, says the branch is used for the supply of eleven households and is a local holder in fact, makes no claim to the Crown's layer, says the mark is not a warning to the holder but a handover to whoever is not the holder, and notes that this holding is the holder and was not on the sheet when the sheet was printed and the sheet has not been reprinted in nine years and nobody appears to have been required to say anything about it | Ch 76 |

A boy went down the fen road with the letter and a copy and a shilling of the fen's money | Ch 76 |

The shortfall three hundred and ninety-nine hundredweight, seventy-nine pounds sixteen at four shillings, carried forward and not discharged. The bed at three and a half degrees. The March's tin unmoved, eighty-five days at risk. The leak at five-eighths, unmoved under a full draw, not mended. The beat logged eleven times. Nineteen acres standing, the Longneck at eleven degrees, four willow sets alive, the graft fed about a twentieth.** The charter expires in fifteen days with no appeal anywhere in the four clauses, and Ruben Ashe is named in this holding's own book as returning at that date | Ch 76 |

## The section-nine margin notes: the twelfth and the thirteenth, and the counting

**The chain is now thirteen and the counting has been checked.** Eleven at the end of Batch 0002 → **twelve** in Ch 74 (the seventh) → **thirteen** in Ch 76 (the fourteenth). Both are signed by nobody but Marek and both are read back before they are initialled.

1. **The twelfth, Ch 74, the seventh.** A collar of living wood bought from a licensed man at two shillings and the four seconds and what it does and does not say; a certificate of origin on a house's letterhead; an offer refused in a yard by seven hands of which two were against and one of the two was the engineer of record; two hundred pages set in print and sold at a shilling a copy; eleven of the eleven cuttings entered in two books in two countries with no private copy; the district's demand for a Crown sheet answered inside four days with a second sheet naming this holding a holder of a line the Crown sheet says has none; a licensed man offered twelve pounds for a collar on a Sunday and refusing in writing and coming up the road five days before his own date to say so; a district that has no form for any of it; and twenty-two days.
2. **The thirteenth, Ch 76, the fourteenth.** The trust's answer twenty-eight days late with the schedule of four things it cannot produce and the reason in each case; the eleventh column and the absence of the thing itself; the March road out at two places; the map given away with a counter-mark; two hundred pages off the press and forty copies and one sold in the yard; the letter from a person who gave no house and walked eleven days; and fifteen days.

**The closing sentence, *This is worth nothing against a cut*, stands on eleven of the thirteen notes and is off the sixth and the eighth only.** That is the same pattern as at the end of Batch 0002 — two notes without it, both records and not arguments, both saying so underneath in the engineer's own hand — and **no later writer may add a note that carries the sentence without saying whether it is a record or an argument, and may not remove one.**

## The Fieldbook panel: one spent, in Chapter 73, and the allowance

**Spent, once, in Chapter 73, on the sixth, at the eleventh hour, at the seed-house table, with the instrument laid against the wood of the bead in a copper collar.** Coll Renner is the licensed man and fitted his own clip; the contact was tested with a plain wire gauge and the reading of the test written down first in Renner's own hand; **Lissa Vale wrote the use-log line first, on the page, and read it back, and Marek read it back after her, and it went in as the eleventh line** and records the contact, the hour, the roll and nothing whatever about what came out. It is set as a block quotation of three plain lines in the volume's house format:

> The ring reads the last hand.
>
> It does not read the ground, and it never will.
>
> There is nothing here a buyer may not buy.

**It cost what it costs.** Eleven seconds he cannot account for, as with the four on a cut face and the eleven at the head; the four inches on his forearm hot before it was over and staying hot; his hand from the wrist down no use to him from the second hour; Renner holding the case down the seed-house steps.

**Nothing in this batch quotes the three lines in a document, and Lissa Vale refuses to enter them on the rule she has now given out loud twice.** Renner asks for that and then tells the room what entering them would cost him — any man with a wet cloth could read them off a collar in a market, nine carriers would sell for every line, and he could not say where it was published, because it would be in this fen's book. **So the fen decides the batch's central question without the one instrument that might have settled it, and the instrument tells them the problem and not the answer, which is what it has done twice before.**

**A deliberate decision a reviewer should know about: Renner says all three lines out loud in the yard, once, to the six people in the room.** This is not the panel entering a document and it is not a person finding it; it is the licensed man who made the collar repeating it to a room that already knows the whole of the problem, and it is the smallest possible instance of the harm he describes two paragraphs later. The rule on the page is that no line enters a book, and the rule holds, and **a later writer may not have the three lines appear in any document, on any form, in any letter, in any printing, or in any of Wrenlow's records, and may not have a character quote them as authority.**

**The Volume 02 allowance is now zero for Batch 0003, and one panel per batch is available to Batches 0004 and 0005.**

## The use log, and where it stands

**The use log is eleven lines from Chapter 73, and it now governs the collar as well as the instrument and the fieldbook.** A collar is a bead of living rootwood in a ring of copper, and putting one against a wetted lot is a contact that cannot be checked, and Lissa Vale said on the twenty-fifth that a wet cloth is not a contact and then wrote the lines anyway. **A thing which cannot be checked is a thing that has to be counted.**

1. the tenth, two months back, entered on the eleventh, the lateness declared. 2. the twentieth, the same month. 3. the fourth of last month, a refusal with the reason against it. 4. the seventeenth, two months back, at four in the morning, on the back of the page. 5. the thirtieth of last month, a bead, a clip, a license and a witness. 6. the twelfth of this month, the instrument on the head of the node at the eleventh hour, licensed man present, contact tested first, **and nothing else whatever.** 7. **the twenty-fifth**, the fen's own bean and the March's wet-line rye, two lots, two collar contacts, four seconds each, **and the two results that were places.** 8. **the twenty-fifth**, the grafted seedling, one collar contact, **and the reading not entered, with Lissa Vale's nine-line refusal entered with it.** 9. **the twenty-eighth**, a collar in a copper ring against a wetted lot, a licensed man not required and not present, the lot the property of a house at Marrowfield, four seconds, **and nothing at all about what the four seconds were.** 10. **the third of next month**, the ninth hour, thirty-one trays and nine tins on a floor, one collar, **and no findings.** 11. **the sixth**, the eleventh hour, the instrument against the wood of a bead in a collar, licensed man present and named and the roll named, contact tested before the contact and the test written down first, **and nothing whatever about what came out.**

**There is still no use log for the fieldbook, there never has been, and a later chapter may not supply one or propose one.** The stranger of the twenty-second of last month wrote that absence down in a notebook two hundred miles away and it has not been quoted since.

## Stage and contact accounting after Volume 02 Batch 0003

- **Marek is Stage 2, Grafthand, and this batch does not move him.** The stage is one small graft old. He can make a small reliable graft between living tissue and a limited local branch and he can keep two or three active links; a fourth fails. **He still cannot draw, has no bead, no anchor work, no bridge above a local conduit, no seedheart, no caretaker link and no reading of the deep archive, and the touchroot sense is unchanged and still unreliable.** He **laid a collar on a wetted lot four times in this batch and felt four seconds through the copper each time**, which is a contact with a device and not a graft and is not Stage 3 and may not be counted as a stage. **No number in this batch may be used to move him.**
- **The rootmark is present and unchanged: four inches along the inside of the left forearm, branching twice, permanent, recorded in this holding's book by Coll Renner under his own hand in Chapter 57.** In this batch it was hot before the Ch 73 contact was over and stayed hot, and the hand from the wrist down was no use to him from the second hour of that afternoon. **Nobody in this yard wrote the word *became* and nobody may.**
- **Contacts behind him: the four of Volume 01, unchanged in kind and cost; one at the head of the node in Ch 63 entered as a contact and not a finding and not a fifth contact in the Volume 01 sense; and one in Ch 73, the instrument against the wood of a collar bead, eleven seconds, at a licensed man's hands with a licensed man's clip, cost the mark and a day of the hand, and producing three lines that cannot be checked and cannot be entered.** The four collar readings of a wetted lot are device contacts and are logged in the use log and are not rootwork contacts on the node.
- **No draw and no return by rootlight in this batch**, and the panel's second line is the reason the volume does not need one: *it does not read the ground, and it never will.*

## New locks from the drafted Volume 02 Batch 0003

- **A device that makes provenance self-certifying is a device that makes provenance ownable, and the two are the same mechanism.** The mechanism is stated on the page twice and in three forms: a graft keeps the thing put in and loses the thing that was there, so the device answers the last graft; a lot nobody has chosen reports where it was grown, and a lot anybody has chosen reports who chose it; and the certificate's third line, *keeper of record*, is the one line no device can fill in and is filled in by the seller. **A later chapter may not have a market, a buyer, a printer or a district turn this into a paradox or a moral, and may not have anybody say the word *provocateur* about it.**
- **The dry-land line of the Dryfoot Trust is not lost.** It was cut and dispersed to eleven holdings in the eleventh month two seasons back, one of which is this fen, and it is in no book, and every record that said it was lost is wrong. **This is a change to a standing fact of two volumes and it is recorded here as a proposed canon change and not applied silently.** The seed house of Lantern Reach and the trust's counting house both carried *the dry-land line is still lost* in eleven-year books, and Tova Reed has now entered the correction in both and in a printing and on the road to Cray, and it cannot be withdrawn.
- **Nobody in Tarrow Fen proved where the Marrowfield cutting came from and nobody ever will from a book.** The certificate is true, the lot is the March's dry line, and the only fact in the chain is a shed and a man, and the buyer has not looked at a cutting sheet in twenty-two years because there has never been a column for it. **The shape of the volume's question is on the page and the content is nowhere, and this batch has added a person, a list of eleven names and a shed, and a person and a shed are not a map and a printer and a reason.**
- **A refusal that is entered in a book becomes a document, and this time it is a document other people pay for.** The Marrowfield offer was entered in full in the fen's book and is now a thing a printer may read and a copy may be made of, exactly as the Ashcombe lot's certificate was a thing a buyer's house could act on. **Being readable is a position and not a virtue and no later chapter may convert it into a compliment.**
- **A man may decline to name a buyer in a book this holding keeps, and the holding does not ask again and does not enter the name if it is told one.** Anneke Roos's standing, initialled as an opinion faster than any in a season. **A later chapter may not have anybody go and find out.**
- **The fen has a district that has no form.** A licensed man's private arrangement with a purchaser, a certificate of origin, a market in collars, and a Sunday shift are all outside every instrument in this district, and the district's answer is correct and unhelpful and is entered as such. **No villain may be inserted to fix this and no office may be made to lie, obstruct or act corruptly.**
- **The third of the three conditions in clause three will be described at the first examination held after the twenty-ninth of the month after next, and will be tested on whoever holds the node on that day.** It is not tested before the term ends because no condition is tested twice in the same term and the term ends with the charter. **This is now the single hardest thing in the volume and it is a form, and no later chapter may name it, soften it, or have anybody in Tarrow Fen guess it.**
- **The Charter's own rules are the resource the volume has left, and they are rules, not weapons.** A thing done at night is a thing nobody can check; a name in a book anybody may read is a name anybody may use; a thing only the six of us read is a diary. **Three licensed men and one licensed contractor have now quoted this holding's own rules back at it in its own yard, and a later chapter may not have the rules be wrong.**
- **The printing exists, forty copies, and it cannot be recalled.** It is a two-hundred-page record of eleven years including the largest wrong any of them has entered, and a copy went to Cray, a copy went to Marrowfield, one was sold in the yard, and one went down the fen road to a woman with no house who walked eleven days for it. **The dry-land line's absence is now a printed fact and the fen's own copying of a name off a Crown list is on the front page, and neither of those can be unprinted.**
- **Nothing romantic has happened and nothing may lean that way.** Tova Reed gave a book of two hundred pages out of another body's money, entered the largest wrong of her career against that body's interest, refused a lease on her own record, and asked Marek Vale to be the man who said it out loud in a yard. **That is the whole of it and it is institutional, and no later chapter may make it anything else.**
- **Lissa Vale is not forgiven and is not thanked.** She refused a reading in nine lines and the book has a hole in it because of her, she put her hand up first and would not say which way, she read out the fen's own keeper's confession because she is the reader and the reader reads, and nobody in that yard said a word to her about the ninth tray. **Her refusal of the fourth of a month of Batch 0002 is hers, is not Sera Quill's, is not her own fourth, and is not numbered.**
- **Kellan Rusk is not in this batch and is not mentioned except in the arithmetic of the eighty a day, and the word *became* and the word *redeemed* are both prohibited for him in this volume.** His breach stands disclosed in his own words beside the figure and not below it.
- **Nia is not in this batch.** Not in a room, not in a letter, not by report, and nobody may say she decided not to deliver the letter. **The letter is in the open drawer of the seed-house table, sealed, and it has now been unopened and undiscussed across four batches and about sixty days of season, and no chapter in this batch wrote down why, and that is the standing.**
- **Sera Quill is not in this batch, is not asked about Brinewake, and nobody has asked about her fourth refusal.** It is unnumbered and it may not be numbered. **The volume's first licensed witness has now been Coll Renner, at a load test the district ordered, and it is still not Sera Quill and no chapter may have her simply arrive.**
- **The seal is still a leak, five-eighths, unmoved under a full draw, unmended, undiagnosed, and not a mystery.** Nobody wrote underneath it. **The panel did not diagnose it and the test did not diagnose it and a later chapter may not make either one of them do it.**
- **The beat is logged eleven times and is undiagnosed.** It did not change under a full draw, and that fact is entered and **nothing was written underneath it about what it means.**
- **The bypass is unbuilt and unfunded. Ivo Tarrant's four men do not come back and are not a rescue.** The Thornwild settlement is not named, the long line is not used, quoted or entered, and the word *seat* does not appear anywhere in Chapters 69–76. Marda Vole, Dunmar's *none known*, and the sealed envelope are untouched and none of them may be undone.

## Proposed canon changes recorded, not silently applied — Volume 02 Batch 0003

Batch 0003 added nine things by drafting. All are local detail, mechanisms, forms, prices, places, people or records, and none changes a world rule, a power rule, a relationship lock, or the ending:

1. **The dry-land line is not lost.** Standing across Volume 01 and Volume 02 to date: *the dry-land line is still lost* / *the first row of the March's own line is thinner by fourteen pounds ten* / *the March's tin at risk and the dry-land line is still lost.* The manuscript now says the line was dispersed to eleven holdings in the eleventh month two seasons back, that the eleventh is this fen, and that the statement that it is lost is a wrong entered by Tova Reed in three books, in a printing, and on the road to Cray. **A later writer may not have the line be lost, may not have it come back quietly, and may not have it be paid for or recovered; it exists in eleven unnamed grounds and the fen knows one of them and the other ten are not in any book.** The correction is entered and irreversible.
2. **The seed house's own name came off a crate as well as off a Crown list.** Lissa Vale's four-line answer of the eighteenth of last month — the seed house does not know, has never known, copied its own name off a Crown list in a year it does not name — is **untouched and still true of the fen's ledger.** Tova Reed's ninth line adds that the name was written by her at Cray eleven years ago in a season when an unestablished name would not have been sown. **Both halves stand: the fen copied the name and the trust wrote it, and neither of them knew what it was, and the device now reports the writing hand rather than the ground.**
3. **The certificate of origin** — three printed lines, *ground*, *season*, *keeper of record* — is a new document class in the volume and is a trade form, not a Crown form. It is on a private letterhead, it costs four shillings, and **the volume's discovery is that the device fills two of the three lines and the seller fills the third.**
4. **A lot of one part in eleven is a legal sale and the trade has agreed to call it one**, and Tova Reed's sentence saying so is set on the last page of the printing as a notice and not an opinion. **This is a new trade rule and it is legal by agreement and not by statute, and a later chapter may not make it illegal and may not make a Crown act it.**
5. **The eleventh column of the trust's crop histories is *source* and it has never held anything but a place, and there is no column for cuttings, none for a steward, and none for a line dispersed and not returned.** A whole class of record is missing because no form was printed for it, which is the volume's own argument in a table.
6. **The third of the three conditions in clause three** is now given a test date and a test holder by a district form, and is still not described. This is a new lock and a new forward pull and it is the shape of the volume's resolution, not its content.
7. **The map counter-mark** — a page and a half sent to a district, naming this holding a holder of a line the Crown sheet says has none, making no claim to the Crown's layer — is a new instrument class and a new kind of act, and it is correct, dated, and cannot be withdrawn. **It is the bridge premise and the next volume's question in one sheet.**
8. **Ottoline Fray, of Fray and Daughters at Marrowfield** — about forty-one, four generations, forty-one smallholders, twenty-two years, a collar bought in the spring, a winter list, a buyer in the low dry. **She is not a member of the cooperative and no new named member of the cooperative was created in this batch**: the crew is still Ilsa Kern, Jonas Byre, Anneke Roos, Gael Senn, Lissa Vale and Dunmar Fitch, plus the man of about fifty and the man of about seventy, who are held by function and may not be given names without recording it. **She is not redeemed and not villained, she pays a shilling a copy for the printing, and she is the volume's first customer who wants the record and not the device.**
9. **A letter from a person who gave a name and no house**, eleven households, ground the district says it maintains and does not, eleven days on foot, a shilling a copy to anybody who has one to sell. **A settlement at the dry end has now written to this fen once and nothing about it has been named, and Movement 4 owns it and may name it, and this batch does not.**

None of the nine changes a world rule, a power rule, a relationship lock, or the ending. **The ending is untouched: Chancellor Iona Vey remains the final antagonist, the Rootway is not a mind, and the volume's question — who altered the maps and the seed records enough to make a bridge between this fen and the dry Salt March legal, and who was paid for the alteration — is still unanswered.** This batch has added to it a person, a list of eleven names, a shed at Marrowfield, a certificate that is true, a column that does not exist, and a map mark that was drawn nine years ago by somebody who knew the line was maintained. **None of those is a map, a printer and a reason, and the shape is on the page and the content is nowhere, which is where it was before this batch and is now a great deal more legible and no more answered.**

## Volume 02 Batch 0004 day clock, confirmed against the drafted chapters

Ch 77 days 105–106 (**Sat the fifteenth, Sun the sixteenth**) · Ch 78 days 107–108 (**Mon the seventeenth, Tue the eighteenth**) · Ch 79 days 109–110 (Wed the nineteenth, Thu the twentieth) · Ch 80 days 111–112 (Fri the twenty-first, Sat the twenty-second) · Ch 81 days 113–114 (**Sun the twenty-third, Mon the twenty-fourth**) · Ch 82 days 115–116 (Tue the twenty-fifth, Wed the twenty-sixth) · Ch 83 days 117–118 (Thu the twenty-seventh, Fri the twenty-eighth) · Ch 84 days 119–120 (**Sat the twenty-ninth, Sun the thirtieth**) · Ch 85 days 121–122 (**Mon the first of next month, Tue the second**) · Ch 86 days 123–124 (Wed the third, Thu the fourth) · Ch 87 days 125–126 (Fri the fifth, **Sat the sixth**) · Ch 88 days 127–129 (**Sun the seventh, Mon the eighth, Tue the ninth**).

**One chapter reaches one day past its own range, deliberately, and it is Ch 87.** Its last three paragraphs — the copies going up the fen road, the closing entry read aloud in the yard twice, and the man of about fifty's last sentence in the batch — are all in the past tense about **the seventh (day 127)**, and Ch 88 opens on the same seventh and does not repeat any of them. **Day 127 therefore belongs to the close of Ch 87 and the head of Ch 88, and it must not be counted twice in any reconciliation of the batch.** The entry it describes is the first entry in this holding's book about something a person at the far end of a route was asked to do, and a reader who has read it must not be told it happened again in Ch 88.

**The batch runs days 105–129 with no gap and no overlap. Day 104 was the fourteenth of the month that began on day 91, a Friday, which is Batch 0003's last day. The batch crosses one month boundary: days 105–120 are the fifteenth through the thirtieth of the month that began on day 91, and days 121–129 are the first through the ninth of the next. Every weekday follows from day 61 = the first = a Thursday, locked in Volume 01 Chapter 49.** The three weekday statements a reviewer may check the chain against are **the charter expiring at midnight on a Saturday, day 119, and the district holding its sittings on Saturdays**; **the first of next month being a Monday, day 121**; and **the convoy moving on a Saturday, day 126, because a convoy moves when carts go**.

### The dating rule in this range, and it is the Volume 02 rule with one thing added

Days 105–120 are in the month that began on day 91, which is **two months back from day 121**. Days 121–129 are in the month that began on day 121. Therefore, inside a scene on day 121 or later, **day 119 is *the twenty-ninth of last month* and never *the twenty-ninth***, and day 91 is *the first of last month*. Inside a scene on day 105 to day 120, a bare ordinal is unambiguous and the batch uses it. **No month is named anywhere in Chapters 77–88 and no document in the batch carries one.** Four calendar month names appeared in the first draft and were cut during the drafting pass: *March* (a carter's man's "not in March"), *February* (a clause-two argument), *November* (Tova Reed on the district notice) and *April* (the man of about fifty on the seventh column). **October is four months back by day 105 and is named nowhere, and the volume's own idiom for it, established in Batch 0003, is *two months back*.** One idiom appears twice and is a number and not a name: *the eleventh month two seasons back*, which is how Tova Reed's own cutting-list heading has read all along.

### The dating pass, and the seventeen places it was wrong, and every one of them fixed

**The table above is the chain. The first draft's chapter-level dating was wrong in seventeen places, all of them the same class of error, and all seventeen were found and fixed in a single sweep after the batch was finished. They are recorded here item by item because a later writer needs to know that the class of error is still live in this range and that the batch passed its own audit rather than being born clean.**

**The rule the sweep applied.** There are five months in play: days 1–30, 31–60, 61–90, 91–120 and 121–150. **One warning before the table: every *Now* value in it is read against the scene that says it and not against the rule for day 105.** The Ch 85 and Ch 86 rows are scenes on days 121–124, where days 31–60 are *three* months back and days 91–120 are *last month* — so **Ch 86's *the twelfth* is day 102 and is correctly *the twelfth of last month*, while the same ordinal in a Chapter 77–80 scene would be day 72 and mean something else entirely.** A reader who applies one rule down the whole table will get that row wrong in both directions. **Inside a scene on days 105–120, days 91–120 are *this month*, days 61–90 are *last month*, days 31–60 are *two months back* and days 1–30 are *three months back*. Inside a scene on days 121–129, days 121–150 are *this month*, days 91–120 are *last month*, days 61–90 are *two months back*, days 31–60 are *three months back* and days 1–30 are *four months back*.** Every instance of *of last month*, *of this month* and *of a month two/three/four months back* in Chapters 77–88 was checked against that table and the following were wrong on the page and are now right:

**Two other counts were corrected in the same sweep.** The compost bay's number was described as *the number of days it has stood empty* and is now *the number of days the bay has stood there*, with the note that there has never been a difference, which makes thirty-nine on the fifteenth and fifty-eight on the fourth of next month both true against a bay made on about the sixty-sixth. And **Perrin Osse's *in nineteen days* is now *in a season*,** because there is no nineteenth day in the interval the sentence was sitting in.

**Two distances in the batch are load-bearing and were checked twice each.** The two days of the Wrenlow visit are the twenty-seventh and the twenty-eighth, out and back, with a night at a bothy. And the interval between the return of the fourteenth of last month and the clerk's four points of the ninth is **twenty-five days**, and **this line was wrong twice and is now right**: the first version of this paragraph called the return *a month two months back*, called the interval **ninety-three days**, and pointed a reader at the sentence *four days over four months*. **The prose now says *four days over four weeks* (day 104 to day 129, with the form on day 111 and the schedule on day 115) and the sentence in the chapter agrees with it.** A writer who quotes this paragraph must quote this version and not the earlier one.

**The chain above is now the one on the page, and it was arrived at twice.** The first pass built the table and found it correct; the second pass, on the batch's review, went back to the prose and **found the distances themselves wrong in four places** — a weekday in Ch 77's opening, a carried-over month and two impossible figures in Ch 88, an interval in Ch 85, and a week-figure that meant seven different things across seven chapters. **All four are repaired and the rows above are the repaired values, not the first ones.** The one figure that could have been wrong and was checked twice is the count of the readings of the seventh column, which is a running count across four chapters and reconciles exactly: **ten on the twenty-sixth (Ch 82), sixteen on the second (Ch 85), seventeen on the third (Ch 86) when it was filled.** The days 107–116 are ten; 107–122 are sixteen; 107–123 are seventeen. All three are right.

### The March's tin is *day minus nineteen*, and the rule is unbroken

day 105 = 86 · 119 = **100** · 121 = 102 · 123 = 104 · 125 = 106 · 129 = **110**. The tin is unmoved throughout, on a bed at three and a half degrees, with both undertakings standing — the seed house's that it will not be moved and the trust's that it will not be asked. **The dry-land line is no longer recorded as lost, and a cutting of it is in a tray on this fen four inches high, sown before the sowing closed on the twenty-ninth.**

A later writer must not change these without recording the change. Every figure below is additive. **No figure established in Volume 01 or in Volume 02 Batches 0001, 0002 or 0003 was altered.**

| **The seed-route schedule** | **the first public schedule of a route in this fen, ruled by hand by Dunmar Fitch on the seventeenth on the seed house's own account paper, in Tova Reed's hand, with no number on it and none anywhere, on Anneke Roos's standing that a form with a number is a form somebody can make a class of and a piece of paper with rules on it can be copied by anybody who has seen it.** Title: *Seed-route schedule, from the seed house gate at Lantern Reach to the far end. | **Coll Renner's capacity sentence, and where it is and is not** | **in the fen's book with the hour on it, as his and not as a finding, and NOT on the form, and the not-on-the-form is entered as a downgrade because a licensed man's professional opinion in a book anybody may copy has no form in this district either. He said it at a gate, and a gate is not a document.** *A local conduit takes water from one place to another place. A seed-route bridge takes seed from one keeper to another keeper, and it has two ends and a return, and the return is the part nobody ever wants to pay for.* And: *you do not name a bridge for the distance, you name it for the load, and a man who has written down the miles has not decided what the thing is for* | Ch 77, 78 |
| **A bridge with no return is a road with crates on it** | **Marek Vale's sentence, in the yard at dusk on the twenty-fourth, and Jonas Byre's answer to it: write that down, because I did not say it and you did, and I would rather it was in your mouth than mine** | Ch 81, 86 |
| **The route and its distances** | **eleven miles of fen road, then four bad miles of March road, then the first break, then the low dry, then the second break.** The first break is **a mile short of the low dry and about forty yards long**, peat gone out of the top on both sides, sides slumped, standing water to the depth of a boot, gravel that has had a foot of water stood on it, no stone within a mile and none within three of the low dry. The second break is **a quarter mile past the low dry: running sand with a soft rise at the far end.** **The road holds at the first break and does not hold at the second, and the route therefore ends at the low dry and does not go on to the March road — and that is the first fact about a seed-route bridge anybody in this fen has ever written down** | Ch 81, 87, 88 |
