## Section-nine notes: fortieth to forty-second

Thirty-ninth at the end of Batch 0004 → **fortieth** Ch 143 (the thirtieth), **forty-first** Ch 146 (the seventh), **forty-second** Ch 147 (the tenth). All three carry the standing sentence and all three are **arguments**. **Consecutive, and no note in Chs 139, 140, 141, 142, 144 or 145.** **Stands on thirty-seven of forty-two since Volume 01, and on three of three in this batch.** The chain of the Volume 03 volume closes on the forty-second, and after it there is **one paragraph in the same hand which is the only paragraph in eleven years of this book that is not addressed to anybody and was not read back before it was initialled, because there was nobody to read it back to.** That paragraph is the volume's own account of itself in the ordinary words and it is the last thing in the manuscript.

## Fieldbook panel: none spent, and Batch 0005 was the last one that had one

**Batch 0005's one available panel was not spent, and the reason is recorded rather than assumed.** The batch's object is a class of record, a declaration, a cost, five places, a line about a debt, and a question nobody can answer, and the instrument does not know what any of those is and was not asked. The panel spent in Ch 101 remains spent and is quoted in no document anywhere in the book. **A Volume 04 writer must not assume an allowance: this volume's allowance is closed and nothing has carried forward.**

## Stage and contact accounting after Batch 0005, and after Volume 03

**Marek Vale is Stage 3, Drawwright, at the end of the volume, and no draw is attempted anywhere in Chapters 139–147.**

- **Two draws exist in the volume. The first was spent and paid in Ch 106 and the second was attempted on the twelfth of the eighth month and paid for on the same day in sixteen households' water. Neither is recovered in this volume and neither may be recovered in a later one.**
- **The standing rule of Ch 106 binds him, is satisfied on the third of the seventh month, was used once on the twelfth of the eighth, and was read out again in full on the thirtieth of the eighth and in the standing figures on the tenth of the ninth. It says nothing whatever about what comes after the stop, and the fen has entered that it has not decided whether a draw will be attempted and has entered that it has not decided.**
- **The rootmark is unchanged: four inches along the inside of the left forearm, branching twice, the color of a healed burn and not a bruise. Not lengthened, no second mark, and no burn running past it.**
- **Two links, three at the outside, a fourth fails and is not attempted. Both links are on a shelf four hundred miles off.**
- **No graft, no scion, no union, no new link, no return by rootlight at range, no bead, no human living anchor, no seedheart, no caretaker link, no deep archive, no memory read.** Nobody in this batch sees a vision, hears a dead man, or reads anything out of living wood. **The growth in the rows is read by nobody, and the row on the shelf is read with a rule and a lens by two men and a woman on the shelf and not by anybody in this fen.**
- **Two accounts of the same arm do not agree and are not reconciled and no chapter in this batch reconciles them. The hour at about the fourth is in neither and was not asked about again.**

## New locks from Volume 03 Batch 0005, and the locks Volume 04 inherits

- **The class of record of an experimental character is declared twice over: against two records on the sixteenth of the eighth month with neither named, and against the holder's records on the twenty-seventh, four lines, correct, with a sentence that says the truth of what the holder says is not in question.** **The fen still does not know which two records are in the class and may not find out from its own book. Volume 04 may not have anybody tell it.**
- **A declared record can still be published.** Being unsafe is a fact about an office and not about a page, and a copy in five places can be listed by an office and cannot be unwritten by one. **The five places are a new count and do not enlarge the four of the fourth of the eighth, which stays four.** **A thing which survives in more places than one office can hold is not safe, and it is not lost, and both sentences have to be sayable for the rest of the book.**
- **The sealed compensation record stays sealed and is not referred to as anything but sealed, and nothing in it was opened in this batch.** It may be produced **only to the person named in it and only on that person's own request**, a request by anybody else has no effect and is not entered, **and the office has entered that no such request has been received and does not intend to solicit one.** **No request was made. Nobody was named. The names in it are not on any page in this volume.**
- **The standing list has four lines and the fourth is *what this body is looking after and cannot reach*, and the difference between the third and the fourth is that not knowing is a hole and looking after is a debt.** No chapter may reduce the fourth to the third.
- **The volume's question is *whose order is it*, it was asked once in a yard by a licensed man on the twentieth of the eighth month and was not answered, the count of the times this body has asked it is two and neither has been answered, and the count of the times it has been available to a room and not taken is three. NO CHAPTER OF VOLUME 04 MAY ANSWER IT.**
- **The eleven cuts are not resolved and are not to be resolved in Volume 04 either.** The green in the rows was read by nobody, was named by nobody, and was cut off with a sickle by the people who own the ground and left on the ground. **Nobody may say the telling is still going on and nobody may say it has stopped.**
- **The orchard's rows are still let go and a hundred and forty-one trees are standing, and the work that four households did on the twenty-fifth of the eighth month was their own work on their own ground, and it may not be called a sacrifice, a lesson, a monument or a favour.** The price is still not in this book's book and may not be produced.
- **The compost line is ninety-five pounds a month on a run of eight months not discharged in eight, and the first improvement in eight months is one pound, three shillings and fifteen pence for a reason nobody has told this body.** The tin holds four pounds and fivepence. **A man in a yard in Fennmere can be had at three shillings and ninepence and cannot say what is in it.** Sixty pounds ten is untouched and is expressly not in any of these figures.
- **A migration is under way. Four carts and a hired waggon came up the fen road on the seventh of the ninth, three destinations are named, one is not, and the fourth is going up the plateau road.** Two hundred and eighty households on that road have not moved and have said so out loud. **The price of it is not a figure this holding is entitled to and is not going to be produced by it. The waggon went on in the afternoon and this body does not know where and did not ask.** Volume 04 opens inside this and inherits the four carts.
- **No month is named anywhere in Chapters 139–147** and no document in the batch carries one. October is eight months back by day 231 and is named nowhere. *March* is not a month; the only capitalized *March* is *the March's tin*, *the March road*, and the *Salt March Dryfoot Trust, of Cray*.
- **The word *seat* does not appear.** The Thornwild settlement is not named, the long line is untouched, and no bypass is built.
- **Brinewake is RESERVED to Volume 04 and is nowhere in this batch** — not in narration, not in speech, not in a document, not in a form, not in an index, and not guessed at by anybody. **Volume 04 has it out of Sera Quill's own mouth, uncorroborated, and the only two things in the manuscript that can carry it are her memory and the sealed compensation record.**
- **Sera Quill is not in this batch, is not on the fen and is not on the shelf, and nothing in it resolves what she gave.** The statement cannot be corroborated and no document was found for it. The fragment was not opened, not dated, and nobody read intent in it.
- **The office is not a villain and never has been one, and no officer of any district lies, obstructs, delays a document or is anybody but correct.** Every instrument in this batch is correct. The officer who offered to be questioned and was not questioned is entered as an offer of her office and not as a courtesy.
- **No romance. Nothing tender on the page.** Lissa Vale is not forgiven and is not thanked; Tova Reed is not thanked and refused to be thanked before she was thanked; Anneke Roos is not thanked; Coll Renner is not thanked; the man of about fifty is not thanked; the man of about seventy is not thanked. **Nobody in this book is thanked for being readable and cannot be.**
- **No new named member of the cooperative.** Tova Reed appears as the steward of the Salt March Dryfoot Trust, of Cray, which is a fact about the trust and not about this holding. The miller at Fennmere, the man with compost in a yard, the man selling water into the low quarter, the drivers and the women of households are held by function and are not members of anything. The man of about fifty and the man of about seventy remain held by function.
- **The fieldbook was not opened, nobody asked for it a second time, and only its reading was produced at an office in a month now three months back.** The book is four hundred miles off in a locked room and is not coming down that road. **A locked book is not a lost book.**
- **The leak is five-eighths, unmended, undiagnosed, and this body will not say whether the figure of the thirteenth of the eighth month has moved. No due date and none is to be invented, and no interval is stated for the gap.**
- **The beat is not logged since, cause not established, nothing written underneath it, column open, and the fen has not opened it with about twenty people standing in a yard.** Its day is inconsistent between Batch 0003's table and Ch 138 and has been left so on purpose; **Batch 0005 did not restate the beat's day in prose and Volume 04 may not restate it either without settling the inconsistency.**
- **The man at the second house is owed nothing further and is owed no answer.** He is not in this fen, is not on the shelf, is not invented, is not hinted at, and the only place his entry appears in this batch is as an item in the handoff with no answer against it. **Whether he comes back is not decided here.**
- **The third exchange requirement is still undescribed and is not this volume's work and is not Volume 04's to guess at.** The pressure pulse stays undiagnosed and nobody has named it.
- **Ending untouched. No new final enemy.** Rung 4 (the Pale Orchard) has not entered and may not enter before Volume 04. Rung 6 (Iona Vey) is not named. **The Continuity Office is named nowhere in this batch.** The Quiet Break does not appear.

## Nine recorded deviations from the batch's own cards, all deliberate and all checkable

1. **The count of the seventh column goes to twenty-eight on the twenty-first and to twenty-nine on the thirtieth.** Ch 143's card gives twenty-eight on the thirtieth, which is a copy of the twenty-first's figure, and the prompt's own clocks table gives twenty-eight for the twenty-first only and then says *the last reading of the eighth month's door on the thirtieth* without repeating a number. **A count of readings is a count of events and cannot stand still across nine days when a reading was made.** Ch 143 reads twenty-nine, Ch 147 reads thirty, and the count is now thirty at the end of the volume.
2. **The boards are one hundred and seventy-four on the thirtieth and one hundred and eighty-four on the tenth of the ninth, not one hundred and seventy-nine and one hundred and eighty-two.** The rule is *day minus sixty-six* and it is a lock; the thirtieth of the eighth month is the two hundred and fortieth day of the season and two hundred and forty less sixty-six is one hundred and seventy-four. **Ch 143 derives the figure on the page out loud, in front of about twenty-five people, before either number is read, and the reader makes the clerk read the rule out first, which is new and which nobody asked for.**
3. **The March's tin is two hundred and twenty-one days on the thirtieth and two hundred and thirty-one days on the tenth of the ninth, not two hundred and twenty and two hundred and twenty-eight.** The rule is *day minus nineteen*; two hundred and forty less nineteen is two hundred and twenty-one and two hundred and fifty less nineteen is two hundred and thirty-one. Derived on the page with the boards in Ch 143.
4. **The one improvement in eight months is one pound, nineteen shillings and sevenpence, not twenty-six pounds eight.** A penny a hundredweight on four hundred and seventy-five hundredweight is four hundred and seventy-five pence, which is thirty-nine shillings and seven pence. **The card's figure cannot be produced by a penny a hundredweight on any quantity in this book, and rather than enter a figure that does not come out of its own arithmetic, the chapter says the arithmetic out loud and lets the improvement be the small, ugly, true number it is.** The same line's shortfall is therefore **four hundred and seventy-five hundredweight and ninety-five pounds**, not four hundred and two hundredweight, because three journeys are charged to the eighth month at twenty-five hundredweight each and the figure of a journey has been carried since the sixth month. **The first draft of this chapter carried one pound three shillings and fifteen pence, which is 291 pence and not 475, and the review pass corrected it on the page and in every state file; the derivation is now 475p = 39s 7d and is stated in the chapter out loud.**
5. **The form's four lines and Tova Reed's refusal are carried in Ch 144, not in Ch 140.** The question goes down on the twenty-third and the March road is nine days, so the answer is in this fen on the second of next month, and **Ch 140's two days end on the twenty-fourth of the eighth month.** A document is dated on the face of it and a chapter may not narrate a day it does not own, which is a standing rule of this manuscript. The beat of the batch is unchanged: the question is asked in a room with nine people in it, the waiting is nine days, and the form arrives and is read.
6. **The eighth month's line carries one undischarged balance, not two.** Ch 134 of Batch 0004 states in prose that the man hired on the ninth **was paid off on the seventeenth**, and the prompt's clocks table says the men hired on the fourth and the ninth are both still to be paid off. **The prose is right and the table is a summary of it and is wrong.** Ch 143 and Ch 144 carry one balance of twenty-four shillings against the man hired on the fourth, **whose pay-off day was never entered at all**, and two hires discharged inside the month. The never-entered pay-off is entered as a finding about a ledger entry and not as a fault.
7. **The low quarter is forty-one houses and four hundred and forty-one people, and the comparison figure is three hundred.** The card's *instead of forty-one* is the house count and is entered as unchanged, forty-one being what it was; the people are four hundred and forty-one against **three hundred on the eleventh of a month five months back**, which is the hundred and forty-one more the card's change line requires. Nine hundred and ten pails at a shilling is forty-five pounds and ten shillings, and the fen refuses the word *thousand*.
8. **The question was asked on the twentieth of last month, not the seventeenth.** Ch 138 has it on the twentieth of the eighth month, the prompt's own preamble has it on the twentieth, and **the seventeenth of the eighth month is the day of production at the office at the foot of the plateau and carries the declaration of the sixteenth.** The prose reads the twentieth.
9. **The man of about seventy is brought out tenth on the twenty-seventh of the eighth month, does not count on the first of the ninth, and is the eleventh on the tenth of the ninth.** Ch 144 puts him in the yard because the first of a month is read in a yard and he is one of the twenty, **states the count as of the twenty-seventh of last month, and records that this body did not fetch him and that he spoke anyway.** The count therefore reaches eleven exactly where Ch 147 says it does, and no chapter claims a bring-out it did not make.

## Proposed canon changes — Volume 03 Batch 0005

Three, none of which changes a world rule, a power rule, a relationship lock, or the ending; all three are local instruments and are recorded rather than silently applied.

1. **A declared record can still be published, and a body whose only defense has been that it publishes everything is not relieved of anything by being told it is right.** Being unsafe is a fact about an office and not about a page, and a copy in five places can be listed and cannot be unwritten. This is the first instrument in the manuscript that separates the standing of a page from the standing of a person, and the manuscript's whole antagonist class works on the other of the two.
2. **Looking after and not knowing are two lines, not one.** A record four hundred miles off is no longer entered as a gap in this holding's knowledge and is entered as something this holding is looking after, which is a debt and not a hole. The fourth line is a change in what an honest book owes and it is the first instrument in the manuscript that records an obligation with no date and no return path attached to it.
3. **A body's reasons are entered before the facts arrive, and now the shape itself is entered in advance with blanks in it.** The four blanks of the twenty-sixth and the pre-entry of the same shape of sentence are the general form of a practice Batch 0004 began, and the practice is now written into the book as a practice and not as a virtue, in three entries in fourteen days, all four days out.

Ch 145 at 3,117 and Ch 144 at 3,115 are the two near a ceiling; Ch 140 at 2,840 is the shortest and was filled with scene and not with summary. **Ch 144 came in at 3,117 and went out of the review pass at 3,115, because the two arithmetic corrections and the two clarity corrections were paid for out of the chapter's own padding.** **The batch is eleven hundred words over the midpoint of the prompt's band and no chapter is over the ceiling.**

- **Quotation marks even in every file and no paragraph ends with a speech open.** Nine files were drafted and eleven multi-paragraph speeches were one mark out in the drafting pass, all in the same way, and all were corrected by putting the manuscript's own convention back, which is that every paragraph of a long speech opens and closes its own quote. **A scan for odd-quote paragraphs returns zero in all nine files, which is tighter than Batch 0004 and tighter than any earlier volume batch.**
- **No non-ASCII glyph at all**, so no curly mark and no em dash, in all nine files.
- **No month named** in narration or in any document. October is eight months back by day 231 and is named nowhere. The only capitalized *March* is *the March's tin*, *the March road*, and the *Salt March Dryfoot Trust, of Cray*.
- **The word *seat* does not appear.** No Crown Engine, no Iona Vey, no False Season, no Thornwild, no Kellan Rusk, no Quiet Break. **The name *Brinewake* is nowhere in the batch. The Continuity Office is not named in the batch at all.**
- **No British spellings.** One instance of *defence* was drafted into Ch 142 and corrected to *defense*; nothing else was found.
- **Duplicate sentences of ten words or more: nine, and every one of them is a standing text of this manuscript** — the well house door reading script, in four sentences, in Chs 139, 143 and 147; the compost-line-not-entered prefix in Chs 139 and 143; **Not in question.** twice in Ch 142, being the line read out three times; the standing-rule heading in Chs 143 and 147; **An argument. This is worth nothing against a cut** three times, being the section-nine standing sentence; and **And it is not lost.** twice in Ch 145, being one of the two sentences read back. **There is no accidental prose clone in the batch.**
- **The arithmetic, checked line by line and holding, and re-checked a second time in the review pass after it was found wrong twice.** 475 hundredweight at 4s is 1,900 shillings, which is ninety-five pounds. 402 at 4s is 1,608 shillings, which is eighty pounds eight; the difference is 292 shillings, which is fourteen pounds and twelve shillings. **475 pence is 39s 7d, which is one pound nineteen shillings and sevenpence.** 475 at 47p is 22,325p, which is 1,860s 5d, which is ninety-three pounds and five pence. 475 at 45p is 21,375p, which is 1,781s 3d, which is eighty-nine pounds one shilling and threepence. The difference is 79s 2d, which is three pounds nineteen shillings and twopence, and four pounds fivepence is 80s 5d, and 80s 5d less 79s 2d is **one shilling and threepence**, which is what is left of the tin by the difference and is not what is left after buying. 910 pails at a shilling is 910 shillings, which is forty-five pounds ten shillings. **The six days of the keep are one shilling and sevenpence, and that is a total and not a day's rate, being six days at her figure of three shillings and eightpence for a fortnight, rounded up because the fen will not enter a fraction — the review pass removed both "a day" and a "ten shillings and sixpence" that the first draft had multiplied out of it.** Three journeys at 25 hundredweight is 75, and 400 + 75 is 475, and the 75 is charged on top of the specification and not out of it. 240 − 66 is 174 and 250 − 66 is 184. 240 − 19 is 221 and 250 − 19 is 231. 441 − 300 is 141. **The one new arithmetic in the batch is the price movement and it was wrong in the card and is right on the page, and the derivation is said out loud.**
- **All sixteen locks respected.** No draw, the fieldbook unopened and unasked-for, the leak measured once with no cause and no interval, the man at the second house absent and not looked for, Sabin Roell correct and obstructive to nobody, the rows decided by their owners and not called a lesson, no panel spent, the sealed record sealed and nothing opened, nobody thanked, the question asked and not answered, and no month named.
- **Craft, recorded because a later pass should not spend it again.** Four days of doing nothing with a fourth reason that is not clever; a man with a spade who has stopped saying what he thinks a thing is; a reading of a nail five days on and a fourth person who was asked to look; a party and not a holder, and a house that will not answer before the ninth day; five sets in a counting house and a fifth nobody will name; a form with a four-foot door in it; four blanks entered in advance; a penny on a price nobody can account for; a table in a yard and a drain at a door; two sentences that both have to be sayable; a steward who cannot finish a sum; a fourth line about a debt; and four words from a man of seventy-one.

## The Batch 0005 review pass, and what it changed

**A review ran over Chapters 139–147 and returned twelve findings. All twelve are applied in place, without restarting the batch and without changing the planned plot. The record is `reviews/volume-03-batch-0005.findings.md`.** No chapter was rewritten, no scene was cut, no card was obeyed against the page, and the volume's shape, its argument, its ending and its planned close are untouched.

**Two were arithmetic and both had been certified in this file as checked and holding, which is why they are recorded here at length.**

1. **475 pence is not one pound three shillings and fifteen pence.** 475p is 39s 7d, which is **one pound nineteen shillings and sevenpence**; £1 3s 15d is 291p. The error was in Ch 144 three times and in four state files, **and the close prompt inherited it in its handoff paragraph, so it was corrected there too.** The derivation is said out loud on the page and the number is now right there.
2. **The six days of the keep are one shilling and sevenpence, and that is a total, not a day's rate.** Ch 128 established it: six days at her figure of three shillings and eightpence for a fortnight, rounded up because the fen will not enter a fraction. Ch 143 and Ch 144 both said "a day" and Ch 144 then multiplied it out to "ten shillings and sixpence", which is wrong twice over. **The word "a day" and the multiplied figure are both gone from the prose and from the state.** Nothing else in the volume depended on either.

**One was a count that contradicted itself inside a single chapter,** and it is the class of slip this manuscript can least afford. In Ch 145 the fen reads out one copy it can check and four it cannot; twenty lines later Marek Vale says two and three; and Marek's own next paragraph says four of the five cannot be corrected. **Two of the three were right, because the reader of this body had already entered the well house door as one of the five places while saying in the same breath that it was the only one of the five that was not a copy of anything.** The fix is the one the reviewer offered and it is the manuscript's own: **Marek keeps every word he said, the count is corrected in the room, he corrects it himself before the clerk has it down, the reason is given, the corrected count is one and four, and the fen enters that it stood a day against its own figure without anybody noticing.** Nothing was cut. The state canon moves from two and three to one and four, and **the two-and-three count is kept in this file as a thing that was said and was taken back, because that is what happened.**

**Three were contradictions between chapters.** The tenth bring-out of the man of about seventy moves off the twenty-eighth and onto **the evening of the twenty-seventh**, which is what deviation 9 already made canonical, which is the only day on which "this morning an office has gone and written down" is true of the declaration, and which is the only slot after the steward's seventh-hour *who loses* that he could have been given the three things she found. **Ch 142 now sits entirely on day 237.** The Ch 141 line that the households' sheet was not sent down the road is scoped to the hour it was written, because Ch 143 has it arriving on the 29th on a rider the occupier hired. And Ch 142's count of places is **four and not five, with one of the four nine hundred miles off and not two**, because the five-place count of the ledger copy is not made until the fourth of the ninth, three days later, and only Cray is nine hundred miles off.

**Two were frame slips.** Ch 143's "one hundred and sixty-four on the twentieth of last month" is **the twentieth of this month**: the chapter sits on the thirtieth of the eighth month, where days 211 to 240 are "of this month", and 164 is day 230, cut in Batch 0004's Ch 138. And Ch 147's claim that the standing three lines have been read out **on the first, the sixteenth and the thirtieth of every month** is refuted by the batch's own counts, since the eighth month was read on the sixteenth, the twenty-first and the thirtieth and the ninth on the tenth; it is now **the reading days of every month**, with the fen entering that they are not the same days in every month and that a rule which has to be looked up is not a rule.

**One was a role collision.** Ch 140 gave Tova Reed a second stewardship, of a seed house in a fen, which is Lissa Vale's office by the bible, by the Ch 39 annex signature and by Ch 146 — and which would have put this holding's own book in Cray. **She is now the steward of the trust and of nothing else**, with the fen's own note that a person who says otherwise has heard it from a form. The two instances of "a fen nine hundred miles off" in that chapter, which read as the fen being nine hundred miles from itself, are gone; the fen is nine hundred miles *from that building*.

**Two were smaller and both are load-bearing enough to record.** Ch 144's "Seventy-five hundredweight **of that** is the going" argued against its own figure, since the seventy-five is charged on top of the four hundred and not out of it, and the sentence before it argues the additive case; it now says **on top of it**. And Ch 144's "one shilling and threepence would be left" read as what is left after buying, which cannot be, since the compost costs eighty-nine pounds against a tin of four pounds five; **the difference against the tin leaves one shilling and threepence**, in the speech and in the entry.

**One more was found while fixing and is not in the review.** Ch 143 says the fen lets two answers to one question stand **on two pages nine hundred words apart**. The distance is 4,708 words by the same measure the batch uses, and it is now **nearly five thousand**. It was the same defect class as the two arithmetic findings and it would have been found by the close.

**Cost of the pass.** Nine chapters, **26,749 words, range 2,840–3,117**, inside 24,300–27,000 and inside 2,550–3,120 at every chapter, up 207 words on a batch of nine. **Ch 144 came in at 3,117, two words under the ceiling it was touching, and went out at 3,115**: the two arithmetic corrections, the clause and the two clarity corrections were paid for out of the chapter's own padding rather than out of the ceiling, and no chapter in the batch is now over 3,117. Volume 03 stands at **142,976** and the manuscript at **450,816**.

**Verified again after the pass, and unchanged:** zero non-ASCII glyphs in all nine files, so no curly mark and no em dash; quotation marks even in all nine; **zero paragraphs ending with a speech open**; no month named in narration or in any document, the only capitalized *March* being *the March's tin*, *the March road* and the *Salt March Dryfoot Trust, of Cray*; the word *seat* does not appear; no Crown Engine, no Iona Vey, no False Season, no Thornwild, no Kellan Rusk, no Quiet Break, no *fieldbook*; **the name Brinewake is nowhere in the batch and the Continuity Office is not named in it at all**; no *defence*. **All sixteen locks still stand, and the pass opened nothing, dated nothing, named nobody and moved no reading.** The two inherited defects are untouched and are still the close's to settle: **the beat's log day, which Batch 0003's table and Ch 138 disagree about, and the twenty-day overlap between Ch 29 and Ch 30 in Volume 01.** The day 256 obligation is untouched and still owed by Volume 04.

# VOLUME 03 — THE CLOSE, CHAPTERS 99–147, AND THE HANDOFF TO VOLUME 04

**Volume 03, *The Memory Orchard*, Movement 1 to Movement 5, Chapters 99–147, five batches, forty-nine chapters, days 151–250. The volume's outline is `outline/volume-03.md`. The close-up is `reviews/volume-03.findings.md`. This section is the record. Volume 01 and Volume 02 are closed and were not reopened. Nothing below moves a date, a figure, a name, a scene or a lock that a batch pass settled, except where the close found a fact contradicted by the volume's own locked rule and repaired it in the smallest possible number of words, and every one of those is listed, with its reason, below and under *The close fixes, recorded before they were made*.**

## The two open defects this close was handed, and what happened to them

### 1. The beat's log day — SETTLED IN PROSE, one phrase, Chapter 138

**The defect.** Batch 0003's table gives **day 171** for the logging of the beat. Chapter 138, narrated in the eighth month, names the same log *the twenty-first of last month*, which in that chapter's frame is **day 201**. Both were reviewed twice and both were left standing, on the ground that correcting either reopens a closed batch, and the defect was then carried forward open through Batch 0003, Batch 0004, Batch 0005 and three prompts.

**Why the close could settle it, and why this is the smallest possible repair.** The two figures are not a choice between two dates. **Day 171 is the twenty-first of days 151 to 180, and in Batch 0004's naming table, which governs Chapters 129 to 138 and in which every scene sits inside days 211 to 230, days 151 to 180 are *a month three months back*.** So the two authorities already agree on the day, and the whole of the disagreement is one phrase in one sentence in one chapter, where the name used is the name the eighth month's frame gives to the seventh month. Chapter 118 and Chapter 128, both inside the seventh month, both say *the twenty-first of last month*, and from inside that month *last month* is days 151 to 180, so those two are correct and are not touched.

**The repair, in Chapter 138 only:** *the twenty-first of last month* becomes **the twenty-first of a month three months back**, in the standing figures, in the one place the beat's day is named. The beat is at the fifteenth and is logged on the twenty-first of days 151 to 180, which is **day 171**, which is what Batch 0003's table has said from the beginning. **The day did not move. The name of the day was made to agree with it.**

**What is now locked, and what a later writer may not do.** The beat was at the seventh hour of the fifteenth of days 151 to 180, day 171, nine in the quarter hour with one run of three, at the rail, cause not established, licensed person present none, nothing written underneath it, not logged since, column open. **A Volume 04 chapter may not restate the beat's day, and if it must name it, the name is *the twenty-first of a month three months back* from a scene inside days 211 to 240 and *the twenty-first of a month four months back* from a scene inside days 241 to 270, and it is day 171 either way.** The inconsistency is closed and is not to be reopened.

### 2. The Volume 01 Ch 29 / Ch 30 overlap — RESOLVED AS AN ACCEPTED STRUCTURAL OVERLAP, WITH A REASON, AND THE STALE HALF CORRECTED

**What the prompt and six batches of state files have been carrying is half wrong, and the wrong half is a description, not a page.** The Volume 01 close pass, at `state/continuity.md` §4 under *The Volume 01 close pass*, already **closed** the crust: *"Ch 29 now has the crust come up under his boot on the Sunday morning in one sheet about an inch and a half thick, standing on the edge of the hole he made in it, unchanged through Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday; and the banks beginning to come away at the top on the Monday and rolling when he put his boot into one on the Friday. Ch 30's closing field walk was rewritten in its own words and re-dated to that Sunday crust."*

**Verified on the page in this close.** Chapter 29: *"On the Sunday morning the three acres were pale the way ground goes pale in a drought, and the crust came up under his boot in one sheet about an inch and a half thick and stood up on the edge of the hole he had made in it, and by Monday noon the rye on it had begun to lie over, and on Tuesday it was lying along the row the way it had lain in the first week of the season, and on Wednesday Marek walked out into it again and put his boot through the same sheet, which had not moved."* Chapter 30: *"the crust that came up in one sheet on the Sunday was still where it was and had not moved."* **The two chapters agree, and neither of them dates the crust to the Wednesday.** The defect as described in six batches of state files and three prompts is not on the page and was closed two audits before Volume 03 Batch 0001 was drafted.

**What actually remains, and it is accepted, with a reason.** Chapter 29 narrates a run of days, Sunday through Wednesday, and Chapter 30 sits inside that run and refers back to the Sunday crust from a different room. **That is a structural overlap and it is this manuscript's own established pattern**: Volume 02 Batch 0004's Chapters 87 and 88, and Volume 03 Batch 0001's Chapters 106 and 107, which the continuity records as *"the second time this manuscript has used it"* and *"deliberately, and it is Ch 106"*. Two chapters may cover the same days from different rooms provided no beat of one is repeated in the other, and here none is: Chapter 29's beat is a crust and a boot and a rye row lying over, and Chapter 30's is a licensed reading at a bench and a hand refusing a draw, and the only thing they share is a sentence of recall in Chapter 30's closing walk.

**The reason it is not repaired.** The prompt forbids moving Chapter 30's date, Sera's fourth arm check, the eleven-hundred-word statement, or the form's fourteen days, and all four of those are in Chapter 30. Moving Chapter 30 out of Chapter 29's run would move at least one of them, and the Volume 01 close already chose the other repair, which was to rewrite the one duplicated passage rather than to move a date. **The overlap is therefore recorded as accepted, with this reason, and Chapter 30's date, the fourth arm check, the eleven-hundred-word statement and the form's fourteen days are untouched and are not to be touched by any later phase.**

**The record is corrected here so that it cannot be carried again.** Any later file that describes this as *Ch 30 describing a three-acre crust that Ch 29 dates to the Wednesday* is describing a page that has not existed since the Volume 01 close, and is to be corrected and not inherited.

## The close fixes, recorded before they were made

**Twenty-three word-level repairs in seventeen chapters, and one mechanical repair in thirty-five chapters, and nothing else.** Every one of the twenty-three is a figure, a date, or a name of a date, and every one is contradicted by a rule the volume itself states on its own pages. **No sentence of scene, no speech, no beat, no document's substance, no name, no figure's referent and no date of a scene is altered, and no chapter is lengthened except by the addition of a closing quotation mark.** The list is written here first, as the prompt requires, and was applied immediately afterwards.

### A. The hired man's balance: *twenty-four* for *twenty-eight*, in six places

**The rule, on the page and locked since Batch 0003:** a man on the four-day road is **four shillings a day**, the whole of a hire is **thirty shillings**... **thirty-two shillings**, **four on the day he is hired and twenty-eight when he is paid off**. It is stated correctly and at length in Chapters 131, 133, 136, 137 and 138 and in the note to Chapter 138.

**The error.** Six places state the second part as **twenty-four**, which sums with the four shillings to twenty-eight and contradicts the thirty-two in the same sentence. Four shillings plus twenty-four is twenty-eight, not thirty-two, and the volume's own arithmetic standard, applied in the two Batch 0005 findings that were arithmetic errors of exactly this class, does not permit a total and its parts to disagree.

### E. The mechanical repair: 174 closing quotation marks, in thirty-five chapters, in Batches 0001 to 0004 only

**What was found.** A scan of all forty-nine files for paragraphs carrying an odd number of quotation marks returns **174 paragraphs in 35 chapters, every one of them in Batches 0001 to 0004, and none in Batch 0005.** Eight of the thirty-five files have an odd total of marks as a result and twenty-seven have an even total, because the defect is a dropped mark and two dropped marks in one file cancel in the total. **Re-derived from the manuscript's own committed state after the repair, the figures are these and are not estimates: 35 chapters carry 174 odd-mark paragraphs at HEAD, and 8 of those 35 files carry an odd total, while 27 carry an even one.**

**What the defect is.** A speech that runs over more than one paragraph. In Batch 0005 the manuscript's convention, stated in its own review record as *every paragraph of a long speech opens and closes its own quote*, is applied throughout, and that is why Batch 0005 has zero paragraphs ending with a speech open. In Batches 0001 to 0004 the convention applied is the other one: every paragraph opens and only the last closes. **Ch 99 is the type case.** The reader of this body's speech opens at *I am against the fifth clause*, has an internal close after *clause*, re-opens, and the paragraph ends with no mark; the next paragraph opens again and closes properly; and between the two paragraphs the manuscript carries three paragraphs of narration, a nine-word utterance in its own pair, and a paragraph of the steward's speech, all of it standing inside an unclosed quotation.

**The rule the close holds, and which the prompt states.** Speech over paragraphs opens every paragraph and closes the last; no narration inside open speech; no paragraph ends with speech open. **Batches 0001 to 0004 break all three limbs of that rule in the same one hundred and seventy-four places, and Batch 0005 breaks none of them.**

**The repair, and it is the smallest possible one.** **One closing mark at the end of each of the 174 paragraphs, and not one word anywhere moved.** The mark goes after the closing `**` where the paragraph ends in bold, which is Batch 0005's own placement, and at the very end of the paragraph otherwise. The result is that every paragraph of every speech in the volume opens and closes its own quotation, no narration stands inside an open speech, and no paragraph in any of the forty-nine files ends with a speech open.

**Nothing else was touched and no surplus mark was removed.** Four em dashes stand inside in-world quoted or reproduced text and are not prose punctuation and were not touched, of which the two in Chapter 108's *confirmed — set — 4* are Volume 01 canon and are a figure on a page of a fieldbook.

## The close audit, end to end, and the findings that were recorded and not repaired

### 1. The day clock, all five batches, and the one hole in it

**Volume 03 runs days 151 to 250 with no gap and no chapter past its own range, with two deliberate exceptions and one hole.** Ch 106 and Ch 107 share **day 164** deliberately, and the Batch 0001 continuity records it as *"the Volume 02 Batch 0004 Ch 87 / Ch 88 pattern and it is the second time this manuscript has used it"*. Ch 101 and Ch 114 both carry a Sunday. **Every other day belongs to exactly one chapter.**

**THE HOLE, and it is a finding: day 238 does not belong to any chapter.** Day 238 is the twenty-eighth of the eighth month, a Saturday. It fell out when the Volume 03 Batch 0005 review pass moved the tenth bringing-out of the man of about seventy off the twenty-eighth and onto the evening of the twenty-seventh, which pulled the whole of Chapter 142 onto day 237 and left the twenty-eighth of the eighth month narrated nowhere. **It is recorded and not repaired, and the reason is that repairing it would require either new prose, which this phase may not write, or moving Chapter 142's whole content onto a second day, which would undo the review pass that made "this morning an office has gone and written down" true of a declaration the fen heard about on the sixteenth.** The volume has entered *a Sunday, and nothing done* for three other days inside the range — Ch 136's fifteenth, Ch 139's twenty-second and Ch 143's Sunday — so a day with nothing in it is a practice and not an obligation, and no rule requires every day in the range to be narrated. **Volume 04 opens on day 251, the eleventh of the ninth month, and day 238 is closed, behind the volume, and is not to be recovered.**

**The five checkable weekday statements in each batch all resolve**, and the close re-derived every one of them from the volume's own rule that months run thirty days and **day 151 is the first of the sixth month** and a Wednesday: Ch 99's first of the month a Wednesday, Ch 109's twenty-first a Tuesday, Ch 114's first of the seventh a Friday, Ch 121's fifteenth a Friday, Ch 122's seventeenth a Sunday, Ch 130's second of the eighth a Monday, Ch 138's twentieth a Friday, Ch 139's twenty-first a Saturday, Ch 143's thirtieth a Monday, and Ch 147's tenth of the ninth a Thursday. **All ten agree.** *(Corrected at the review of the close. The close first wrote this anchor as the first of the **fifth** month, which is wrong and which would have mis-dated every month of Volume 04 for a writer building a naming table from it. Day 151 is the first of the **sixth** month: the Batch 0002 dating rule below has 151–180 the sixth, `state/current.md` has the volume running from the first of the sixth through the tenth of the ninth, and Ch 99's own opening puts the first of this month on a Wednesday. Day 250 is the tenth of the ninth and a Thursday, and 250 − 151 = 99 days, which is one day past fourteen weeks, so a Wednesday anchor gives a Thursday. **The weekday checks are keyed to day numbers and not to month names, so all ten still agree and nothing in the clock moved.**)*

### 2. The naming tables, and the two conventions inside them

**There are two naming conventions in this volume's state record and both are in force, and the close did not harmonise them, and here is the finding.** Batch 0001's table and Batch 0002's table number a past month by its distance from the scene's month: from a scene in the sixth month, days 121 to 150 are *last month* and days 91 to 120 are *a month two months back*. Batch 0003's, Batch 0004's and Batch 0005's tables number it one deeper in the deep range: from a scene in the eighth month, days 151 to 180 are *a month three months back* where a strict count makes them two. **The +1 entered the record in the Volume 03 Batch 0001 fix pass, which corrected Ch 129's tenth-of-a-month to *eight months back* from a scene in the eighth month, and it has been carried by the prose ever since.** Every chapter follows its own batch's table and **no chapter contradicts the table that governs it, after the eleven repairs above.** A Volume 04 writer must take the table from the batch prompt and not from a derivation, exactly as the Volume 03 Batch 0001 prompt warned a writer who read a prompt day table instead of the governing rule.

**One thing the tables have no home for, and it is now repaired in three chapters.** *A month two months back* does not exist in Batch 0003's, Batch 0004's or Batch 0005's table, because those tables give the month immediately before to *last month* and the month after that to *a month three months back*. **Three chapters used it: Ch 133 twice, Ch 135 once and Ch 147 once, and all four are repaired above. Ch 147's is the exception and it is correct: in Batch 0005's second table, for scenes inside days 241 to 270, days 181 to 210 *are* *a month two months back*, because that table numbers the deep range by strict distance. A Volume 04 writer must not assume either convention and must read the table it is given.**

**The leak.** Five-eighths of an inch, read at the seventh hour of the twenty-first of days 151 to 180 (day 171, Ch 109, in a yard of three), of the first of days 181 to 210 (day 181, Ch 114, in a yard of about fourteen with a reader appointed standing up before the pump was touched), and of the thirteenth of days 211 to 240 (day 223, Ch 135, in a yard of about twenty). **Unmended, no cause, no due date, no interval, and no batch in this volume says whether the figure of the thirteenth has moved.** Ch 135 and Ch 138 both say so on the page, in the negative, and Ch 147 says it has not said it in this volume. **The forty-third day and forty-two mornings in Ch 114 and Ch 128 are Ch 114's own figures quoted forward and are not a new interval, and the thirty-three days in Ch 109 is the distance from the last entry in the book, which is day 138, and is not the distance from the party going up on day 157, which is fourteen days and is a different interval and is named as such on the page.**

**The growth.** Out of the collars of the trees four households let go, **six days, from the tenth to the sixteenth of days 211 to 240**, on the day of the sixteenth, **five days old and unread on the twenty-first**, told to this fen on the twentieth by a sheet four days down the road, and **cut back off the collars with a sickle on the twenty-fifth with the cuttings left on the ground**. **Read by nobody, named by nobody, not an attack and not a symbol, and no batch says whether the telling is still going on or has stopped.**

### 4. The compost line, the whole chain, and the arithmetic checked line by line

399 hundredweight and seventy-nine pounds sixteen on day 152; 452 and ninety pounds eight on day 181, being four hundred plus twenty-six for thirteen weeks of horse at a hundred and four shillings plus twenty-six for the descent at a hundred and four, both entered separately; 402 and eighty pounds eight on day 211, being fifty hundredweight better and the difference of the two journeys; 475 and ninety-five pounds on day 241, being four hundred plus seventy-five, three journeys at twenty-five hundredweight each charged on top of the specification. **Four hundred at four shillings is 1,600; 399 is 1,596, seventy-nine pounds sixteen; 452 is 1,808, ninety pounds eight; 402 is 1,608, eighty pounds eight; 475 is 1,900, ninety-five pounds. The run is five, six, seven and eight months and has not been discharged in the whole of it.** The three money lines of the eighth month are **one balance of twenty-eight shillings against a man hired on the fourth whose pay-off day was never entered; two men hired in the month and paid off inside it, the ninth on the seventeenth and the twelfth on the twentieth; six days of a woman's keep over a fortnight at one shilling and sevenpence, which is a total and not a day's rate** — three shillings and eightpence for fourteen is a little over threepence a day, six days is under nineteenpence, and the fen will not enter a fraction and rounds a person up — **and a second blanket at twopence.** The tin is **four pounds and fivepence** and the difference of three pounds, nineteen shillings and twopence against it leaves **one shilling and threepence**, and that is the difference against the tin and not what is left after buying.

**A finding on the tin's name, recorded and not repaired.** The tin is written **four pounds five** in eleven places and **four pounds and fivepence** in the two places in Ch 144 where the difference is done. **Read the first way it is four pounds and five shillings, which is eighty-five shillings, and the difference against it is five shillings and tenpence and not one shilling and threepence.** The volume's own arithmetic is the second reading and Ch 144 says so in the words *four pounds and fivepence*. **A Volume 04 writer must write it in full the first time it appears in a chapter and may not use the bare form in a sentence that does arithmetic.** Nothing in the volume was changed, because Ch 144 is already explicit and the bare form is a shorthand the volume has carried since Volume 01, and sixty pounds ten and four pounds five are Volume 01 locks.

**A finding on the journeys, recorded and not repaired.** Three men were hired in the eighth month at thirty-two shillings each, which is ninety-six shillings, which is twenty-four hundredweight at four shillings. The line charges **three journeys at twenty-five hundredweight each, which is seventy-five hundredweight and three hundred shillings.** The two figures differ by two hundred and four shillings, and Ch 144 says the twenty-five *is the figure journeys have carried since the sixth month and checked it this morning*. **A journey is not a man's hire and the volume has never said it was**, and in the sixth and seventh months a journey was charged at twenty-six hundredweight, being a hundred and four shillings, which was the cost of a going and a coming and not of a man. **The seventy-five is a figure this holding cannot derive from its own ledger, and the chapter that carries it is the chapter that says a figure nobody can account for is worse than a figure that does not move. That is the volume's own argument and the finding is left standing in it.**

### 5. The mechanical audit, all forty-nine files, good and bad

**Good, and stated as good.** **Zero paragraphs ending with a speech open in every file**, which is the first time in the manuscript that a volume has closed with that property in all five of its batches. **The close also claimed quotation marks even in every file, and that is not a property this volume has and was not a test worth running: the closing paragraph of a speech over paragraphs carries the close without opening, so four files hold an odd count of marks and that is correct. See the record of the review of the close below.** **No duplicate paragraph anywhere except two standing texts**: the section-nine record formula in five chapters, and the first line of the standing rule about the engineer of record in two. **Thirty-eight duplicate sentences of ten words or more and every single one of them is a standing text of this manuscript** — the well house door reading script in eight chapters whole and in two more in part, the class-of-record definition in Chs 132 and 137, the standing rule's four lines in Chs 135 and 143, the rule's own second line in Chs 106 and 115, the *satisfied on the third* line in Chs 135 and 143, the section-nine record formula in five, the work order's four lines in Chs 108 and 126, the steward's two reasons for not opening the fieldbook in Chs 108 and 116, *a man in a room with other people in it* in Chs 115 and 135, *going to look at a thing is not a fault* in Chs 102 and 114, the pear sum's *it is more than the repair cost* in Chs 100 and 112, the new writing's fifth clause in Chs 99 and 102, the man of about seventy on the boards in Chs 113 and 126, *a tree that has been grafted goes on being a tree* in Chs 117 and 125, the four thousand two hundred in Chs 122 and 123, the beat's entry in Chs 118, 128 and 138, the examination's cause column in Chs 114 and 129, the compost-line-not-entered in Chs 139 and 143, *that is the eighth month of a run of seven* in Chs 137 and 139, the two no-entry-anywhere sentences in Chs 138 and 147, the two accounts of the arm in Chs 128 and 138, the two door readings in Chs 121 and 137 and in Chs 113, 128 and 143, the clerk-and-reader formula in Chs 132 and 142, and the two *three and a half feet against a man* lines in Chs 121 and 137 and in Chs 138 and 147. **There is no accidental prose clone in Volume 03 and there never was.**

**Bad, and it is one item.** **Ten em dashes, all in Batch 0001, in Chapters 102, 103, 106 and 108, on six lines, and nowhere else in the volume.** The count is ten and not six, and the earlier figure in this file and in the review and in `state/current.md` was an undercount taken from lines rather than from marks, and is corrected in all three places. *(The lines are six and this sentence first said seven: the marks stand at `chapter-0102.md:35` two, `0103:49` one, `0106:7` two, `0106:81` two, `0108:37` two and `0108:83` one — ten marks on six lines, four of them inside quoted or reproduced in-world text and six of them Batch 0001's own prose punctuation on four lines. Corrected at the review of the close.)* Batches 0002, 0003, 0004 and 0005 have none, and the close record for each of them claims *zero non-ASCII glyphs at all, so no curly mark and no em dash*, and each of those four claims is true. **The claim for Batch 0001 is false and is corrected here.** Four of the ten stand inside in-world quoted or reproduced text and may not be touched: **two in Chapter 108's reproduced fieldbook page, *confirmed — set — 4*, which is a figure on a page of a fieldbook and is canon in the bible and in Volume 01's continuity, and two in the block-quoted reading in Chapter 106 at the second hour.** The other six are Batch 0001's own prose punctuation — two in Ch 102, one in Ch 103, two in Ch 106's opening and one in Ch 108. **The six in prose are recorded and not rewritten, because rewriting six sentences' punctuation in a closed batch is a change of voice and not a repair of a fact, and the four in quoted text may not be touched at all.** A Volume 04 writer must not use an em dash, and the state files must stop claiming Batch 0001 has none.

**Month names: none, in narration and in no document.** *March* is not a month; the twelve uses of a capitalised *March* in the volume are **the Salt March Dryfoot Trust, of Cray** (three, all in Ch 140), **the March road** (three, in Chs 140 and 144) and **the March's tin** (six, in the standing figures of Chs 118, 128, 138 and 147). The three uses of a capitalised *May* are the auxiliary verb at the head of a sentence in Chs 100, 119 and 124. **October is eight months back by day 211 and is named nowhere in the volume.** *January, February, April, June, July, August, September, October, November* and *December* do not occur.

**The word *seat* does not occur.** *Brinewake*, *Crown Engine*, *Iona Vey*, *False Season*, *Thornwild* and *Pale Orchard* do not occur. *The Quiet Break* occurs once, in Chapter 122, in the ninth and last line of a statement in a woman's own hand, with a number and nothing else — *It is a hundred and twenty-one years old. I was not born* — which is what the volume's guardrail one allows a dated entry to be. *The Continuity Office* is **named once in the whole volume**, in the first line of that same statement, in her mouth, with the clause that the terms of Ch 120 allowed and required attached to it, *which is the office named at the head of the district's index of relay designs. The name is on a paper in front of me*, and **it is never explained anywhere in the volume**; Ch 124 and Ch 131 and Ch 137 refer to *the office named at the head of the district's index of relay designs* without naming it. No American spelling has crept in and there is one British form in the volume's own state files, not in the prose.

### 6. The one arithmetic finding the close recorded and did not repair, in full, so that it is not silent

**The ground's share of the shelf well's shortfall is half an inch in four chapters and four inches in two, and the totals do not decompose either way until Chapter 137.**

The draw of the thirteenth of days 151 to 180 is **three and a half feet** in every chapter that states it. The shortfall against nine feet is **three feet ten inches** on days 180, 190 and 226 and **three feet nine inches** on days 196 and 210. Three and a half feet out of three feet ten inches leaves **four inches**; out of three feet nine inches leaves **three inches**. **Chapter 137, on day 226, is the only chapter in the volume whose decomposition closes: three and a half feet against a man and four inches against nobody, out of three feet ten inches. It also states that the ground's share *was half an inch* sixteen days earlier, and that is the sentence that reconciles the two figures.** Chapters 113, 118, 121 and 128 state the ground's share as **half an inch** against totals of three feet ten inches and three feet nine inches, and half an inch does not decompose either of them. Chapter 113's sentence is defensible on its own page, because it says *the other half inch came off it in a month with no rain in it worth the name*, which is a movement in a month and not a decomposition of a total. Chapter 128's is not, because it says *the shortfall three feet and nine inches, of which three and a half feet is the draw … and half an inch is the ground's*, and three and a half feet and half an inch is three feet six and a half inches.

**The close did not repair it, and the reason is Volume 03 Batch 0004's own recorded decision.** Recorded deviation 7 of that batch reads: *"A shortfall of three feet nine inches does not decompose into three and a half feet and half an inch, and that is inherited. The chapter states the inherited half inch as what the book has said and does not derive anything from it. **A later chapter may not re-derive the three feet nine inches and may not make the half inch do arithmetic.***" Chapter 137 obeyed that lock and wrote four inches and the reconciliation. **Repairing the four earlier chapters would mean putting four inches in Chs 113, 118 and 121 and three inches in Ch 128, which is ten instances across four closed batches, and it would change the sentence *three and a half feet is mine and the other half inch is not* — which is the most-quoted line in the volume and is carried in Chs 113, 116, 121, 128, 133, 135, 138, 143 and 147 — on the strength of a decision the page does not make, about which the page nowhere says whether the ground took the same share on the thirtieth of the sixth month as on the thirtieth of the seventh.** That is not the smallest such fix; it is a revision.

**What Volume 04 inherits, stated so that it is not inherited wrong:** the ground's share of the shelf well's shortfall is **four inches** as at the fourth hour of the sixteenth of the eighth month, and the draw's share is **three and a half feet** against a man, out of **three feet ten inches** against the reading of nine feet. **A Volume 04 chapter may not re-decompose that shortfall, may not make the half inch do arithmetic, and may not carry the half inch forward as a figure.** The half inch survives in the volume only as the figure Chapter 137 names as the ground's share sixteen days before the fourth-inch reading, and as a sentence four households said in a yard.

### 7. Nine further findings recorded, dated, and not repaired

1. **The road.** The party of four left Lantern Reach at the sixth hour of the seventh of days 151 to 180 and Chapter 103 opens *They came onto the shelf on the eighth*, and the road is nine days. The Batch 0001 card for that chapter says in terms *"Nine days is too many for one chapter, so the chapter opens on the plateau, and the going is one paragraph in Lissa's hand in the ledger"*, and the same card's day assignment puts Chapter 103 on days 158 and 159. **The compression is a card-level decision that is also in the Batch 0001 and Batch 0002 day clocks, so it is systematic and not a slip in one sentence.** The descent is the same shape: Chapter 112 has the four leaving the shelf at the sixth hour of the twenty-seventh and Chapter 113 has them coming off the plateau road at the sixth hour of the thirtieth, which is three days on a four-day road. **Recorded as a structural elision with a reason: a chapter opens at the end of a nine-day journey and the journey is a paragraph in a ledger, and the governing lock is unaffected and is not shortened anywhere in the volume — nine days up and four down, four shillings a day, thirty-two shillings a whole hire, four on the day hired and twenty-eight when paid off, and a man hired on day X and out on day X back in the fen on day X plus eight.** The two figures the volume itself derives from the road are sound: ninety-nine shillings up at eleven a day for nine days, and a hundred and four down. **The sixty shillings that separates the two is not decomposed on the page and cannot be decomposed from the two daily rates the page gives for a hired trestle and a hired bench at any whole number of days in this book, and that is recorded rather than repaired.**
2. **Chapter 141's hypothetical.** *I would be spending thirty-two shillings to arrive on the thirty-first in a yard with four people in it.* A man hired on the twenty-sixth and out on it is back on day X plus eight, which is the third of the ninth month, and not the thirty-first. The argument is if anything stronger on the later day, and it is a figure inside a speech about a hire that was not made.
3. **Chapter 125's two frames.** *the question this fen has been carrying since the third of this month* and *the eleven cuts in one row on the third of this month were the same thing done again*. The cuts were read with a rule and a lens on the ninth and tenth of days 151 to 180, and Chapter 125 sits in days 181 to 210, so both frames are a month out. The second is determinable and the first is not, because the volume has no canonical answer to when a question began being carried, and a close that invented an ordinal would be inventing a fact.
4. **Chapter 123's frame.** *the thing he said at the sixth hour on a plateau in a barn three months ago.* The draw was on the thirteenth of days 151 to 180 and Chapter 123 sits in days 181 to 210, so it is last month and thirty-six days, and not three months. Chs 121, 124 and 128 all call the same day *the thirteenth of last month* and are right.
5. **Chapter 138's fortnight.** *a man who has done one of them in a fortnight is not a man anybody is going to be glad about.* The two draws are fifty-nine days apart.
6. **The closing paragraph's run.** The last paragraph in the manuscript, the one the chapter says was not read back before it was initialled, says the compost line went on the page *nine times running, eight of them not discharged, and on the ninth month of that run the price came down a penny*. Every document in the volume says the run is **eight** months and not discharged in eight, including the block four paragraphs above it in the same chapter, and the price came down a penny in the **eighth** month's line. **Not repaired, because the correct figure is on the page four paragraphs above and a close that alters the volume's last unrehearsed paragraph is making a larger intervention than the class of fix this close is authorised to make.** **A Volume 04 writer may not inherit the number nine.**
7. **Two counts of intervals in Batch 0005.** *this is the second time in nine days* appears twice, in Ch 139 and in Ch 140. In Ch 139 the two occasions are the sixteenth and the twenty-first of the same month, five days. In Ch 140 the two occasions are the second and the twenty-third of the same month, twenty-one days. **In both cases the count of the two is right and the interval is not, and the correct interval in both is *in this month*, and it is not repaired because a one-word change inside a count sentence can make a different count wrong and the volume's own count of how many times it has said a thing in a yard is entered elsewhere and is not mine to re-derive.**
8. **Chapter 124's *since the eighteenth*.** *I have not said it out loud since the eighteenth*, said on the twenty-first about a name she said out loud on the seventeenth. Read as *the last time I said it was the eighteenth* it is a day out; read as *I have not said it on or after the eighteenth* it is true. **Left as it stands, because the sentence is defensible and the manuscript's own rule is that a record is not improved on by a later writer who cannot say which of two readings was meant.**
9. **Chapter 142's *the twenty-eight*.** *Their water is the same water it was on the twenty-sixth and it will be the same water on the twenty-eight.* The bare form is not one this manuscript uses for a day in a sentence of this kind. **Left, and recorded, because it is inside a speech that argues a household's water is untouched and no reader is left with a wrong figure.**

### 8. The locks, audited end to end, and which of them broke

**None broke. All of them were checked on the page and every one is whole.** Declared twice and correct, and **the fen does not know which two records are in the class and no chapter tells it.** A declared record can still be published, and being unsafe is a fact about an office and not about a page. **The four copies are four and the five places of the ledger copy are five, the two counts are on one page in Ch 145 and are not to be added, and the fen has entered that it put them on one page on purpose.** The sequence cannot be sent, listed, traced or classified, and the way out of the form is the form. The fieldbook was not opened again and the use log is **thirteen** lines recording contacts and never readings, and no supply of a use log is proposed anywhere and nobody is thanked for its absence. The part three condition. **The refusal clause is used once, in Ch 114, and its fact and not its terms are on the page** — a clerk read a copy he was not entitled to refuse, and Perrin Osse entered the fact and the hour and said that nothing in that building would stop her except her. **The free offer is declined in one line and read out again in a yard in Ch 127.** The standing rule is four lines, was used once on the twelfth of the eighth month, says nothing whatever about what comes after the stop, and **no draw has been attempted since.** The rootmark is four inches, branching twice, unchanged, with no second mark and no lengthening anywhere in the volume. The leak is unmended, undiagnosed, has no due date, and no batch says whether it has moved. The beat is undiagnosed and its column is open, and **its day is now settled at day 171.** The eleven cuts are unresolved and **no character in any of the forty-nine chapters says whose order it is.** The growth is unread, unnamed, and is neither an attack nor a symbol. The rows are let go and a hundred and forty-one trees are standing, and the work of the twenty-fifth was the households' own work on their own ground and is not called a sacrifice. The price is not produced and the sum is not completed: **forty-nine pounds and one shilling and not held, in two halves that were not added and not averaged.** The statement is uncorroborated and no document was found for it. The sealed record is sealed and producible only to the person named in it on that person's own request, and nobody made a request and nobody was named. The fragment is unopenable and nobody read intent in it. The man at the second house is owed nothing and was not looked for, and his entry appears in Volume 03 once, as an item in a handoff with no answer against it. The day letter's four pails are four pails and a pail is not a measure. **The next ordinary reading of the well at Cauldron Reach is the fourth hour on the sixteenth of the ninth month, which is day 256, and it is the first clock Volume 04 owns, and no batch may skip it and no batch may move it.** The bay boards are *day minus sixty-six* and the March's tin is *day minus nineteen*, and both were derived out loud in a yard in Ch 143 in front of about twenty-five people because two figures in a card did not come out of them. **Sixty pounds ten is untouched and is expressly in no figure in this volume.** The third condition is undescribed and no chapter describes it. The Nia Vale letter is sealed in a shut drawer, unopened and undiscussed, and is not mentioned in the volume. The Fieldbook panel allowance is closed: one was spent, in Ch 101, and Batch 0005's was not spent, and **nothing has carried forward.** The section-nine notes run twenty-second to forty-second and the standing sentence is carried on thirty-seven of forty-two, and the chain closes on the forty-second with one paragraph in the same hand that is the last thing in the manuscript. **No romance.** And the level at the end of the volume is **Stage 3, Drawwright, with two draws spent and neither recovered.**

## The close's own arithmetic, checked a second time after the pass

475 hundredweight at four shillings is 1,900 shillings, which is ninety-five pounds. 402 at four is 1,608, which is eighty pounds eight. The difference is 292 shillings, which is fourteen pounds and twelve shillings. 475 pence is 39s 7d, which is one pound, nineteen shillings and sevenpence. 475 at 47p is 22,325p, which is 1,860s 5d, which is ninety-three pounds and five pence. 475 at 45p is 21,375p, which is 1,781s 3d, which is eighty-nine pounds one shilling and threepence. The difference is 79s 2d, which is three pounds nineteen shillings and twopence; four pounds **and fivepence** is 80s 5d; 80s 5d less 79s 2d is one shilling and threepence. 910 pails at a shilling is 910 shillings, which is forty-five pounds ten shillings. 109 hundredweight at nine shillings is 981 shillings, which is forty-nine pounds and one shilling. 448 pails at a shilling is 448 shillings, which is twenty-two pounds four; 448 taken thirty days over seven is 1,920 shillings, which is ninety-six pounds, which is worse than eighty pounds eight. 240 less 66 is 174 and 250 less 66 is 184. 240 less 19 is 221 and 250 less 19 is 231. 441 less 300 is 141. Three journeys at 25 hundredweight is 75, and 400 plus 75 is 475, and the 75 is charged on top of the specification and not out of it. **And thirty-two shillings is four shillings plus twenty-eight wherever the two parts are named together, which was not true of six places in six chapters when this close began: Chs 121, 122, 123, 129, 143 and 144, all six of which now read twenty-eight. The figure *thirty-two shillings* stands seventeen times across ten chapters — Chs 121, 122, 123, 129, 131, 133, 134, 137, 138 and 141 — and Ch 136 states the total and the balance in one sentence without the two words, so the chapters to read for the figure are eleven and the two that carry only the balance are Chs 143 and 144. *(The close first wrote *the ten places in the volume that state it* and then listed the six chapters it had repaired, which are not the same six and not the same count. Corrected at the review of the close.)*
