# VOLUME 03 — THE REVIEW OF THE CLOSE, AND WHAT IT CHANGED

**The Volume 03 close was reviewed as a phase and not as a batch. Five findings: three blocking, two of them about the record rather than the pages, and two minor. Four were applied and one was checked against the volume's own arithmetic and declined. Four chapters lost one character each. No sentence, no figure, no date, no name and no beat moved, and nothing in the volume's argument, its ending or its locks was touched.**

## 1. Applied — four doubled closing marks, Chapters 123, 126, 127 and 128

**The defect.** The close's quotation pass put one mark at the end of each of 174 paragraphs and in four of them it put a *second* one. `chapter-0123.md:77`, `chapter-0126.md:89`, `chapter-0127.md:55` and `chapter-0128.md:67` each ended `.**""`. All four were correct before the pass: each is the closing paragraph of a speech carried over paragraphs, each ends in bold, and each already ended `.**"`. The heuristic read a paragraph whose only mark was a closer and appended another.

**Fixed.** One character removed from each line, at the end, and not one word moved. Each line now ends `.**"` as it did before the close.

**What this does to the count, and why that is correct.** The close recorded *quotation marks even in all forty-nine files* as a property the volume had reached for the first time. **It has not, and the even/odd check was never a test of this manuscript's convention.** In the convention, a speech carried over paragraphs opens every paragraph and the closing paragraph carries the close *without* opening, so a speech of seven paragraphs holds eight marks and a chapter built on it can hold an odd number. The four files above now hold odd counts and they are right. **A later writer or a later pass must not run an even/odd check on this manuscript and must not add a mark to a paragraph that already ends a speech.** The property the volume does have, and the one worth auditing, is that **no paragraph ends with its speech open**, and that holds in all forty-nine.

## 2. Applied — the day-151 anchor, which was the wrong month

**The defect.** The close wrote its derivation anchor as *day 151 is the first of the **fifth** month and a Wednesday*, in `reviews/volume-03.findings.md` and in this file. **Day 151 is the first of the sixth month.** The Batch 0002 dating rule in this file has 151–180 the sixth and 181–210 the seventh, `state/current.md` has the volume running from the first of the sixth through the tenth of the ninth, and Ch 99's own opening sentence puts the first of this month on a Wednesday.

**Fixed in both places, with the reason beside the figure.** The weekday checks are keyed to day numbers and not to month names, so all ten still resolve and no day moved: day 151 a Wednesday gives day 250 a Thursday, which is what `state/current.md` says and what Ch 147's tenth of the ninth says. **The error was latent and it was expensive to leave: a Volume 04 writer building a naming table from that line would have mis-dated every month in the new volume by thirty days.**

## 3. Declined — Chapter 118's *the sixteenth of a month two months back*, which is right

**The finding.** The review held that the close's repair of Ch 118 stopped short: that the referent is day 166, the sixteenth of the sixth month, that from Ch 118's own scene on day 190 the frame must be *last month*, and that the same block quote already calls day 163 *the thirteenth of last month* and day 180 *the thirtieth of last month*, so one paragraph would be naming the same month two ways.

**Checked, and declined. The referent is day 136 and the close's frame is the correct one.** The sentence is the well on the shelf: *Five feet and two inches on the thirtieth of last month … three feet ten inches against the sixteenth of a month two months back.* **Three feet ten inches closes against exactly one reading in this volume, and it is the nine-foot reading of day 136 — 9 feet less 5 feet 2 inches is 3 feet 10 inches.** Day 166 read five feet five inches (Ch 108, and Ch 113's block gives both), so a shortfall of 3 feet 10 inches cannot be measured against it: against day 166 it would be 3 feet 7 inches. The volume says so in its own standing text — **Ch 113, at day 180: *The same well, at the fourth hour of the sixteenth of last month … nine feet* … and the shortfall against the sixteenth of last month is three feet and ten inches** — which is day 136 named from a different month, and the same figure under both of the volume's two naming conventions. Ch 121, at day 201, calls the same reading *the sixteenth of a month three months back*, which is Batch 0003's table being one deeper, exactly as §2 of the close audit records. **Day 136 is the sixteenth of the fifth month, and from a seventh-month scene that is *a month two months back* in Batch 0002's own table, which is what the page says.** The draw of the thirteenth of last month is day 163 and it falls inside the interval the paragraph is measuring, 136 to 180, and the paragraph names three dates in two months, correctly.

**Nothing was changed. The finding is declined on the arithmetic and recorded here so that neither the close's repair nor this refusal is re-litigated.** The one thing standing inside that paragraph that does not close is the half inch: three and a half feet and half an inch is not three and a half feet and four inches, and that is the recorded inherited finding of §4 of the close-up, in four chapters, under the Batch 0004 lock.

## 4. Applied — three figures in the record, none of them on a page

- **The ceiling.** The close recorded the volume's longest chapter, 3,119, as *reached twice, by Ch 123 and Ch 136*, and attached *neither may be lengthened* to it. **It is reached four times: Ch 108, Ch 118, Ch 123 and Ch 136.** Corrected in `reviews/volume-03.findings.md`, in this file and in `state/current.md`, and the lock now names all four.
- **The thirty-two.** The close recorded *four plus twenty-eight in all ten places in the volume* and then listed six chapters, which were the six it had repaired and not the places the figure appears. **The arithmetic is right and the six repairs stand in Chs 121, 122, 123, 129, 143 and 144. The figure *thirty-two shillings* stands seventeen times across ten chapters — Chs 121, 122, 123, 129, 131, 133, 134, 137, 138 and 141 — Ch 136 states the total and the balance together without the two words, and Chs 143 and 144 carry the balance and never name the total.** Corrected in all three files so that an auditor reads eleven chapters for the figure and two for the balance.
- **The em dashes.** Ten marks stand on **six** lines, not seven, all in Batch 0001 and four chapters: `0102:35`, `0103:49`, `0106:7`, `0106:81`, `0108:37`, `0108:83`. Four of the ten are inside quoted or reproduced in-world text and may not be touched. Corrected in this file and in `reviews/volume-03.findings.md`.

## 5. Recorded, not repaired — two more of the close prompt's own figures

**Both are in a document and not on a page, and both would have been inherited.** The close prompt's cuts paragraph says **Ch 108 was drafted at 3,937 and cut to 3,102, and Ch 108 is 3,119** — so a writer auditing the ceiling against that figure would have let Ch 108 grow by seventeen words, and Ch 108 is one of the four chapters standing at the ceiling. **And it says Ch 140 at 2,840 is the shortest chapter in the volume: Ch 140 is the shortest in Batch 0005, and the shortest in Volume 03 is Ch 106 at 2,620.** Recorded here and in `state/current.md` and in the close-up, and the prompt itself is left as it was written, because it is the record of what the close was given.

## 6. What the review did not dispute, and what this pass did not touch

**The 174 marks, the twenty-three word-level repairs, the six balance repairs, the twelve date-frame repairs, the Ch 129 thirty-first, the Ch 128 fourteen days, the Ch 126 date and hour, the Ch 138 beat-day settlement, the Ch 29/Ch 30 overlap as an accepted structural elision, the day 238 hole, the nine-day road, the well's four inches, the compost chain, the ninety-six pounds, the sixty pounds ten, the day 256 obligation, and every one of the locks in §8.** All stand. **The volume is 142,952 words across forty-nine chapters, the manuscript 450,792 across 147, the range 2,620–3,119, and no chapter is outside 2,550–3,120.** The four chapters this pass touched are shorter by one character each and no figure moved.

**The fleet has no Volume 04 prompt and the close was forbidden from writing one, which is per instruction and not a defect. The next phase needs a volume or batch plan for Volume 04 and not a batch prompt.**

# VOLUME 04 — BATCH 0001, CHAPTERS 148–157, MOVEMENT 1, *NINE DAYS OF WATER*

**Volume 04, *Salt Without Rain*, Chapters 148–157, days 251–268, Movement 1. The volume's outline is `outline/volume-04.md`, and that outline was written by the phase that drafted this batch, because no Volume 04 outline existed. Volume 01, Volume 02 and Volume 03 are closed. Chapters 99–147 are the only prose that existed before this one.**

## The dating rule inside this batch, which has no month turn in it and one naming table

**Days 241–270 are the ninth month and days 271–300 the tenth. This batch runs days 251–268 and is therefore entirely inside the ninth month and has ONE naming table, and the next batch crosses the turn and will have two.** Day 250 was the tenth of the ninth month, a Thursday, and is Volume 03's last day.

| Day | Named, in Chapters 148–157 |
|---|---|
| 1–30 | *a month eight months back* |
| 31–60 | *a month seven months back* |
| 61–90 | *a month six months back* |
| 91–120 | *a month five months back* |

**October is the first month and is named nowhere in the batch, and a named month is not carried in a distance; the ordinal distances the batch runs on are not in question.** *March* is not a month. **The batch carries four forms of the capitalised *March* and all four are the region and the trust and not a calendar: *the March's tin* (Chs 148, 154, 157), *the March road* (Ch 149, twice), *the Salt March Dryfoot Trust, of Cray* (Ch 149), and, once, *nine thousand people in the March* (Ch 149).** Volume 03's lock allowed three forms; the fourth is a region phrase inside a speech and is recorded here so that a later writer does not treat it as a fourth kind of thing.

## Volume 04 Batch 0001 day clock, confirmed against the drafted chapters

Ch 148 days 251–252 (**Fri the eleventh, Sat the twelfth**) · Ch 149 days 253–254 (**Sun the thirteenth, Mon the fourteenth**) · Ch 150 day 255 (**Tue the fifteenth**) · Ch 151 day 256 (**Wed the sixteenth**) · Ch 152 days 257–258 (Thu the seventeenth, Fri the eighteenth) · Ch 153 days 259–260 (**Sat the nineteenth, Sun the twentieth**) · Ch 154 day 261 (Mon the twenty-first) · Ch 155 days 262–263 (Tue the twenty-second, Wed the twenty-third) · Ch 156 days 264–265 (Thu the twenty-fourth, Fri the twenty-fifth) · Ch 157 days 266–268 (**Sat the twenty-sixth, Sun the twenty-seventh, Mon the twenty-eighth**).

**The batch runs days 251–268 with no gap, no day shared between two chapters, and no chapter past its own range. Day 268 is the twenty-eighth of the ninth month, a Monday. Day 269 is the twenty-ninth, a Tuesday, and day 270 is the thirtieth, a Wednesday, and day 271 is the first of the tenth month, a Thursday. Batch 0002 starts at 269 and crosses the turn, and the first of next month is a Thursday, which is the day the ninth month's compost line falls on.**

**The five weekday statements a reviewer may check, and all five resolve:** the waggon in the yard on the fifteenth, a **Tuesday**; the reading of the well at Cauldron Reach on the sixteenth, a **Wednesday**; the door read whole on the twenty-first, a **Monday**; the give-away on the twenty-sixth, a **Saturday**; and the volume's first standing figures read on the twenty-eighth, a **Monday**.

**Staging.** Chapters 148, 149, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156 and 157 are at Lantern Reach, on the fen road, or in the low ground four hundred yards below the north gate. **Two scenes are narrated from outside and neither has a fen character in it: Ch 151's whole chapter at Cauldron Reach, four hundred miles off, and the paragraph of Ch 150 about the waggon's arithmetic, which is a fen character in a fen yard.** The Fennmere yard in Ch 152 is nine miles off and walked out of and back from on the seventeenth, and the Pans well is eleven miles off and walked out of and back from on the eighteenth. **No character is on the shelf and back at the fen inside ten days.** The sheet from the fourth house at Cauldron Reach was written on the sixteenth and arrives on the twentieth, on the four-day road, at the household's own cost, which is the fourth time in a season this body has been beaten home by a household's own expense.

Two stakes stand in the two faces that were not read. The occupier's whole answer is four sentences and ends: a thing comes up where nobody is doing anything to it, and that is not a finding, that is the difference between a thing and a finding.** **NOBODY MAY SAY THE TELLING IS STILL GOING ON AND NOBODY MAY SAY IT HAS STOPPED** | Ch 151 |

Two hundred and nine at the Pans well eleven miles off, on the eighteenth, at about the second hour of the afternoon.** Differences: **fifty-seven** and **a hundred and fifteen** and **fifty-eight**. **Two hundred and nine against ninety-four is two and a bit times, and it is not two and a quarter times, because two and a quarter times ninety-four is two hundred and eleven and a half and this body does not have that number** | Ch 152 |
| **The four men and one sentence** | in the low quarter on the seventeenth, **four men said the same sentence in the same words, and not one of the other forty-odd people said anything: *Is the road taking it off us?*** The engineer of record answered the same question four times in the same words, in this order, before he looked at anybody's face: **I have got a pail and a watch and I have not got an answer, and I am not going to give you one today, and I would rather say that than give you a figure that belongs to me.** And to the second question, *then who is taking it off us*: **I do not know, and I have not got a charter and I have got no standing on that road, and if I told you a name I would be telling you a name I got from a sheet with no address on it, and that would be worse than nothing, because you would use it and I would have given it to you for free.** The count of men in that quarter who have said that sentence is **four** and the count of people in it is **four hundred and forty-one**, and the fen is not going to divide one into the other | Ch 152 |
| **A supply and not a theft** | the reader of this body's distinction and the volume's frame: **a man emptying a well and charging by the pail, and being a man with a cart and not a man with a licence, is a supply, and a supply is a thing the law has an opinion about and the law is nine miles away in a building and does not live in a yard. And if this holding says he is a thief in a yard then the next thing anybody in that quarter will say is that the well was always ours, and the well was not always ours, and there is a charter on it and the charter is somebody's and the somebody is Garrow Nye** | Ch 152 |
| **The return of the eighteenth, four lines** | **a licensed holder of a well may supply water to a quarter in which wells are off, and a supply so made is a licensed use and is entered as one**; **the rate is one shilling and fourpence the hundredweight, of which seven pence is the tariff and nine pence is the holder's**; **the parties to a supply are to be identified and returned on the form provided, and a form not returned is a form outstanding and an outstanding form is a matter for the office and not for a third party**; **this return is made in the ordinary course and no part of it is a finding against any person, and nothing in this line states that any water has been taken by anybody who was not entitled to take it.** Signed at the foot by the desk and not by a person. No office has written a word of it and nobody has lied on it | Ch 153 |
| **The margin, and it is not a fraud** | **a shilling and fourpence is sixteen pence. One thousand and forty-five hundredweight at sixteen pence is sixteen thousand seven hundred and twenty pence, which is one thousand three hundred and ninety-three shillings and fourpence, which is sixty-nine pounds and thirteen shillings and fourpence. They paid fifty-two pounds and five shillings. The difference is seventeen pounds, eight shillings and fourpence**, derived a second time as **fourpence a hundredweight on one thousand and forty-five hundredweight is four thousand one hundred and eighty pence, which is three hundred and forty-eight shillings and fourpence.** **The difference is a road and is in nobody's pocket and is the price of eleven miles** | Ch 153 |
| **A pail is not a hundredweight** | the two have been carried as one by this body for a month, **and that carrying is entered as a practice and not as a fact, and this body can check neither of them.** The man who hauls is not a clerk and is not wrong about his own pail | Ch 153 |
| **The sixth no** | the count of things this holding has been told no by this season is **six**, and the sixth is a form in the ordinary course with no part of it a finding against any person. The answer entered: **we cannot name a single party to a licensed supply in the low quarter and we will not try, and the reason is that there are four hundred and forty-one people in that quarter and we do not know which of them bought a pail and which of them was given one, and a form that asks us to say would make us the people who know, and we are not.** And: **the difference between not knowing and refusing has been the whole argument of this book for a year and is not going to be collapsed in a month because a piece of paper came in the post** | Ch 153 |
| **The three who lose** | **one, the low quarter. | **Nothing, four times** | this body can do nothing about the first three lines and the fourth is a fact about a yard, and **there is no form on which this body could put a line about a man who has not spoken to three people four hundred miles off, and there is no address on the sheet, and this holding has looked and has not written and is not going to invent a way of writing in order to have the feeling of having written.** The word nothing is entered four times on that page | Ch 153 |
| **The contact on the boards** | the twenty-first, at the fourth hour, at a boarded floor over a shaft in this holding's own low ground that came off on the twenty-first of a month two months back. **The use log's fourteenth line**, written first and read back twice, with the contact tested with a plain wire gauge and **the reading of the test written down before the instrument was laid on the boards.** Out and back the same day, the seventh hour. **The fieldbook is not in the case; the fieldbook is four hundred miles off in a room with a lock; the instrument is not the book and the book is not the instrument and the two have been confused in a room in this book before** | Ch 154 |
| **The batch's one Fieldbook panel, spent in Chapter 154** | the instrument's and not a person's, read out once at about the fourth hour and a half with four people on the boards, and **no document in this book quotes it as an instruction or as a reason**: *This is not the same as the mouth. / A place can be dry and not be empty. / What is under a floor is not under your hand. / Ground that is held is ground somebody is working.* **Four lines and not three, because the volume's instrument reads a node and has never read a page and the chapter says so out loud on the page rather than in a state file.** The licensed man said it on the boards; nobody thanked him and he was not thanked | Ch 154 |
| **The cost of the contact** | **the mark hot for the rest of that day and the hand from the wrist down no use for about a day, and the man of the north row with the cough carried the case up the slope because he asked and because nobody else offered in time.** **The rootmark is four inches along the inside of the left forearm, branching twice, and is not longer this morning than it was on the eleventh, and there is no second mark, and the burn that ran past it into the elbow is not a mark** | Ch 154, 155 |
| **The Pans well stopped** | brought by a haulier, a man of about forty, on the twenty-first at about the sixth hour, four things in order: **it stopped at the fourth hour yesterday morning, not the afternoon**; he was there at the fifth and put a pail down four times and there was nothing in it that was not in the bottom of it; **the holder's man came out at the seventh hour and has a book and has not said anything to him that he could repeat and he did not ask and is not going to**; and **he is telling this body and not the district and did not come nine miles for a form.** He is held by function and his name is not in this book's and is not going to be | Ch 154 |
| **The standing rule, used once, and used outside one of its four lines** | four lines, every one about a stop. Begun at the fourth hour and twenty minutes of the twenty-second on a shaft in this holding's own low ground, **with about four people on the boards and no yard called.** Stopped at the fourth hour and forty minutes **at four feet, by a licensed man, in a low ground with about four people in it and no yard called**, entered by the licensed man in his own hand with the hour on it. **The line of the low ground is open in this column and nothing has been written underneath it and the fen has not opened it with about four people standing in it. The third line does not say in a yard. This body read that line as though it did, out loud, in this yard, for two years, including the reader and the clerk, and the rule has no clause for a yard and there is no fifth line and there never has been one. The count of the times a rule of this body has been used outside one of its own four lines is one** | Ch 154, 155 |
| **Why the rule could not be satisfied, and who broke it** | the rule's first line requires that the draw not be begun on ground whose return is not carrying. **Nobody in that yard can say whether the return under that floor is carrying. The instrument and a man of about thirty-five are the only two sources in this book with anything to say about it; one is a piece of metal that cannot be checked and the other is nine miles away, is not a party, and cannot be asked in a room.** The reader of this body entered that the rule has handed its whole of itself to a man because the only person who can answer its first line is a stranger, and that it is the worst-written rule he has ever read and that it is the worst-written rule in this book and that it is his own. **The engineer of record began the draw anyway, and did not tell anybody in this holding that he was going to, and said why in a yard the next morning in six sentences: *I did not want about twenty-five people and a rule and a licensed man and a clerk standing on a floor while I did it, because I knew what the rule's first line said and I knew I could not satisfy it, and the only way I could get past that without breaking the rule in front of anybody was to do it when there was nobody there to break it in front of. And that is a thing you do when you have decided you are going to do a thing, and not a thing you do when you have decided the right thing.*** **The fen entered that this is NOT one of the six noes, in a separate line on purpose, because a thing a man does to himself is not a refusal and must not be counted as one** | Ch 154, 155 |
| **The cost of the draw** | **darkened veins past the mark into the elbow, on the left arm, from about the fifth hour of the twenty-second until about the third hour of the twenty-fourth; fever twice in the night, and he was not alone on either night and did not ask for company and did not send anybody away; numbness in three fingers, the two middle ones and the ring one, and the third finger is the one he rules with; loss of taste from about the eleventh hour of the twenty-second until about the ninth hour of the twenty-third; the hand from the wrist down no use for two days.** **Two accounts of the same arm in this book do not agree and were not reconciled: the reader's says a day and a half, the engineer of record's says two, and there is an hour at about the fourth that is in neither, and the fen entered both again and entered that it does not reconcile them** | Ch 155 |
| **The miller's board** | from nine miles off, in the miller's own hand: **the sixteenth, two hundred and forty-four; the twenty-second, the morning, before anything, two hundred and forty-four; the twenty-third, the morning, two hundred and thirty-three.** **A fall of eleven on a board that read two hundred and forty-four four days running**, entered as a difference and not as a cause, with a fourth line carrying no figure at all, the first such line in nineteen years of that board: **the wheel was not turned by the water on the morning of the twenty-second and I turned it by my own arm for a count of ninety and I have written what I did because I am a miller and not a clerk and a number without what I did to make it is a thing somebody will use against me in a year** | Ch 155 |
| **The low quarter's fifth house** | a woman of a household in the low quarter came up on foot on the twenty-third and did not stop at the gate and came the last four hundred yards down into the low ground. **The well they were drawing off went off at about the second hour on the twenty-third; it had been off before that at the first hour of the month and had come on on the nineteenth and had been on four days. There were five houses on that row with water on the fourteenth and there are four, and the one that went is not hers. She timed the pail: a hundred and fifty-one every day since the seventeenth, and on the twenty-third she timed it four times and there was nothing to time. She said, first, that she does not know that it is this holding, and that four men have said the other thing at her in four days and she is not going to be the fifth, and that she did not ask the man with the cart where the water comes from, because he is a man with a cart and she is a woman with a pail, and that is how it is done down there and has always been done and it is not going to be her who changes it this week** | Ch 155 |
| **The word refused** | **the man of the north row with the cough said the word nest on the twenty-third at the wall side of the low ground, once, not to anybody, and Soren Rill was four feet away and heard it.** The refusal, given as a refusal and not as a definition: **a nest is a thing a thing makes when it is stopping. That is what a nest is. It is a place a thing builds and then stays in, and it is not a road and it is not a queue and it is not a thing that is on its way anywhere. A nest has one thing in it and one thing in it has a number. What is under that ground is not that.** The evidence given: **he has read that ground four times and it is not one thing, because he has watched it refuse — in a year he is not going to name, a crew with a licence and a schedule put a probe into it and the ground closed over the probe and took the schedule with it and the schedule came up in a different place eleven feet on, and he has never seen a thing do that twice, and he has been waiting two years to see it do it twice and it did not. So there is no number under that ground, and a thing with no number under it and a road on it is not a nest.** **THE WORD HE REFUSES TO GIVE IS NOT ON ANY PAGE OF THIS BOOK AND IS NOT TO BE GUESSED AT BY ANYBODY** | Ch 156 |
| **The checkable half, and the half he will not give** | **a thing under that ground does not go where the ground goes, and it is doing work, and the work is not water and is not seeds and is not anything anybody in this yard can name, and it is the sort of work that stops if nobody does it.** And: **the half I will not tell you is what it is, and I am not going to be asked again by this body, and if I am asked again by a person in an office I will say no in one word, and I have said that to four offices in nineteen years and have never once had to say it twice to the same one** | Ch 156 |
| **The ask and the price** | **a pail, a measure, and an hour. Not the boards pail — this holding's pail — and any measure that will hold an exact amount and not a bucket.** He declined to say what it was for, **and the reason entered as the reason, which is that there is none he is willing to put in a book of a body of sixteen households on one head.** **The person who keeps the seed house asked who brings it back and he said not him, and the clerk entered it in the form he said it and was told not to improve it and not to let anybody in the book say later that he promised.** He said the price out loud before anybody asked: **one pail, and the losing of a man you have had for four days, who has not been paid and is not going to be paid and is not asking, and who has told you two things in a dark yard with a lamp on it that are worth about four years of work to a man who does this** | Ch 156, 157 |
| **What this holding gave away, and what it cost** | **a pail, a measure that will hold an exact amount, and four hours of a licensed man's time, from the fourth hour of the twenty-eighth to the eighth hour of the twenty-eighth.** Given on the twenty-sixth at about the third hour of the afternoon **in a yard with about thirty people in it, the largest this holding has had on a working day since the flood.** **The pail may not come back. No promise was given and a time was given.** The steward asked who loses and entered that **this body cannot tell**, and that **this holding is now a party to one thing it cannot price, which is the first time in eleven years that has happened.** A licensed man refused to go, and the reason is on the page: **a licensed man under a ground is a thing that can be written about afterwards, and I would rather there were four people in this yard who can say afterwards that there was no licensed man under that ground at any hour on the twenty-eighth. I will be here at the fourth hour and at the eighth and I will write down both, and I will not write down what happened in between, and if anybody asks me in four years I will say that I was not there and that I did not ask** | Ch 157 |
| **The two pails** | **this holding has two pails and has had two pails for eleven years and nobody in this yard knew that until Friday morning, when a stranger asked for one.** The examiner counted them twice and did not round. **The pail given is the boards pail, washed on Saturday morning, and the wash is entered because the last thing it carried was a man's fever and the man does not want it recorded and it is recorded** | Ch 156, 157 |
| **The four answers** | **the count of answers the engineer of record has given in this batch and the count of the four that are in this book's book is one.** On the fourteenth he gave the seedwright of the trust a date instead of a figure; on the fifteenth he gave nine feet two inches in a yard and was asked whether that was the figure and answered that it was a figure; on the twentieth he gave a third answer to a fourth person; **on the twenty-fourth he told the seedwright of the trust that the ground under the low quarter is going to move before the end of next month, and he said the eleventh, and he cannot defend it and has not got a second reading** | Ch 156, 157 |
| **The date with nothing against it** | **the eleventh of next month, in a room with four people in it, of which one was the clerk, entered as a date and not as a finding and read back to the reader of this body on the evening of the twenty-fourth, in a room with about nine people, without saying who had said it.** The reader asked for it in a yard on the twenty-seventh and got **yes**, and the count and the day, and not the thing. The reader's two sentences, and the second is the batch's fault line: **a man who cannot defend a thing and holds it anyway has not kept a private record, he has started one — and a body that has a name can hold a thing it cannot defend, and that is how a name becomes a party** | Ch 156, 157 |
| **The seedwright's sentence** | said once, in a room with four people in it, and **the reader of this body was not in the room and has never read it back and did not read it back that morning, and the fen entered that he was not in the room**: **a thing that is true and in one room is not a secret yet. The day it is in the same room again is the day it is a secret, and I am telling you the day now so that you cannot have it later, and I am not going to be thanked for it and I have said that before I was thanked.** And: **I am not going to write it down. The seedwright of the trust was asked for a number by the engineer of record and gave him the one she had, and was asked to enter it and did not enter it, and is not going to enter it, and the reason she gave is that a thing that one person can carry is not a thing a body can be asked to carry, and that is the sixth time in a year she has refused to have that written as a refusal** | Ch 156 |
| **The volume's third question** | **people are walking toward water. Nine of them went down this fen road on the fifteenth with a chest of twenty-six trays and four days of water, a hundred and forty-one more are at the bottom of a quarter nine miles off, and a man with a cart is filling pails from a well eleven miles off, and this body cannot tell whether they are walking toward a thing that is walking with them.** Asked once, in a yard of about thirty on the twenty-sixth. **The count of the times it has been asked is one and the count of the times it has been available to a room and not been taken is one, and the two counts are not to be added to the count of the first question.** The difference is on the page in the fen's own words: **the first question asks who gave an order. The third does not ask that, and nobody in this book could answer it, because an order has a person at the end of it and this body has not got one and has looked and not found one** | Ch 157 |
| **The man of about seventy, twelfth time in a season** | fetched on the afternoon of the twenty-eighth, given the three counts, the two sums, the three answers, the date with nothing against it, and the pail and the measure and the hour, and asked for the last count to be repeated and said **three words: write it twice.** Nobody explained it, he was not asked what it was about and was not going to be, **and the fen does not know what it means and has entered that it does not know** | Ch 157 |

## Recorded deviations from the batch's own cards, all deliberate and all checkable

1. **The batch's outline gives the batch ten chapters and the day clock 148–157 as days 251–268. The prose runs the same days and no chapter crosses its own day.** Two chapters run on one day and are entered as such: Ch 150 is the fifteenth alone and Ch 151 is the sixteenth alone, and Ch 154 is the twenty-first alone. **The reason is that Ch 151 is the volume's first clock and is not to be shared with a fen scene, and that Ch 150's waggon is an arrival and is not to be spread over two days.**
2. **The board figures and the tin figure are derived, not stated.** Day 251 less sixty-six is one hundred and eighty-five and day 251 less nineteen is two hundred and thirty-two in Ch 148; day 261 gives one hundred and ninety-five and two hundred and forty-two in Ch 154; day 268 gives two hundred and two and two hundred and forty-nine in Ch 157. **All three are the day-minus rules and all three are arithmetically true, and the reader of this body made the clerk read the rule out loud before the first of them, which is now the third time he has done that on a reading day and which nobody asked for.**
3. **The margin between the licensed rate and the price of a pail is seventeen pounds, eight shillings and fourpence, and the card's arithmetic in the outline did not exist and was wrong when first derived.** 1,045 hundredweight at one shilling and fourpence is sixteen thousand seven hundred and twenty pence, which is sixty-nine pounds and thirteen shillings and fourpence; against fifty-two pounds and five shillings the difference is seventeen pounds, eight shillings and fourpence. **A first draft of the chapter carried twenty pounds and eighteen shillings, which is what twenty shillings and fourpence a hundredweight on one thousand and forty-five gives if a shilling is treated as twenty pence. In this manuscript a shilling is twelve pence, and a first shilling and fourpence is sixteen pence, and the page is now right and the derivation is said out loud twice.** The same correction moved the tariff line in the return from nineteen pence to **seven pence, with nine pence the holder's**, so that the four lines of that document add up.
4. **The projection of the bill in Ch 148 is two thousand eight hundred and fifty pails and one hundred and forty-two pounds and ten shillings**, being ninety-five a day for the nineteen remaining days of a thirty-day month plus the one thousand and forty-five already hauled. **A first draft carried one hundred and forty-one pounds and six shillings, which is not that multiplication, and the page is now right.**
5. **No character says the word the man of about thirty-five refused, and the word is not on a page.** The outline's card for this beat said the team has to distinguish a territorial living community from a monster nest in Movement 3; **Movement 1 must not get there, and the outline's own Movement 3 card is what carries it.** The batch's contribution is the refusal, the checkable half, and the price.
6. **The engineer of record is not on the plateau and is not on the shelf in this batch, and no chapter has him read deep memory or see a vision.** The word *rootmark* appears in the standing figures and nowhere as an instrument; the fieldbook is not opened; the instrument is laid on a floor, not on a node.
7. **The low quarter's water is not a pail of the fen's own.** The batch deliberately carries **a pail as a hundredweight as a practice and not as a fact**, and enters that this body can check neither. The conversion was not made good anywhere in the batch and is not to be made good in Batch 0002 without a household or an office putting it in a document.
8. **Soren Rill gives a year once and refuses it.** He says the ground has been in that shape longer than the charter at the bottom of the other road and **asks that the year not be put on it**, and the fen entered that. **The year is not on a page and no chapter may put it there.**

## Proposed canon changes — Volume 04 Batch 0001

Four, none of which changes a world rule, a power rule, a relationship lock, or the ending; all four are local instruments and are recorded rather than silently applied.

1. **A licensed supply to a quarter where wells are off is a licensed use, and the margin between a licensed rate and the price of a pail is the price of a road.** This is the first instrument in the manuscript that puts the Crown's frame on a page in a form nobody can call a lie, and it is the volume's engine: a body that has become a name cannot fill in a form about four hundred and forty-one people it cannot see.
2. **The refusal of a word, and a price said out loud before anybody asks.** The man who refused the word nest gave a checkable half, refused the other half in one word, said what a refusal is for, said the price of what he was asking before he was asked, and said he would not be brought back. **This is the first time in the manuscript that a character has named the cost of his own request in advance, and the fen entered the whole of it.**
3. **A rule's first line can be unsatisfiable and the breach is entered in a line of its own that is not the line of a refusal.** The reader of this body entered that the rule is the worst-written rule in the book and that it is his own, and the fen entered the engineer's breach on a separate line, **because a thing a man does to himself is not a refusal and must not be counted as one.** This is the first instrument in the manuscript that separates a self-inflicted breach from an external no, and the volume needs both counts to stay distinct.
4. **The first line of a standing list is a question and the third is a different question, and the counts of questions are kept apart.** The volume adds a third question and states in the fen's own words that it is not the first two, **and it is the first time in the manuscript that a body has entered a question and then declined to add its count to the count of an older question.** The count of a question is the count of a question.

## The review of Volume 04 Batch 0001, and what it changed

The `next-0004` phase was reviewed as a phase: the ten drafted chapters, the volume outline the same phase wrote to govern them, and the Batch 0002 prompt it queued. **Nine findings, two blocking, applied in place. No chapter was rewritten and no sentence that carries a fact, a name, a date, a beat or a guardrail was moved.** The full record is `reviews/volume-04-batch-0001.findings.md`. The review phase's log records that the `novel-reviewer` subagent could not be loaded and the review fell back to the writer agent, so this was a hand review and the findings file says so on its face.

**1. The Cauldron Reach speech contradicted the wall, and the wall was right — applied.** Ch 151's occupier said the sixteenth of last month was five feet and three inches. It is **five feet and two inches**, and every other authority agrees with the wall: the wall block in the same chapter, `outline/volume-04.md`, the batch summary, this file, and Volume 03's canon, which has day 196 at five feet three inches and day 226 at five feet two inches. The spoken clause was the single outlier in a chapter whose whole subject is that the wall outranks the explanation. **The same speech also gave the series in a different order from the wall and mislabelled one month, and both were corrected in the same pass.** The occupier now says, in the same words the narrator uses for the wall, that she is giving them in the order they are on the wall, and the eight readings run 9 feet, five and a half, five five, five four, five two, five three, five two, five one — **line for line and figure for figure with the block, in wall order.** This is load-bearing: the day-286 reading belongs to Batch 0003 and is built off this series.

**The series, settled, and Batch 0003 may not re-date any of it.** Carried as day numbers, because a name changes at the month turn and a day number does not: **day 136 read nine feet, day 164 five feet and a half, day 166 five feet five inches, day 170 five feet four inches, day 180 five feet two inches, day 196 five feet three inches, day 226 five feet and two inches, day 256 five feet and one inch.** From a scene inside days 241 to 270, which is Batch 0001 and Batch 0002, day 256 is *the sixteenth of this month*, day 226 is *the sixteenth of last month*, day 196 is *the sixteenth of a month two months back*, day 180 is *the thirtieth of a month three months back*, day 170 is *the twentieth of a month three months back*, day 166 is *the sixteenth of a month three months back*, day 164 is *the fourteenth of a month three months back*, and day 136 is *the sixteenth of a month four months back*. **The shortfall of three feet and eleven inches closes against day 136 and against nothing else, and no chapter may decompose it.**

**2. The outline carried a money figure the batch had already corrected on the page — applied.** `outline/volume-04.md` said the margin over eleven days was twenty pounds eighteen shillings. It is **seventeen pounds, eight shillings and fourpence**, which is what 1,045 hundredweight at fourpence gives and what the prose gives and what every state file gives. The figure had been corrected twice in the manuscript already, once on the page in Ch 153 and once in this file, and the outline is the document a later phase reads for the rate structure, so the contradiction was one line from becoming fact. **The outline now carries the right figure and the derivation is unchanged and is stated in this file at item 3 below.**

**3. A false mechanical claim in the audit trail — applied.** Both `state/chapter-summaries.md` and this file asserted **zero duplicate sentences of nine words or more across the batch.** There are two, and both are deliberate: the guarantee's operative clause read out of the document and said again in speech in Ch 149, and the standing figures refrain in Chs 154 and 157. **Both claims are withdrawn and replaced with the two named repetitions and the reason neither is a defect.** This is the failure mode `reviews/README.md` records this repo being bitten by twice, a state file certifying a property nobody ran, and it was found by a review that checked rather than by a writer that assumed.

**4. The length band had been widened to fit the output — the claim is fixed and two chapters are declared.** See the length section above. The band is 2,600–3,120, the target; 2,550–3,120, the floor Volume 03 closed on; and the two chapters outside it are named as exceptions in `state/current.md`, in this file and in `state/chapter-summaries.md`. **The queued Batch 0002 prompt was carrying the widened 2,550–3,200 and now carries the real band plus a sentence saying that a chapter landing outside it is a fact to report and not a band to widen afterwards.**

The half-inch lock in the outline did not parse — applied and rewritten as a lock.** It read *the figure Chapter 137 named as the ground's share sixteen days before the four-inch reading*, which conflated a draw on the head of a well with a reading of this well and gave an interval that does not close: the four-inch draw is Ch 135, dated the twelfth, and the reading beside it is day 226, which is fourteen days later and not sixteen. **The outline now says what the canon is: the half inch is Ch 137's figure and is the ground's share as of day 196, and it may not be carried forward as a figure, added to or taken off any later reading, or made to do arithmetic; and the four inches is a draw and not a reading and may not be dated sixteen days before anything.** Batch 0003 reads the day-286 well and this is the sentence it will have been reading.

**6. All three now carry the outline's rule, which is a rule: a day is an ordinal, *of this month* or *of last month*; a day of the first month is a bare number only; and a named month is not carried in a distance, while the ordinal distances the batch and the queued prompt are both built on — *a month two months back*, *the thirtieth of a month three months back* — are the house idiom and are not in question.

**8. `outline/series.md` gives Volume 04 a third question the volume outline does not carry — flagged, not resolved, and nobody may resolve it.** See `state/open-threads.md`. The series card is the contract where the two documents differ, and the difference is now written down instead of being silent.

**9. Paragraph length and bold density — measured, and the prose left alone.** The review's own figures put this batch slightly below Volume 03 on paragraph length and called the drift series-wide. Measured against the manuscript's own convention, **every paragraph over 200 words in the batch is a block quote or an italic document note** — sixteen of them, the longest at 516 words in Ch 157 — **and not one is narrative prose.** That is the shape Volume 03 runs in: its longest paragraph is 761 words and eighty-eight of its paragraphs exceed 200. Breaking the 380-word note in Ch 152 would have meant breaking the batch's central turn out of the document it belongs to, in a manuscript whose block quotes are how a fen's records are made audible. **Declined, and recorded here so that a later pass does not re-attempt it.** The bold density is a property of the whole manuscript and is not this batch's to change alone.

**What the review confirmed and did not touch.** The calendar, which the review checked first and which holds throughout. Zero paragraphs ending with a speech open, in all ten files, which is the binding Volume 03 lesson. # VOLUME 04 — BATCH 0002, CHAPTERS 158–167, MOVEMENT 2, *WHAT SHE SAID IN A ROOM*

## The dating rule inside this batch, which has a month turn in it and two naming tables

**Months run thirty days. Days 241–270 are the ninth month and days 271–300 are the tenth. This batch runs days 269–285 and therefore crosses the turn between Ch 158 and Ch 159 and therefore has TWO naming tables and not one.** Day 268 was the twenty-eighth of the ninth month, a Monday, and was Batch 0001's last day. Day 270 is the thirtieth, a Wednesday, and is the last reading day of the ninth month. Day 271 is the first of the tenth, a Thursday. Day 285 is the fifteenth of the tenth, a Thursday. **Day 286 is the sixteenth of the tenth, a Friday, and is the fourth hour and the next ordinary reading of the well at Cauldron Reach. It is the first day of Batch 0003, no chapter of this batch owns it, and none of them read it, predicted it, or put it on the standing figures.**

**Ch 158 is the only chapter inside days 269–270, and it is named from the ninth month.** Every past day in it is a ninth-month distance: the twenty-eighth of this month is the hour; day 262, the draw, is **the twenty-second of this month**; day 261, the leak, is **the twenty-first of this month**; day 256, the Cauldron Reach reading, is **the sixteenth of this month**; day 248, the day letter, is **the eighth to the seventeenth of this month**; day 226, the Cauldron Reach reading before it and the green in the older row, is **last month**; day 223, the earlier leak figure, is **the thirteenth of a month two months back**; day 171, the beat, is **the twenty-first of a month three months back**; day 136, the nine feet, is **the sixteenth of a month four months back**; and the fourth cart, gone up the plateau road on the seventh of the eighth month, is **a month two months back**, and the not asking is a month old and is entered as a month and not as a day.

**Chapters 159 to 167 sit inside days 271–285 and are named from the tenth month, and the whole of the ninth month changes its name in the space of one chapter, which is the whole reason a day number is not a name.** From those chapters: days 1–30 are *a month nine months back*; 31–60 *a month eight months back*; 61–90 *a month seven months back*; 91–120 *a month six months back*; 121–150 *a month five months back*; 151–180 *a month four months back*; 181–210 *a month three months back*; 211–240 *a month two months back*; **241–270 are *last month***; 271–285 are *of this month*, *the first*, or the bare ordinal. **These two conventions are not the same and the difference is a recorded feature of this manuscript and not a defect to be harmonised by a later writer. What a chapter may never do is carry a name across the turn.** The second table is the convention of Volume 03 Batch 0005's second table and is the convention this batch's prose follows.

| **BRINEWAKE** | **SPENT. Spoken once, out of Sera Quill's own mouth, in a room with about eleven people in it, on the sixth of this month. The clerk wrote it once and did not write it twice. Nothing corroborates it and nothing can. A record, a log, a district index, a clerk and a licensed man did not supply it, and nothing in this batch corroborates it, and nothing in this batch says that it exists.** On the page it is attached to a place, a relay, a warning that was not in the log and a number of people, and **to no date, to no year, to no office and to no Quiet Break.** It does not appear again anywhere in Volume 04 after Chapter 162. **Because of that lock, the four-line entry read out whole in Chapter 167 carries a BLANK where the place-name stands, the blank has been in the book since the sixth, the clerk put it there and has not filled it in since, about eleven people read four lines with a blank in the middle of one of them, nobody asked about the blank, and the fen entered why and entered that nobody asked** | 162, 167 |
| **what corroborates it** | **nothing.** The record of compensation is sealed, is produced to the person named in it and on that person's own request, **no request has been made, nobody has been named, nothing has been opened, and this body has no standing to become a person who could.** The only two things that can carry what she said are her memory and that record. **No chapter of this volume may open the second and no chapter of this volume may have anybody make the request, and Sera Quill did not make it and was not asked to** | 162 |
| **what she wanted for it** | **not money. To be entered in this holding's own book, under her own name, with the date, as the person who said it** — and her reason, that in four years there is going to be one person who can say she said it, and if she is not on the page then the page says a thing happened to a room. And before that, when asked what she wanted this body to do with a number like that: **nothing. I do not want it used. I do not want it printed. I do not want it in a yard in nine miles and I do not want it in a yard here. I have had one of these and I am not going to have a second one that I chose** | 162, 167 |
| **the cost of entering it** | **the reader named the wrong half as wrong before he said it: if this holding writes it down an office can list it, and a thing in a list is a thing that has been had; and if it does not write it down then a woman said a thing in a room and it is gone, and in four years she will be the only person who ever said it and this book will be the proof that nobody was listening, and that is worse than the list.** The fen said yes and **the payment for it is this holding's own exposure and it is not hers and it went in this holding's book and not in hers**, and **this body has been a name for a month and has now made itself a party, and the reader of this body said in a yard on the twenty-seventh of last month that this is how a name becomes a party and did not think about it for a day then and has thought about it for two days since.** She is on the page once, she did not ask to be, she was not asked whether she wanted it, and she would have accepted it either way, and **the clerk entered that and read it back and did not improve on it** | 162, 167 |

| **the sum that will not be entered** | the low quarter had five wells off on the fourth day of this month, and from the second to the seventh it has had the licensed supply at a shilling a pail and for every one of those six days water at no price out of a source nobody has named, **and the number of pails in the second supply is in no book because there was no gate, and the two supplies can be added and cannot be divided, and a figure which is the sum of two things one of which was never measured is not a figure, it is a shape, and the person who keeps the money will not enter it and will not be asked to** | 163 |

He knows the form would close the licensed draw, which is the only supply the quarter has got, and that the water a party put in there at no price has stopped and nobody knows where it came from or where it went, and he brought it in the rain anyway. A holder whose well is broken and who does not say so is a holder whose break is somebody else's water. I am not going to be thanked for saying so and I am not going to be forgiven today either, because it is not that kind of day. | **the man of about thirty-five comes back** | on the eleventh, on foot, at about the fourth hour of the afternoon, unasked. **I have been on that ground for nine days. | **it is not late** | the one sentence he said that is not the word he has refused and is not an answer to anything. **Nobody in that low ground asked him what he meant and the fen entered that nobody asked, and entered that this body does not know what it means and has not written and ask and is not going to. The word he has not said is not on any page of this book, and *is not late* is a sentence and not a word for it, and no name may be built on it in this volume** | 165 |

Three, a form on a bench in this room with a date and a well and a licensed man and a number on it, and a man of about eleven miles' road who brought it in the rain and has not been answered. Four, a woman in this room who has not been forgiven and has not asked. Five, a name at the foot of a sheet in eleven miles that this body has no address for, and that this body has read out loud in a yard once this month and did not ask the man whether he wanted it read out loud.** Five things, four lines, **the difference of one is entered as a difference and not as a decision, and the fen entered that not deciding is also a decision and has entered that it is not going to decide it this month either** | 166 |

I am not the person you bring a thing to when it is not one, and you have known the difference between those two since the fourteenth of last month and so have I, and if you cannot hold the difference then you do not need me, you need a book, and you have one, and it is on the middle of this table and anybody may read it.** The reader of this body was not in the room. **The engineer of record did not answer her and nobody in that room answered her, and the time between the question and the end of the room is about nine seconds and the fen entered it and does not know what to do with it.** **This is the first time in eleven years that a person in this building has refused a role and not a figure, the refusal is the standing and not an exception to it, and the count of that standing in a season is five, of which four were about figures** | 166 |
| **the third thing this holding has not learned** | said at the seventh hour in a yard of about nine, out loud and not in the book first: **this holding has spent a month learning that a body with no standing can still be asked to put its name to a form, and a month learning that a man with a private record is a party, and it has not yet learned the third thing, which is that a person who is offered the job of being the one you tell is going to be offered it again, and is going to say no again, and the second no is easier and the third one is not.** And the reason for saying it in a yard: **a thing has to go into a yard before it is a thing everybody knows, and this holding has watched that take nine years once** | 166 |
| **the clerk's observation, fifth in the chain** | entered on the fourteenth of this month, on his own motion, unasked, and never explained and nobody asked: **the book cannot check her** | 167 |
