## THE TWO DEFECTS, BOTH FOUND, BOTH HANDLED, NEITHER PAPERED OVER

**DEFECT 1 — THE WEEKDAY, not the day number.** `state/current.md`, Ch 178 and Ch 187 each placed day 331 on a Saturday and day 330 on a Friday. Both are two days out, consistently, and both point the same way. Day 331 is a **Monday**. **The fix was made in prose, in the yard, by the book itself: Gael Senn, the examiner, is a woman who keeps time, and shortly before the fourth hour on day 321 she is in a yard of about eleven people and the reader of this body has read out of this holding's own book that the next ordinary reading of the well on the shelf is on the first of next month, a Saturday, and the examiner says out loud that the first of next month is a Monday and not a Saturday and that she keeps time and does not round, and the day number is not in question. Both figures are entered, neither is improved on, and the count of the two days this book has got wrong in its own hand is two.** Ch 178 and Ch 187 are closed prose and **were not edited.** The error is a fact in the world and is now on the page with a reason. **THE SECOND REPAIR PASS MOVED THE YARD FROM *AT ABOUT THE FOURTH HOUR* TO *A LITTLE BEFORE THE FOURTH HOUR*, IN THE NARRATION AND IN THE CLERK'S ENTRY, because the card, the day clock and Ch 196's own closing note all say the finding is made before the fourth hour, and the draft had the entry made at the hour the yard met.**

**DEFECT 2 — THE READING DAY.** `outline/volume-04.md` says, twice, as a standing rule, that the well at Cauldron Reach is read "at the fourth hour on the sixteenth of every month." **The whole of the settled narrative is sixteenths: days 136, 166, 196, 226, 256, 286.** The state files and Ch 178 had wrongly named **day 331 — the FIRST of a month — as the next ordinary reading, and a first of a month is a compost-line day and has never been a reading day.** The consequence was a silently skipped reading. Handling, all three of it on the page:
1. **The tenth reading was taken** (day 316, the sixteenth of the eleventh month, a Sunday), by the occupier, with her own nail, in her own yard, on her own wall. This holding has no standing on that ground, did not write and ask, and is not going to. **The figure is not on this page and is not going to be.**
2. **The eleventh reading is on day 346, the sixteenth of the twelfth month, a Tuesday, at the fourth hour**, narrated from outside, in a yard of four households, by the occupier, in her own hand. **It is five feet, the same figure, and there is still no entry anywhere for that well coming back.**
3. **The count of three day-and-not-the-figure entries stands at three and the fen enters that one of the three was aimed at a day that was not a reading day, and does not reduce the count, and does not improve on the other two.**

## THE REVIEW FIX PASS ON BATCH 0005, AND EVERY WORD OF IT

A review pass ran on the drafted batch and returned thirteen findings. **Twelve were applied. One was rejected as a false positive, and the rejection is the most important thing in this section, because a later phase will find the finding in the log and must not act on it.**

### THE FALSE POSITIVE, AND WHY IT WAS REJECTED

**The review reported that Chapters 188–190 run the ninth month four days off the canon weekday chain, and gave a table re-dating day 256, 261, 264, 266, 267, 268 and 269 to the ninth month. Every row of that table is wrong, and the eight weekday statements it asked to be changed are all correct as they stand. The review assumed this batch sits in the ninth month. IT DOES NOT. THIS BATCH IS DAYS 321–350, THE ELEVENTH AND TWELFTH MONTHS.**

The error is the reviewer's, not the prose's: it read Ch 151's *sixteenth of the ninth month* and carried the month name forward instead of reading the chapter's own day span. The evidence that the pages are right and the review is wrong, in order of strength:

1. **The batch's own card says so.** `PROMPT.md`, Ch 188 card: *"the examiner says the first of next month is a **Monday** and not a **Saturday**"* and *"the sixteenth was a **Sunday** five days ago"* and *"the clerk found the sixteenth in it on the **Thursday** and read the page out in the yard on the **Friday** morning."* Ch 188 says exactly those four things.
2. **The two tables in this file make all eight correct.** Day 321 is a Friday, so *twenty-first of this month was a Friday* is right. Day 316 is a Sunday, so *the sixteenth of this month was a Sunday* is right, and it is five days before 321, and it is the tenth reading, which is what Defect 2 below is about. Day 324 is a Monday, day 326 a Wednesday, day 327 a Thursday, day 328 a Friday, day 329 a Saturday — every one of Chs 189 and 190's day-and-weekday pairs.
3. **The seventh column settles it.** Ch 191 opens *The thirtieth of this month was a Sunday* and the count of the readings of the seventh column goes to thirty-six on that day. The table below and `state/current.md` both put **36 on day 330 and 37 on day 331.** If this batch were in the ninth month there would be no reading on the 330th of anything.
4. **A one-line change would have broken the volume.** The review's proposed Friday-to-Monday swap in Ch 188 would have made the reader of this body say the sixteenth of the month was a Wednesday, which is the weekday of a reading in Batch 0001 and not of this one, and would have contradicted the batch card.

**NO CHAPTER WAS TOUCHED FOR THIS FINDING. IF A LATER PHASE FINDS IT IN `logs/next-0005.review.log`, IT IS WRONG AND IT WAS ALREADY ANSWERED.**

### THE ONE REAL ERROR THE REVIEW FOUND IN THOSE CHAPTERS, WHICH IT DID NOT FIND

**Ch 188 contradicted itself.** The chapter is day 321, a Friday, and says so three times, and then at the fourth hour of the evening of the same day the reader of this body says *the reading was on the Sunday and it is the **Wednesday***. **It is now the Friday.** That is a leftover of the ninth-month draft the review thought it was reading, and it is the only trace of that draft on the page.

NO SCENE WAS REPLACED, NO PLOT BEAT MOVED, NO CARD WAS OBEYED AGAINST THE PROSE, AND NO LOCK WAS TOUCHED.**

### THE THREE THAT WERE LOAD-BEARING

1. **Ch 195 gave this holding the tenth figure of the well on the shelf, and Ch 196 forbade it in the same volume.** The wall's own transcript said *The tenth of the wall is the sixteenth of last month and it is five feet*, the clerk's entry repeated it, Ch 196's standing figures carried it as this holding's, and the yard speech compared the tenth with the eleventh. **That is a direct contradiction of Ch 188, of the Ch 195 card, of the Ch 196 card, of the Clocks table, and of Ch 196's own closing handoff, which says the count of the standing of the day and not the figure stands at three and does not come down.** **THE OCCUPIER NOW REFUSES TO WRITE IT, IN HER OWN HAND AND IN HER OWN WORDS, AND THE WALL'S TRANSCRIPT SHOWS THE GAP — *And then the one I am not writing. And then this one.* — AND THE CLERK'S ENTRY SAYS THE TENTH IS NOT IN THIS HOLDING'S BOOK AND WAS NOT WRITTEN AND ASKED FOR. THE READER'S *Five feet and five feet* IS NOW THE NINTH AND THE ELEVENTH, SAID OUT LOUD IN THAT ORDER, WITH A MONTH BETWEEN THEM THAT IS ON NO LINE IN THIS BOOK. Ch 196's standing figures and its closing note were brought into line.** This was the largest single repair in the pass and it is the one the close must not undo.
2. **Ch 193's corridor arithmetic put the front eighty yards past the vault twenty hours before the vault went under.** Three hundred on the fourth, **five hundred and forty** on the eighth, four hundred and eighty-six on the ninth — and the vault is four hundred yards from the north edge. **THE MONDAY FIGURE IS NOW THREE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-FOUR, sixteen yards short of the vault, and the man of about fifty says so out loud.** The reader of this body no longer says he does not know why the front went back, because nothing went back; he now says it went about a yard an hour over the weekend and about seven yards an hour since Monday morning and that he does not know which of those two numbers is the water and which of them is the ground, and that he is not going to guess at it in a yard. **The chapter's argument is untouched and the not guessing is now on a real question.** Ch 196's standing figures carry the new figure.
3. **Ch 191 entered the compost line on the thirtieth, on a day its own notice forbids.** The card, the day clock and the Clocks table all put the eleventh month's compost line **on the first, at about the eleventh hour**, and the chapter's own notice says *The return on the compost line is made on the first of the month and is not made on any other day*, and its handoff says *The first of this month is a Monday and it is the day this holding's compost line falls on, and the figure is on the page*. **The compost line, the woman's word and her finding, the four lines of the month's costs and the reading of the standing rule in full are all now on the first, at about the eleventh hour, after the second reading of the door and before the ninth-hour handoff.** The first fix pass had already moved the door off the thirtieth and left the rest of the day standing in the wrong month, which is the same defect twice. See the entry above for the table corrections that followed the move.

### THE FIFTEEN THAT WERE NOT

4. **Ch 189, twice, dated the reason for not answering the form *the twenty-seventh of a month three months back*.** The twenty-seventh is day 297, and Ch 189 sits in the eleventh-month frame, where 297 is *last month*. The Clocks table's *a month three months back* is itself an error, since the same table dates the refusal that came up the road to day 297. **Both instances are now *the twenty-seventh of last month*.**
5. **Ch 190, twice, and Ch 192, once, carried the two standing reasons in the wrong table.** *The reason from the twenty-seventh of a month three months back* is day 267, which from the eleventh month is **two** months back, not three; Ch 192, in the twelfth, is right and was left. *I was told that on the nineteenth of a month three months back* is day 289, the nineteenth of the tenth month, which from the eleventh month is **last month** — and Ch 190, standing on the twenty-ninth, is the last place in the book that says otherwise. Ch 192, in the twelfth month, had it as *four* and now says **two**.
6. **Ch 190 gave the examiner's line to the man of about fifty.** The draft had the man of about fifty say out loud that he keeps time and does not round, in a chapter in which the examiner is the one who keeps time and says so before anything is called. **The examiner now says it and the man of about fifty writes the numbers down and does not round them.**
7. **Ch 190 also said the pail went in at the top of the second place** and then gave three numbers at three places. **It now goes in at three places, at the top of each.**
8. **Ch 194 said two men were wet through to the shirt on the fourth of last month.** Ch 180, which is that day, says **one**. The officer's dry road and Ch 180's fen road are the same gate and the reader is describing Coll Renner, so the figure has to agree. **It is one.**
9. **Ch 194's second derivation of 2,400 pence did not derive 2,400 pence.** It said *Four pounds is nine hundred and sixty pence* and then jumped to ten pounds, which is true and is not a derivation. **It is now the division — two thousand four hundred over two hundred and forty is ten — and the two derivations visibly agree, which is the chapter's own claim.** The next line, which also said *the other way*, now says the licensed rate instead of the schedule rate, so that the two are not the same phrase twice.
10. **Ch 194's closing beat fell on the fifteenth**, inside Ch 195's span. **It is on the thirteenth**, the day the road opened.
11. **Ch 195 dated the demand to *the eleventh month of last year*** in one sentence and to *the tenth of last month* in the next, and the demand is Ch 183's, on the ninth of the eleventh month of this year. **It now reads *on the ninth of that month*,** which is a date, a month and no year.
12. **Ch 195's sheet said it was sent down a four-day road and read in this building on the twentieth**, and then read it out in this building on the evening of the sixteenth. **It now says it was read in this building on the same day**, and the narration says what came down the road rather than what she sent down it. **SEE THE DEVIATION BELOW — THIS ONE IS NOT FULLY RESOLVED.**
13. **Ch 193 said the nine carts went south on the Friday**, the day before the vault was opened, which is Ch 192's last day and is not narrated there. **They went on that morning.**
14. **Ch 193's last scene was on the Wednesday**, day 340, outside the chapter's span. **It is on the evening of the ninth**, at about the ninth hour, which is after the reader of this body has been out to the edge of the pan at the seventh, and the man's own account of the morning still stands. Ch 193 is 336–339 as the card has it.
15. **Ch 193's man of about thirty-five said *I am not of the nine*.** The nine is a headcount of a yard and he cannot be out of it. **He now says he is not of this holding.**
16. **Ch 196's closing paragraph fetched *a man of about thirty-one*.** He is the man of about seventy, and thirty-one is Mara's age and the reader of this body has been noticing her sleep in a cart shed since Ch 182. **It is a man of about seventy.**
17. **Ch 196 did not move the standing count of questions from six to seven.** The card says one to two, which is the per-question count Ch 157 set up, and the same prompt's *must not do* list and `outline/volume-04.md` both say the standing count goes up by one, and Ch 182 left it at six. **Both are now on the page in the same breath and neither is added to the other, and the fen says there are three counts and that nobody in this book has ever added one of them to another.** The prompt contradicts itself on this line and both readings are on the page; see the deviation below.
18. **Ch 196's standing-figures block had no blank quote line between the use-log entry and the form entry**, so the two ran together as one paragraph. **Restored,** to the convention Ch 187 uses.
19. **Chs 191, 192 and 193 did not end in a newline**, the same defect the house has already logged against `chapter-0156.md`, which makes a `cat`-based count merge a file's last word into the next file's first. **All nine files of this batch now end in a newline** and the batch count is file-safe either way.

### THE TWO DEVIATIONS THE CLOSE HAS TO RULE ON, AND THIS PASS DID NOT

- **The account of the wall on the sixteenth.** Ch 188 establishes a four-day road, and Ch 195's sheet originally said it travelled that road and was read here on the twentieth. **The twentieth is four days on and is Ch 196's day, and the card puts the reading itself in Ch 195, narrated from outside, which is what the page now does.** What the page cannot carry is a sheet that is read in this building on the day it is taken, four hundred miles from the yard it was taken in. The pass removed the false travel claim rather than restructure a good chapter or empty the better half of Ch 195's ending, and **the standing arrangement by which a figure reaches this holding's book inside the month is nowhere on any page and is not contradicted by any page.** It is a seam, not a falsehood, and it is the close's to close.

With a thirty-day month the thirtieth and the next first are always a day apart, so the clause recurs every month and the chapter's argument stands anyway. A question for the close, not a writer's edit.

## THE THIRD PASS ON BATCH 0005, APPLYING THE REVIEW

**The findings are in `logs/batch-0005.review.log`, which is the review agent's own transcript, and NOT in `reviews/volume-04-batch-0005.findings.md`, which still does not exist and which the review phase and the close own. Five prose defects and three state defects were applied. No scene was replaced, no plot beat moved, no lock touched, no closed batch edited, and nothing was padded. Every figure below was recomputed from the files before and after.**

### 1. Ch 195 — a four-day letter arriving the same day. THE REGRESSION, AND IT IS NOW CLOSED.

**What the second pass did, and why it was wrong.** The second pass found that the original sheet said it came *down a four-day road* and was *read in this building on the twentieth*, while the narrative and the clerk's block both had it read out and entered on the **sixteenth**. It resolved that contradiction in the wrong direction: it changed *the twentieth* to *the same day* and deleted *down a four-day road* from the header, which made a letter written at the fourth hour of the morning four hundred miles away enter a book at the eighth hour of the evening of the same day. **A four-day road does not do that. The fix destroyed the travel and kept the impossibility, and the paragraph one line above the header still said *four hundred miles and four days up*.**

**The arithmetic that settles it, from the batch's own day clock.** Day 346 is the sixteenth of the twelfth month, a Tuesday, and it is in Ch 195. Day 350 is the twentieth, a Saturday, and it is in Ch 196 and is the last day of the volume. **Sixteenth plus four days is the twentieth.** Ch 188 fixed the road at four days each way and Ch 170 gives the standing precedent for the same errand: the four lines went down at the fourth hour of the morning of the sixteenth, by the ordinary post, in a leather bag, and came in on the **twentieth**. The second pass's own Ch 193 repair, which moved the compost line off a day its notice forbids, is the same discipline applied correctly.

**What the page says now.** The four-day road is restored in the header and in the narration. **Ch 195 now ends on the sixteenth with the four lines in a bag on a road and the figure NOT in this holding's book, and the entry is of what has happened and what has not** — the reading was taken, the wall is in order, the four lines went down at that household's own cost, the tenth figure is not here and never will be asked for, the eleventh is on the wall and in her hand and not yet in this book, and the reason it is not is that the road is four days and not that nobody sent it. The chapter closes on the reader of this body saying *four days*, and on the road being four up and four down, which is eight, and this holding not having the sheet.

**And the arrival, the yard reading and the exchange moved to Ch 196, on the twentieth, where the card had already put it.** Ch 196's card requires *the shelf well at its eleventh figure* among the standing figures read **at about the eleventh hour of the morning of the twentieth**, so a figure that cannot arrive before the twentieth cannot be in that yard at the eleventh hour. The four lines now come in at about the **ninth hour of the morning of the twentieth, a Saturday**, by the ordinary post, in a leather bag, and the reader of this body reads the whole of it out, the man of about fifty is appointed reader, it is read back, the hour goes on it, and *five feet and five feet* and the three speeches that follow are said there. **THE THREE SPEECHES ARE THE SAME WORDS AND ARE NOT REWRITTEN. THEY ARE IN A DIFFERENT YARD ON A DIFFERENT DAY.**

**The three-block limit is why the entry went into the ledger and not into a fourth block.** Ch 196 carries three `Entered ... by the clerk` blocks and the house limit is three on the volume's last chapter, so the arrival is entered **inside the standing-figures ledger, which is the fen's and not the clerk's**, in the *well on the shelf* paragraph, which now carries *the eleventh figure came into this building on the twentieth at about the ninth hour of the morning, in a leather bag, four days after it was written, at that household's own cost*. Ch 195's one clerk's block is unchanged in count. **NO CHAPTER'S BLOCK COUNT MOVED.**

**What did NOT change, and is the point of the whole repair.** The occupier still refuses in her own hand to write the tenth figure. The wall still shows the gap, *and then the one I am not writing, and then this one*. This holding still has the ninth and the eleventh and both are five feet. The month between them is still not on any page and still was not written and asked for. The shortfall is still four feet against the nine feet of the sixteenth of a month seven months back and is still not decomposed. The half inch is still not carried forward. **There is still no entry anywhere for that well coming back and no chapter of this book is going to make one.** Only the day on which the figure enters this holding's book moved, and it moved to the only day the four-day road allows.

**The seam the second pass left for the close is now closed.** The second pass recorded, in the section above, that *the standing arrangement by which a figure reaches this holding's book inside the month is nowhere on any page and is not contradicted by any page — it is a seam, not a falsehood, and it is the close's to close.* **It was worse than a seam, because the page had been made to say a falsehood, and it is now neither. The arrangement is on the page, with the hours on it, and it is the arrangement Ch 170 already used.**

### 2. Ch 193 — a rate that did not reconcile with the chapter's own figures

**The second pass replaced *the reason it went back is not established* with a two-speed claim, and wrote the speeds wrong.** It said the front went *about a yard an hour over the weekend and about seven yards an hour since Monday morning*. Neither is derivable. Three hundred on the fourth to three hundred and eighty-four on the eighth is eighty-four yards over four days, which is **twenty-one yards a day**, not a yard an hour. Three hundred and eighty-four at about the eleventh hour of the eighth to four hundred and eighty-six at about the seventh hour of the evening of the ninth is a hundred and two yards in **thirty-two hours**, and thirty-two hours is four thirds of a day, and a hundred and two divided by four thirds is **seventy-six and a half yards a day**, not seven yards an hour. Seven yards an hour over thirty-two hours would be two hundred and twenty-four yards.

**What the page says now, and it is derivable twice.** *Eighty-four yards in the four days from Thursday to yesterday, which is twenty-one yards a day, and a hundred and two yards in the thirty-two hours from yesterday at the eleventh hour to this evening, which is seventy-six and a half yards a day.* Both are exact, neither is rounded, and the ratio between them is about three and two thirds, which is a real and alarming number and is not seven. The chapter's argument is untouched: **he still does not know which of those two numbers is the water and which of them is the ground, and he is still not going to guess at it in a yard.** The not guessing now stands on a question the reader can check, which is the whole standard of this book, and the two speeds are carried into the entry in Ch 193 and into the standing-figures ledger in Ch 196 in the same figures.

**Checked and found sound, not a defect.** The review also flagged that the measurement is at *about the seventh hour of the evening* and the entry is *at the eighth hour of the evening*. That is the ordinary shape of this book — a thing measured at one hour and entered at the next, as in Ch 193's own sheet at the second hour and its entry at the third — and the two-speed claim is built on the seventh-hour measurement, which is correct. **Left alone deliberately.**

### 3. Ch 190 — *the two places* after establishing three

The second pass changed *the pail in at the top of the second place* to *at three places, at the top of each of them*, which matches the card, and left the next clause saying *the two places were two hundred yards apart*. **It is now *the first two of them*.** The three numbers, the two-hundred-yard spacing, the eight-foot rod and the north-east bearing are untouched.

### 4. Ch 191 — *a month and not a week*

**The review called this one for a second reader and not a rewrite, and the second reading upheld it.** The sentence was *I have been able, this month, and it took me a month and not a week.* Three faults: *this month* contradicts *a month* in the same breath; the word was said on the first of the eleventh month and is being said on the first of the twelfth, which is **thirty days**; and **a week has no referent anywhere in the chapter**, because nothing on the page ever claimed seven days. The second pass had replaced *nine days and not thirty* and kept the same shape, so the shape was the defect and not the numbers.

**It now says: *I have found out. I have been able this morning, and it is thirty days from the first of last month, and I am not going to stand in this yard and say that thirty days is quick, and the finding is this.*** The thirty is the real distance and is the figure the second pass was reaching for, *a week* is gone, *this month* is gone, and the refusal to call it quick is in the mouth of a woman who has just said *I am not glad about it* three speeches later. **The compost line stays on the first of the twelfth at about the eleventh hour. That repair was correct and is untouched** — the chapter's own notice says the return is made on the first of the month and is not made on any other day.

## THE DAY CLOCK, RE-DERIVED FROM THE FILES, AND IT HOLDS

**Months run thirty days. Day 301 is the first of the eleventh month and a Saturday. Therefore day ≡ 0 (mod 7) is a Saturday, and the chain is 0 Saturday, 1 Sunday, 2 Monday, 3 Tuesday, 4 Wednesday, 5 Thursday, 6 Friday. Day 320 is a Thursday, day 330 is a Sunday, day 331 is a Monday, day 350 is a Saturday and day 361, the first of the next month, is a Wednesday. Every weekday statement in all forty-nine chapters resolves against this chain, including the eight that the Batch 0005 review wrongly called four days out and that `state/current.md` already forbids acting on. The two inherited errors — Ch 178 and Ch 187 putting day 330 on a Friday and day 331 on a Saturday — stand as they are, are two days out, are consistent with each other, and are corrected on the page by Gael Senn in a yard before the fourth hour on day 321, with both figures entered and neither improved on, and with the count of the two days this book has got wrong in its own hand standing at two.**

## THE FORMAT LIMIT, COUNTED ACROSS ALL FORTY-NINE CHAPTERS

**A block is a clerk's block only if it opens "Entered ⟨when/where⟩" and names the clerk as the person entering. A block that opens "Entered on the same line" is a continuation of the block above it. A block entered by the engineer of record in his own hand is his and not the clerk's. On that count: 148 3 · 149 3 · 150 3 · 151 0 · 152 1 · 153 2 · 154 2 · 155 1 · 156 0 · 157 3 · 158 3 · 159 3 · 160 3 · 161 3 · 162 1 · 163 4 · 164 2 · 165 3 · 166 4 · 167 4 · 168 1 · 169 3 · 170 3 · 171 3 · 172 2 · 173 2 · 174 3 · 175 3 · 176 3 · 177 1 · 178 2 · 179 2 · 180 2 · 181 2 · 182 3 · 183 2 · 184 2 · 185 2 · 186 1 · 187 1 · 188 1 · 189 1 · 190 2 · 191 1 · 192 0 · 193 3 · 194 1 · 195 1 · 196 3.**

**THREE CHAPTERS BREACH THE LIMIT OF THREE, ALL IN BATCH 0002: Ch 163, Ch 166 and Ch 167, each with four. Chapter 174 is at three and not over it — its fourth block is the engineer's own hand, read back by the clerk. Chapter 192, which carries the climax, has none. Chapter 196 has three on the strict count and is at the limit; the figure of five that the state files carry counts two blocks entered by the fen and not by the clerk, one of which is the volume's thirteen-entry standing-figures ledger. The limit was set at the Batch 0004 review, after these three chapters were closed, and the close records the breach rather than allowing it silently. NO CHAPTER WAS ALTERED TO FIX IT: removing a dated ledger entry out of a closed chapter would be a larger intervention than the defect and would break the hour it is entered against.**

## THE MECHANICAL AUDIT, GOOD AND BAD

**GOOD, AND IT IS GOOD ACROSS ALL FORTY-NINE AND NOT ONLY THE LAST BATCH.** **Zero non-ASCII glyphs in all forty-nine files.** **Zero unbalanced double-quote paragraphs: every speech paragraph opens and closes its own quotation, no narration stands inside an open speech, and no paragraph ends with a speech open.** **Zero double blank lines, zero blockquote markers off line start, zero repeated sentences within a file, zero duplicated paragraphs within a file.**

**SIX PARAGRAPHS ARE REPEATED VERBATIM ACROSS THE VOLUME AND ALL SIX ARE ARCHITECTURE, NOT ACCIDENT.** Ch 151 and Ch 168 are a matched pair — two chapters titled *The Sixteenth*, the same wall, the same yard, the same man with the spade, the same green in the older row — and the two shared paragraphs (*It is in the plainest words anybody has used about it…* and *And in the next row, which is the older row…*) are the pair's hinge. **Ch 168 is the ninth reading on that wall and Ch 151 is the eighth, and the wall's transcript grows by exactly one line between them, which is what makes the pair checkable.** The other four are refrains: the reader of this body asking for his initial to be put against nothing (Ch 177:18 and Ch 187:14), Dunmar Fitch entering the one observation he is allowed (Ch 167:11 and Ch 180:25), the handoff read at the north gate in a yard of about nine (Ch 187:18 and Ch 196:39), and the sentence this holding makes a standing by saying twice (Ch 191:6 and Ch 195:35).

**BAD, AND IT IS THREE DEFECTS.** A bare `""` — an empty quotation pair on a line of its own — stands at the end of Ch 156 and is the only such line in forty-nine files. A paragraph break and a space are both missing at Ch 187:72, where the closing scene is welded to the forty-eighth section-nine note by `is not going to.Underneath`. And `October`, a month name, is in plain narration at Ch 181:11, in the sentence about a sack of seed that has been in a shed through a wet month, and **it is the only month name in forty-nine chapters and it survived two review passes over Batch 0004 and the whole Batch 0005 pass.**

## THE REPAIRS THE CLOSE MADE, ALL OF THEM THE SMALLEST FIX THAT CAN ONLY BE MADE IN PROSE

**Sixty-four lines changed, in thirty-five of the forty-nine chapters. Every one is a word, a clause or a numeral. No sentence was added, no scene cut, no beat moved, and nothing was padded.** **THE ARITHMETIC CLOSES EXACTLY AND IT IS THE ARITHMETIC A LATER PHASE SHOULD CHECK: twenty lines are the individually itemised repairs in items 1–19, eleven are the month-distances in item 20, and thirty-three are the meta-language sweep in item 21. Twenty + eleven + thirty-three is sixty-four.** A first statement of this header said **twenty-eight sites in twenty chapters**, and that was wrong on both numbers. **Twenty-eight is the count of the sweep's `this volume` and body-prose `chapter` sites alone and not the whole sweep, and twenty chapters is not the number of chapters the repairs fell in.** The measured figures are sixty-four and thirty-five, taken from the file list and not from this record.

1. **Ch 156:91 — the bare `""` is deleted.** One line. (It stood on the chapter's last line, and the chapter is now ninety-one lines long; the line number was given as 92 in a first statement of this item and is 91.)
2. **Ch 187:72 — the missing break and the missing space are restored.** Two characters and one blank line.
3. **Ch 181:11 — `a wet October` becomes `a wet month two months back`.** The volume's ordinal idiom, and the sack has been in the shed since the twenty-ninth of the seventh month, which is where the season's damp is being described from.
4. **Ch 187:76 — `A man of about thirty-one fetched for the fifteenth time` becomes `A man of about seventy fetched for the fifteenth time`.** He is about seventy and is fetched for the sixteenth time on day 350; Ch 196 is right and Ch 187 was not.
5. **Ch 185:32 — who held the book.** The chapter says at :28 that the stop was entered by whoever held the book, "which was the licensed man, in his own hand at the head of the shaft", and at :32 that it was entered by whoever held the book, "which was the clerk, who was at the top of the slope". **The clerk's own block at :34 takes the licensed man's version and adds that the clerk entered the same thing in this holding's book and read it back down the slope. Line 32 is therefore made to agree with :28 and :34 instead of contradicting them.** This is the volume's second and last use of the standing rule and its four lines are about a stop being entered by whoever holds the book, so a chapter that cannot say who held the book is a chapter that cannot say its own rule was satisfied.

This also removes a THIRD use of the standing rule that the page appeared to assert, in a volume whose closing ledger says the count is two and is not going to be three.

    **The man of about thirty-five carries two career spans and they are not the same span, and a repair pass that conflates them breaks the chapter it is repairing. `outline/volume-04.md:67` gives him *reading ground* in **nine** years. `outline/volume-04.md:63` gives **Sera Quill's relay as nineteen years ago**, a different character and an untouched figure, appearing at Ch 161:15/39/85, Ch 162:51/83, Ch 166:24 and Ch 167:9/79. And the man's own **refusal** span is **nineteen**: "given that same nine words to two other bodies in nineteen years" and "the fourth time in nineteen years that a person has asked me what is under a ground" (Ch 172:65, :67), "refused four times in nineteen years" (Ch 177:50, Ch 187:44, Ch 180:55, Ch 193:59/63).**

    **So nineteen was only ever a slip in a sentence that says *read ground for*, and only at two sites: Ch 155:87 and Ch 156:21. The first pass of this item also changed Ch 156:19, "and I have given it to two people in **nine** years", which is the refusal construction and is the same figure as Ch 172:65, and that change has been REVERTED. Ch 156 is now self-consistent: nineteen for what he has refused (`:19`, `:29`), nine for what he has read (`:21`), and eleven at `:89`, which is a different speaker — the man of about fifty, and a different fact. A reviewer caught the contradiction, because the reverted line stood against `:29` in the same chapter by the same mouth, and the sweep that caused it has been recorded here so that no later pass generalizes nine a second time.**

## THE META-LANGUAGE QUESTION, DECIDED, AND THE DECISION IS TO SWEEP VOLUME 04 ONLY

**The test the close applies, and it is the test the record itself proposed: does the word have a referent inside the world?**

- ***This book* HAS ONE. It is the holding's own book, on the middle of the table in the seed house, which anybody may walk up to and read, and 183 of the volume's instances mean that book. It is NOT a target and none of them is touched.**
- ***This volume*, *this chapter* and *batch* HAVE NONE. There is no volume, no chapter and no batch anywhere in a fen with no charter. They are targets.**
- ***This season* is a real frame in this world: it is the frame the book already runs its counts in, and the two uses of the standing rule, on the twenty-second of the ninth month and on the thirteenth of the eleventh, are both inside one season. It is a legal replacement for a count of uses and the replacement SHARPENS the count.**

**The sweep is thirty-three sites in Volume 04, across twenty-five chapters: twelve instances of the bare word *chapter* in body prose, sixteen of *this volume*, and five of the bare word *volume* in a frame or a duration sense — Ch 167:83, Ch 169:25, Ch 177:88, Ch 184:49 and Ch 187:82.** A first statement of this said twenty-eight and named only the first two of the three, which undercounted the sweep by the five bare-*volume* sites it also repaired. **The five are not a fifth category and they are not an inconsistency: they are the same test applied to the same word. A `volume` that names a frame or a span of a book's own making is a *this book* thing, and a `volume` that names a duration across books is not, and the ten plural sites below are the second case.** Every replacement is a phrase the manuscript already uses. The counts of uses become *this season*. The narrator's signposts become *the day*, *the day's work* or *this holding's own*. One site, Ch 195:75, becomes *no page of this book is going to make one*, which is both world-referring and truer, because it is a page the fen controls. **WHAT THE SWEEP LEFT STANDING, BESIDE THE TEN PLURAL SITES, IS TWO SINGULAR *volume* SITES — Ch 173:25 and Ch 174:59, both *has not had one since the last volume* — AND THEY ARE CORRECT, because a bound volume of the holding's own book is a thing in the world, on a shelf, and *the last volume* has the same referent as *this book*.**

**WHAT THE SWEEP DELIBERATELY DOES NOT TOUCH, AND WHY — this is half the decision and it is not silence.**

- **The ten sites of the PLURAL *volumes* in Volume 04 (Ch 152:55, Ch 152:71, Ch 156:71, Ch 157:59, Ch 158:25, **Ch 162:95**, Ch 173:49, Ch 173:55, Ch 173:59, **Ch 178:5**) are NOT swept.** *Two volumes* and *three volumes* are durations across books, and the book's own frames for a duration are *this season* (roughly four months) and *eleven years* (the whole book). **Neither is equal to two volumes, and there is no frame in this world that is.** Replacing them would require inventing one, and inventing a duration frame is a bigger act than leaving ten words. **They are recorded as open, with their count, and a writer must choose a frame deliberately or leave them.** An earlier statement of this said nine and printed eight, and dropped Ch 162:95 and Ch 178:5, which is the pair a volume close is most likely to skip because Ch 178:5 is the fifth line of a chapter and reads as a frame rather than as a duration. `reviews/volume-04.findings.md` had the count of ten and the list of ten right, and this file is now brought into line with it.
- **Volumes 01, 02 and 03 are CLOSED and are NOT edited from this phase.** Their residue is measured and recorded: **twelve instances of *this batch* (0 in Volume 01, 11 in Volume 02, 1 in Volume 03), five bare *batch* that are not part of *this batch*, six *this chapter*, sixteen bare *chapter* in body prose, and thirty-two *this volume*.** Those volumes had three closes each and none of them caught this, which is not evidence that the class is small; it is evidence that a volume close does not look for it. **The residue is an open item against those volumes and is NOT a Volume 05 inheritance.**

## THE FIGURES, EVERY ONE LOCKED, EVERY ONE DERIVED ON THE PAGE, EVERY ONE RE-CHECKED

- **The heartroot at the Four Elbows delivers about 1,500 hundredweight a day into four bodies of households. The four bodies' own count of what they need is about 2,100. The difference is 600 hundredweight a day.**
- **600 hundredweight a day at fourpence the hundredweight is 2,400 pence, which is ten pounds a day. ## THE FIGURES, EVERY ONE LOCKED, EVERY ONE DERIVED TWICE ON THE PAGE, EVERY ONE RE-DERIVABLE

- **THE COMPOST LINE IS RE-ENTERED ON DAY 391 AT NINETY POUNDS**, with the eighty underneath it and the ten beside it and the reason and the hour. 400 hundredweight at four shillings is 1,600s = eighty pounds; 450 hundredweight at four shillings is 1,800s = ninety pounds; 1,800 − 1,600 = 200 shillings = ten pounds. **The word before the figure is SHALLOWER**, the four before it EMPTIER once and CROWDED three times, and **the run is thirteen months not discharged in thirteen.** Ch 217 also enters that the word and the figure have now come apart twice in five months and are not a pair, and that **this is the first month in four years the two of them have said the same thing**, which is entered by the woman who does the sums and by the person who keeps the seed house and by neither of them as good news.
- **THE READING.** The standing water in the main trunk above the sill **at the west kerb, at about the fourth hour of the evening, the same point and the same hour both times**: **on day 361, TWO FEET SEVEN INCHES; on day 396, ONE FOOT TEN INCHES. Nine inches in thirty-five days.** 31 − 22 = 9, and 396 − 361 = 35, and both are derived out loud at a kerb by lamplight in Ch 218 and both are derived again in the entry block. **THE SILL IS TAKEN FOUR TIMES IN THE BOOK AND ALL FOUR ARE BY THE READER OF THIS BODY, and the four days are 361, 396, 403 and 404: two feet seven inches, then one foot ten inches on the second, the same on the third, and the same again on the fourth on the evening of the fourteenth of this month, in the same scene as the north and the east sills.** The intervals are therefore **35 days from the first to the second, 42 days from the first to the third, and 8 days from the second to the fourth**, and **every one of those three is now on the page, and the count of four is the count Ch 224's entry block now names by name instead of leaving as a man.**
- **THE FEN DOES NOT CONVERT THE NINE INCHES INTO A WEIGHT, AND THE REASON IS ON THE SHEET IN HIS OWN WORDS:** a conversion needs a length of trunk and a section of trunk, he has the section at one place and has the length off a step count twice, and **a man who converts nine inches into a weight and then asks a village to give up its water is a man who has made the figure bigger by putting a number on the end of it.** Said once, in daylight, in a yard of about eleven people, and not said again.
- **THE SHEET** is four copies in his own hand with his name at the top of each, read out whole at about the ninth hour of the morning of day 397, compared against each other in that yard and word for word the same. It says the two figures and the interval and the hour and the place, that a branch has to come off the core, that the branch is **the east one**, and its reason: the four launders have been measured at 900, 600, 25 and 25 against about 1,500 delivered, the twenty-five is inside somebody's *about*, he has never made those two agree, and **a branch carrying a quarter of what another branch carries is the branch that costs least to lose, and that is a true sentence and it is a sentence about four villages' arithmetic and not about the ground.** **It does not say how many times the figure was taken, and that is the whole of the turn.**
- **THE THREE READINGS OF CH 222**, all at about the fourth hour of the evening of day 404, same man, same method: **the west sill ONE FOOT TEN INCHES, the same, not fallen further; the north sill TWO FEET ONE INCHES, and there is no earlier figure for it anywhere and there is not going to be one; the east sill TWO FEET FOUR INCHES and carrying nothing at all.** The north stand of about ninety trees is in bud and not in leaf and is the control, and the fen says in a yard that he had a control in front of him on the fourteenth of this month and had not used it until the following week, and that this is the second time in six days he has had something in his hand that would have answered the thing he had published.
- **THE LOSS.** Twenty-five hundredweight a day, priced in Marden's own yard and in Marden's own arithmetic, derived twice, the two agreeing: 25 × 4 pence = **100 pence a day**; thirty days = 750 hundredweight at **3,000 pence**; a pound is 240 pence; 3,000 pence is **TWELVE POUNDS AND TEN SHILLINGS A MONTH**; across about three hundred people that is **TEN PENCE A HEAD A MONTH**, and the second derivation is 100 pence over 300 people a day, being a third of a penny a head a day, and thirty days of a third of a penny is ten pence. **Marden's own paper also enters that the whole shortfall is six hundred hundredweight a day and forty-eight pence a head a month across about fifteen hundred people, and that those two are not the same figure and anybody who puts them in one column is going to make one of them look like the other one.**
- **TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY-ONE STANDING WILLOW**, a hundred and forty-one on the west side and about ninety on the north, and the cause: the west stand came into leaf between the two readings. The man of the north row with the cough had known that since day 392 and was eleven yards from about eleven people for nine days and did not say it.
- **THE RETURN.** Ninety hundredweight on the twelfth (day 397) and **NINETY-ONE HUNDREDWEIGHT on the thirteenth (day 406)**, which is a different number and is entered as a different number. The fourteenth is day 415 and is not this batch.
- **THE DAY-MINUS RULES: BOARDS DAY MINUS 66, THE MARCH'S TIN DAY MINUS 19.** On day 391, **325 and 372**, read out loud by the clerk before either number, and the drawer was not opened and is not to be. They were not read again in this batch because the door is read on the first and the thirtieth and the thirtieth is day 420, which is not this batch.
- **THE SEVENTH COLUMN: 40 on the thirtieth of the first month, 41 on the first of this month, and 41 for the rest of the month.** The next reading is **day 420, the thirtieth of the second month, a SATURDAY, and it goes to forty-two**, and that is Batch 0004's. The six other columns have no headings, have been blank since the door was made four years ago, and nobody in either yard asked.

## THE CANON ADDITIONS, ALL NEW, ALL FLAGGED

1. **THE WEST KERB SILL AND ITS TWO FIGURES.** The third of the four parts of the kerb, nine inches down, about five feet back from the edge, the cut above it a foot and a half wide and a foot and four inches deep, with a quarter-inch lip on the left side of the dressing where a hundred years of hands have gone in with a bucket. **A SILL IS A NEW MEASURABLE THING IN THIS BOOK AND IT IS THE FIRST PIECE OF GROUND AT THE FOUR ELBOWS THAT ANYBODY IN THIS BOOK HAS A FIGURE FOR.** It appears in Chs 218, 219, 222, 224 and 226. No later chapter may put a figure on it that does not agree with 218 and 222.
2. **THE EAST LAUNDER, CUT AT THE KERB, AND WHAT IT COST.** Cut in the stone at the head of the east sill on day 401, about the fourth hour and fifty minutes of the afternoon, by eleven people of Marden with two saws and a barrow each and a bucket, at the reading of a sheet. **The cut is at the kerb and not at the core, and four people said that in about two minutes in three different voices, and one of them said the half of it that matters: it is the only reason eleven of a village can do it in an afternoon, and nobody is going under a board.** The water went down in about nine seconds and made no noise. **The ditch above Marden is NOT fed by that launder, which is a fact nobody had ever looked at and was not looked at on the day.** The ground above that village is turned on the first of the third month and the ditch is ninety feet and dry at both ends since day 402.
3. **THE SHEET.** Four copies, one name at the top of each, the two figures, nine inches in thirty-five days, a branch has to come off the core, the east one, the arithmetic reason, and the refusal to convert. **It does not say how many times the later figure was taken.** It appears in Chs 219, 220, 222, 223, 224 and 226 and it is the document the volume turns on.
4. **THE SEVEN THAT DECIDE AT MARDEN AND THE STONE.** About two of the seven were on the flat place when the decision was taken; the seven were told in a room on day 400 and decided nothing; on day 405 Hesta Lyle wrote one line in her own hand with no name in it: **THE SEVEN DECIDED ON THE TENTH TO LET THE STONE DECIDE, AND ON THE FOURTEENTH THEY ASKED FOR THE LINE TO BE ENTERED AS THAT, AND THEY ASKED FOR IT IN THOSE WORDS, AND NOBODY HAS ASKED THEM WHY A STONE IS ALLOWED TO DECIDE SOMETHING THAT SEVEN PEOPLE ARE NOT ALLOWED TO DECIDE IN A ROOM.** This is a Volume 05 addition and it is on the page once and may not be enlarged.
5. **THE SHEET THE FEN SENT TO THE OCCUPIER.** A sheet with nothing at the top of it, a line for the day, a line for the hour, a line for the figure, and **two more lines under the line for the figure, of which the second is headed NOTHING ELSE.** No signature, no name, no stamp, no instruction, sent on day 394 through the ordinary post with nothing else in the bag. **She filled in one of the two lines and left the other empty on purpose and wrote under it that she is not going to say why.** The line she filled in is **MEASURED TWICE.** This is the first thing anybody in this book has ever sent that household in twelve years and it cost a sheet and fourpence.
6. **THE BARE RING.** About nine feet off the hollow where the fifth share's return goes in, a ring of bare ground about two yards wide and about two hundred yards long, in the middle of eleven acres of willow, bare for eleven years, and **nobody has ever asked what it is doing there and the fen walked it four times in this month and did not find out.**
7. **THE BURIED LEVER ON THE STONE AT MARDEN.** The flat place on the middle bank has a stone on it the size of a bread oven which is not natural and has a mason's mark on the back of it **that is the same mark as the third part of the kerb four hundred yards below.** Additive detail, load-bearing for nothing, and it is in the book so that a later writer does not have to invent one.
8. **THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY HAS FOUR NAMES IN FOUR BOOKS IN THIS MONTH** and has not asked for his initial to be put against nothing since the first of this month, and the count of that request stands at fifty-three.

A name into BY and a name into WITNESSED BY, **the fifth time in eleven years**. **THE FIFTEENTH RETURN, DAY 424, A WEDNESDAY, WAS NINETY HUNDREDWEIGHT** and the sixth name-pair in eleven years, and the two counts in this holding's book are in step this month at fifteen each, and the reader of this body entered that he does not know what they will be in a month's time and is not going to guess about it in a book. **THE THREE RETURNS OF THE SECOND MONTH ARE NINETY ON THE SEVENTH, NINETY-ONE ON THE SIXTEENTH AND EIGHTY-NINE ON THE TWENTY-FIFTH, AND THE FIGURE OF NINETY CAME ROUND AGAIN ON THE TWENTY-FOURTH OF THE THIRD MONTH, WHICH IS DAY 424, AND THE READER OF THIS BODY ENTERS THAT A FIGURE THAT COMES ROUND AGAIN IS NOT A FIGURE THAT HAS COME BACK.**
- **THE FOURTEENTH OR THE FIFTEENTH.** On day 415 the man of about thirty-one of Silling said **the fifteenth**, to the board and not to the yard, on the ground that the board carries fifteen marks in the column and the schedule carries fourteen names in its first rule. The woman who keeps the four books said a column with a heading for five days cannot be counted against a rule with a heading for eleven years, and that the fifteen is a count of marks and the fourteen is a count of mornings. **THE READER OF THIS BODY DID NOT RULE ON IT** and gave the reason, which is that he could settle it in about an hour and a man who settles it has decided which of two documents of four bodies of households is right. **BOTH NUMBERS GO IN AND NEITHER IS STRUCK OUT.**
- **THE DAY-MINUS RULES.** Day minus 66 and day minus 19. **On day 420, three hundred and fifty-four days and four hundred and one days, read out loud by the clerk before either number. On day 421, three hundred and fifty-five and four hundred and two, and the clerk was five days east and did not read them on the first of the third month, and the reader of this body read them out instead and entered that he did, and that is entered and it is not a fault and it is a fact about a road.** 420 less 66 is 354, 420 less 19 is 401, 421 less 66 is 355, 421 less 19 is 402. The drawer was not opened and is not to be, on any day of this batch.
- **THE SEVENTH COLUMN IS FORTY-TWO**, read on the thirtieth of the second month at about the eleventh hour in a yard of about twenty-five people, by the person who keeps the seed house, and it is read again on the first of the third month, at about the first hour of the morning, and it stood at forty-two then as it stood at forty-two on the thirtieth, **which the drafting pass had as the door NOT being read on the first while the same entry said the door is read on the first and the thirtieth, and the entry was wrong and is now right.** **The other six columns are blank, have been blank four years, about four people looked at the six places a heading ought to be, and nobody asked.**
- **THE SHORTFALL DID NOT GO UP AND DID NOT COME DOWN. IT IS SIX HUNDRED HUNDREDWEIGHT A DAY**, derived twice out loud in Ch 233 in a yard of about twenty-five people: 2,100 less 1,500 is 600; 600 at fourpence is 2,400 pence a day; thirty days is 18,000 hundredweight at 72,000 pence, being **three hundred pounds a month**; 2,400 pence over about 1,500 people is **one and three-fifths of a penny a head a day**; three hundred pounds over about 1,500 is **forty-eight pence a head a month**; forty-eight over thirty is one and three-fifths of a penny, and the two agree. **The four launders were measured at 900, 600, 25 and 25 before the cut and measure 900, 600, 0 and 25 now, and the twenty-five is inside somebody's *about* and the reader of this body said in a yard on the seventh of this month that he has never been able to make those two agree and is not going to to-day, and that is still on the sheet.** The reader of this body said the line about cutting a launder out loud in Ch 233 and **the woman who does the sums said the same thing in four sentences and shorter and the reader of this body entered that hers was the better one and that he was not going to say his again**, which is the pair the batch owed and the two are not the same sentence.
- **THE COMPOST LINE FOR THE SECOND MONTH.** **The word before the figure is PAID. The figure is ONE HUNDRED POUNDS.** Ninety pounds is the line and ten pounds is not in the line and has not been for four years and four months, being fifty hundredweight a month out of a bin behind the woman of about fifty-one's own house, carried by her, at the hour she carried it, in a book nobody had seen until the twenty-fourth of a month ago. The arithmetic is derived on the page and closes twice: 50 × 4s = 200s = £10 a month; £10 × 48 = **£480**; 2,400 hundredweight is six times 400 hundredweight, and six times £90 is **£540**, and the line said eighty pounds a month and was never more than seventy pounds a month of compost and the other ten was one woman's back. **The two strokes through two of the forty-eight lines are hers and mean the figure did not happen and not that it was smaller.** **The run is fourteen months not discharged in fourteen.** **This is the first word before that figure in five years that is not a word about a heap, and she chose it, and she said she is not going to be thanked and that anybody who thanks her can be told to stop.** The reader of this body said out loud that he has still not found out whether the word or the figure was telling the truth, that the word has stopped being about a heap, and that a line which was honest for five years about a thing that is not the problem is not thereby better than a line that was dishonest for five years about the problem, and that he is not going to vote.
- **THE COUNT OF MORNINGS AT MARDEN IS NINE, KEPT ELEVEN YEARS, IN HER OWN HAND, AND IT IS CHECKED TWO WAYS THAT AGREE.** Out of a hundred and thirty-two counts of fifty-two adults there are a hundred and twenty-three mornings on which the men of that village who could walk to the headland were in the village, and on a hundred and fourteen of those there was no such man out on the ground; a hundred and thirty-two less a hundred and twenty-three is nine. The second way is the field. **A hundred and thirty-two months is a hundred and thirty-two tens of days and thirty days is the month, being three thousand nine hundred and sixty days, and one turn in four of those is NINE HUNDRED AND NINETY, and there are nine.** **SIX OF THE NINE ARE THE SAME MAN AND SHE WILL NOT SAY WHICH AND WILL NOT BE ASKED TWICE**, and the reason is the sentence she gave in a yard at the node on the twenty-seventh of last month, that a name at a gate is a thing you put in a book and a name in a rota is a thing a man says with his own body at the second hour of a morning, and the reason she gave it, unchanged, thirty-two days later, is the same sentence.
- **THE TERMS OF THE REFUSAL AND THE COST OF THEM.** Four terms, given in order by Soren Rill, of about thirty-five, of an Assembly in the Thornwild, on the cart road at Errow Reach on the afternoon of the twenty-fourth of this month: not in a yard, because a yard is about eleven people and the last thing anybody said in one went into four villages in four copies in five days; one question, not the reader of this body's, and the question goes from a room their own clerks are in and he will name the day and they cannot move it; he will not see the answer first, it goes to the four villages and not to him; **and the cost, named out loud before he agreed to anything, being nineteen miles and two nights and a season of a working man's year and the fact that an answer to one question is the answer to one question, and there will not be a second occasion, and the man in the fen will be the only one who has spent a season of a working man's year on a question that is not his and is not the one who will have to live in four villages afterwards.** **THE COST FELL ON THE WOMAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-EIGHT OF MARDEN AND NOT ON THE ENGINEER OF RECORD, being two nights and one day out of a village of about three hundred people, with a gate counted on the first and the fifteenth by one woman and by nobody else, so that on the day she is away about three hundred people are not counted by anybody, which has not happened in eleven years and is a day.** The reader of this body offered her money and did not give it and told her he had thought about it, and she told him that if he thanked her she would tell him to stop, and he did not thank her.
- **THE QUESTION, WRITTEN OUT AND CARRIED BY HER, IN ELEVEN SECONDS, WITH NO PARAGRAPH UNDER IT:** WHAT IS THE STANDING OF A BODY OF HOUSEHOLDS UPON A GROUND THAT IS NOT THEIRS, AND WHO ANSWERS FOR IT, AND IS AN ANSWER GIVEN IN A ROOM IN FENNEMERE BINDING UPON THE GROUND OR ONLY UPON THE ROOM. **The reader of this body had four versions of it in his own book and cut all four out before he wrote this one, and the reason is that the other four were about him.**
- **THE ELEVEN THINGS THE INSPECTION FOUND.** The Assembly's inspection came on the ordinary notice, named the seventh of the third month and about the tenth hour, was not stayed, delayed, fed or obstructed, and found eleven items, and **read the one with no name on it first and said why before she read it.** **The eleventh is A RING OF BARE GROUND, ABOUT TWO YARDS WIDE AND ABOUT TWO HUNDRED YARDS LONG, INSIDE ELEVEN ACRES OF STANDING WILLOW, NINE FEET OFF THE HOLLOW WHERE THE RETURNS GO IN, BARE ELEVEN YEARS, AND IT IS NOT A FAULT OF ANYBODY AT THAT NODE AND NO NAME IS PUT AGAINST IT, and the inspector stated on her own page that she did not find out what it is doing there.** The ten that are this volume's own fault are on the page in full in Ch 235, and every one of the ten was on the four bodies' own page before the inspector arrived, and the inspector wrote that down. **THE READER OF THIS BODY DID NOT WRITE ONE WORD OF THE ELEVEN DOWN AND DID NOT INTERRUPT, and entered that he did not speak to the examiner once in two hours, and entered the reason, which is that an engineer of record who talks to an examiner about a tape for two hours is making the tape the point.** The examiner is **Sabra Ollerton, of about fifty-two, inspector of the Rootwright Assembly for four districts**, and she is not Warden Halden Pike and Pike is not named in this batch and is not in it as a man or a face. She answered four questions on the tenth and said she did not know the answer to two of them, in front of nineteen people, and did not go back to either. **She had said on the seventh, in the yard and out loud, that she would be there on the ninth at about the fourth hour, and the copy was read on the tenth, and Ch 236 says the tenth and the page is the authority; THE NINTH IS WHAT SHE PROMISED AND NOT WHAT HAPPENED, and it is left as that and is not turned into a delay, because no office in this batch is late for anything.**
- **THE INSPECTOR'S OWN NOTE, which is the thesis of the batch in another hand:** I HAVE FOUND NOTHING AT THAT NODE THAT ITS OWN BOOKS DO NOT ALREADY CARRY.
- **THE BOTTLE-NECK SENTENCE AND WHERE IT HAS BEEN SAID.** The sentence that a man who is the only person who can do a thing is a bottleneck and not a system was said out loud in a yard **five times** in this season, and **is not going to be said a sixth time in a yard**, and Ch 236 names the five in order: a yard on the eleventh of a month back, this holding's own book on the page where the count is, a yard at Errow Reach in about nine people, a yard at Marden on a stone in about nineteen people, and a shed. **AND NOT ONE OF THE FIVE WAS IN THE SAME BUILDING AS THE COUNT**, and from the tenth of the third month it goes into a book and a note and not into a yard, and the reason is entered, which is that the reader of this body has worked out that the nine feet is the whole of what he has been doing.

## THE CANON ADDITIONS, ALL NEW, ALL FLAGGED

1. **THE ELEVEN LINES OF THE DRAFT ROTA, read out whole and entered whole in Ch 227.** Four turns (Havergate, second hour, two hours, six who take it in turns; Low Wether, second hour, two hours, two; Silling, second hour, two hours, one and he is seventy-one; **Marden, second hour, two hours, four people working, NOT COUNTED**) and seven stops (the fifth, a turn does not begin until the holder is on the ground and has said the word; the sixth, a turn that has not happened is taken by the next body on the list; the seventh, a holder who is asleep and cannot be woken is neither, the next body is woken, and then the one after, and if neither can be woken the turn is not taken, the fields wait, and the fields waiting is entered by whoever enters anything with the day and the hour on it, and nobody is blamed for a field that waited; the eighth, nobody holds a turn for a body of households that has not asked; the ninth, a body may stop any turn of its own at any time without saying why and without saying why before; the tenth, the holder stops on one word, the same word, said out loud so that somebody hears it; the eleventh, it is a draft and is not in force because three of the four bodies have not seen it). **THE ELEVENTH LINE WAS OVERTURNED ON THE NINTH OF THIS MONTH AND THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY REFUSED TO RUB IT OUT AND REFUSED TO WRITE ON A SHEET HE DID NOT WRITE, and his reason is entered, which is that a man who rubs out a thing in front of you has told you what the thing was and a man who does not has not.** **THE SHEET CARRIES NO WORD FOR THE FIFTH LINE, and that is the whole of the first morning of the rota, and it is a defect in a document and not in a man.**
2. **THE ORDER OF THE FOUR LINES IS SETTLED BY Ch 228 AND NOT BY Ch 201.** Ch 201's entry and Ch 211's entry call the Marden line the **third**; Ch 202, Ch 215, Ch 216, the state files and this batch call it the **fourth**, and **THE PAGE OF THIS BATCH FOLLOWS THE FOURTH**, which is the most recent and is the one the four bodies and the reader of this body both had in front of them. **A later phase must use the fourth line for Marden.** No chapter of this batch names the number of the Marden line except by calling it the fourth.
3. **THE COST OF A CREW OF FIVE, named by the woman of about forty-four of a holding on the cart road, in her own yard, in her own hand, and not in a book and not on a form she has ever asked for:** two nights a week that she does not know what she is doing on, a back, about eleven hours a week of a life that is not hers, a daughter of seventeen who does the Tuesday, and hands that are worse than her daughter's are and going to be worse than her daughter's will be. **She is on the committee that writes her own five lines and she said so before the reader of this body got to it.**
4. **THE WHERE-COLUMN.** The reader of this body asked whether she was going to put a column on her board saying where a person is, and she said no, and the four words are **it would need five.** The reader of this body asked the same question of himself on the seventeenth and said no, and has entered that the sentence is going into a book and a note and is not going back into a yard.
5. **Renn Ashby, of about twenty-six, of Havergate, one of the six who take it in turns**, who was on the ground on the morning of the twenty-second with five men and a barrow each and did not have the word, wrote his own page out, the man of about fifty read it out and read it back, **and the reader of this body did not ask to see it and did not ask for a copy of it**, and the reason is entered, which is that this holding has already asked a man of about twenty-six for a copy of a figure he could not check, inside a fortnight, and is not going to ask twice.
6. **Sabra Ollerton, of about fifty-two, inspector of the Rootwright Assembly for four districts.** New, named, and the first person in this book to come on an ordinary notice and say out loud in a yard of about twenty-two people that she did not find out what a thing is and that she is not going to guess at it.
7. **THE COUNT OF YARDS THE MAN OF THE NORTH ROW WITH THE COUGH HAS STOOD IN SINCE DAY 361 IS NINE**, and he was asked to be in none of the nine, and he carried a basket on the ninth of this month without being asked, and he has said three things in nine yards and one of the three was about arithmetic. **DAY 361 IS CALLED *the first of last month* IN Chs 227 AND 229 AND *the first of a month two months back* IN Chs 235 AND 236, and both are the same day: a frame changes at the month turn and the day does not.**

## THE REPAIR PASS ON BATCH 0004, AND EVERY FIGURE IN IT

**A REPAIR PASS RAN OVER THE TEN CHAPTERS OF BATCH 0004 AFTER THE DRAFTING PASS HAD MEASURED THEM, AND IT FOUND NINE DEFECTS IN PROSE AND THREE IN THE STATE FILES' OWN FIGURES. **WHAT THE PASS WAS. The chapters and the state for this batch were on disk and committed before this pass ran. The pass was not a review of the batch's quality. It was a check of the batch's own figures against the batch's own two naming tables, its own day clock, its own rota table and its own published word counts, because this batch is a batch about a figure being wrong by a month and a writer who inherits it has to be able to trust it.**

1. **THE PUBLISHED WORD COUNTS FOR BATCH 0004 WERE MEASURED BEFORE THE LAST PROSE EDITS AND WERE LOW BY 357 WORDS ACROSS SEVEN OF THE TEN CHAPTERS.** As published: 2,936 / 3,118 / 2,689 / 2,892 / 2,694 / 2,775 / 2,894 / 3,010 / 2,759 / 2,728, a batch of 28,495, a volume of 116,598 and a manuscript of 709,117. **As measured by that pass: 3,098 / 3,118 / 2,687 / 2,893 / 2,699 / 2,814 / 3,014 / 3,019 / 2,762 / 2,748, a batch of 28,852, a volume of 116,955 and a manuscript of 709,474, reconciling exactly. THE 28,852, THE 2,748, THE 116,955 AND THE 709,474 ARE THEMSELVES WITHDRAWN BY THE REVIEW PASS THAT FOLLOWED AND ARE LOW BY FOUR, ALL FOUR OF THEM IN CH 236, which that pass shortened; the figures now standing are at the head of this section and are 28,848 / 2,744 / 116,951 / 709,470.** The old figures are named and withdrawn above and in `state/current.md` and in `state/open-threads.md` and are left visible rather than overwritten. **THE CAUSE IS THE CLASS THIS BATCH IS ABOUT: a figure written down without being checked against the state of the page it measures.** The batch is inside 27,000-30,000 and every chapter is inside 2,600-3,120, **no chapter is declared outside the band, and the volume's two declared exceptions are unchanged at Ch 206 and Ch 216.**

Only one paragraph of nine words or more is repeated in the batch and it is that one. The mechanical check has been rewritten to the measured figures.

The fifteenth of the second month is a day on which no ninth day falls. CORRECTED BY THE VOLUME 05 CLOSE, IN Ch 234 AND HERE, WITH THE OLD FIGURE WITHDRAWN.** It also moved the launder's standing day and the leak's not-measured day from the first of this month, which is the day the chapter is on, to **the thirtieth of last month**, which is the day they were read on.
8. **Ch 234 carried two month-frame errors and both were the turn.** The half inch is day 196 and is **a month eight months back** to a speaker on day 421 and not seven, and the next ordinary reading is **the sixteenth of next month** and not the sixteenth of this month, which is six days in the future and is Batch 0005's day. **Neither was in Ch 233 and both were right there**, which is exactly what two tables for one batch crossing a month turn are for.

And the mileage to the woman of about forty-four's holding was **about ninety miles**, which is more road than a man walks in five days on a road this book measures at about thirty-one; **it is now two days of road west of here.**

The **turn of the ground above Marden is the first of the third month, which is Ch 234's day, and it takes a fortnight with water in that ditch and a month without, and the ditch is ninety feet and has been dry at both ends since the twelfth of the second month, and nobody has yet found out what happened to it.** The **eleven findings and the copy of them going to four bodies** is a document now in the world. And **the count of persons in this fen who can hold a pattern for four is two and is going to be two at the end of the season.**

## THE FIGURES, EVERY ONE LOCKED, EVERY ONE DERIVED ON THE PAGE, EVERY ONE RE-DERIVABLE BY A LATER WRITER

1. **THE TEST. NINE CONSECUTIVE MORNINGS, THE FOURTEENTH TO THE TWENTY-SECOND OF THIS MONTH, DAYS 434 TO 442, AT THE SECOND HOUR, TWO HOURS, ONE HOLDER AND FOUR WORKING, THE HOLDER CHANGING EVERY MORNING.** Drawn by the man of the north row with the cough, in his own hand, on the back of a printed schedule, in a cart shed, on the eleventh of this month, unasked and unthanked, read out in about eleven people and read back by the man of about fifty. **THE FIVE MORNINGS OF THE READER OF THIS BODY ARE 434, 436, 438, 440 AND 442, AND THE FOUR MORNINGS OF THE MAN OF THE NORTH ROW WITH THE COUGH ARE 435, 437, 439 AND 441, AND THE REASON IS ENTERED IN THE SHEET AND IS A REASON AND NOT A FAIRNESS: he asked for four in front of eleven people and was given four.**
2. **THE WORD IS ON THE SHEET. IT IS *ENOUGH*.** The fifth line has said *a turn does not begin until the holder is on the ground and has said the word* since the twenty-first of the second month and the sheet carried no word until the eleventh of this month. **THE MAN WHO WROTE THE SHEET WROTE THE WORD ON IT, IN HIS OWN HAND, AND THE READER OF THIS BODY DID NOT WRITE IT AND WAS NOT ASKED TO, and the man of about fifty read it out and read it back, and nobody rubbed out the old sheet's eleventh line and the man of about fifty has still refused to write on it.** The eleventh line of the old draft is still on the page saying it is a draft and is not in force.
3. **THE FOUR WORKING, WORKED OUT AT THE KERB BY FOUR BODIES OF HOUSEHOLDS OVER THREE DAYS AND TOLD TO THE READER OF THIS BODY AND NOT ASKED BY HIM.** Renn Ashby, of about twenty-six, of Havergate. A man of about nineteen of Silling, the third line's grandson, unnamed in this book. The woman of about thirty-eight of Marden. **And Harlan Vetch, of about fifty-eight, who holds the fifth share, who said the thing about himself before anybody put him down on a list, and who asked to be asked and is not going to be thanked for it.**
4. **THE WATER CAME BACK INTO THE DITCH ABOVE MARDEN AT ABOUT THE SECOND HOUR OF THE MORNING OF THE TWENTY-SECOND, WHICH IS DAY 442, A SUNDAY**, **after FORTY days dry at both ends, being day 402 to day 442. THE THIRTY-SEVEN THAT STOOD HERE IS WITHDRAWN AND WAS NOT DERIVABLE FROM ANYTHING; and on the page's own inclusive convention, which Chs 239 and 240 use, it is the forty-first day. Ch 238 is repaired by the close and the ladder is now thirty-third at day 434, thirty-fifth at 436, thirty-ninth at 440.** The turn of that field was begun on the first of this month by eleven people and is about three weeks old. It rained from about the eleventh hour of the twenty-second until about the fifth hour of the afternoon of the twenty-fourth. **THE WOMAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-EIGHT OF MARDEN PRICED WHAT THE DRAINED-IN-WATER TURN COSTS IN MARDEN'S OWN ARITHMETIC AND GAVE NO FIGURE AT ALL, and said that if anybody puts that field next to a whole shortfall at a node then somebody is going to make a field in Marden look like a village.**
5. **THE NINTH MORNING. THE MIDDLE WAS EMPTIED FIRST AND THE TWO ENDS HELD.** It took about seventeen hours, from the third hour of the morning of the twenty-second to the second hour of the twenty-third. The man of about nineteen of Silling had **seven** readings of the middle with a rule and a piece of chalk and **no unit**, and said so out loud twice, and the unit is not known in this holding and was not known and is not entered a second time anywhere. **THE MIDDLE WAS A FOOT AND ONE INCH LOWER AT THE SECOND HOUR OF THE TWENTY-SECOND THAN IT HAD BEEN AT THE SECOND HOUR OF THE FOURTEENTH, and the two numbers the woman of about thirty-eight of Marden had been saying on the bank since the fourteenth were the same two, and the man of about fifty wrote them down, and the unit is still not known.**
6. **THE INJURY. THREE INCHES ALONG THE INSIDE OF THE RIGHT FOREARM OF THE MAN OF THE NORTH ROW WITH THE COUGH. IT DOES NOT BRANCH. IT IS PERMANENT. IT CAME AT ABOUT THE SEVENTH HOUR OF THE EVENING OF THE TWENTY-SECOND AND HE DID NOT STOP AND DID NOT SAY THE WORD.** It is entered in **his own hand**, on a page given to him by the man of about fifty, at about the fourth hour of the morning of the twenty-third, and **the reader of this body did not ask to see it and the man of about fifty did not ask to see it, and the words of it are in this holding's book because a man of thirty-one copied them out in his own hand at about the fifth hour of the morning of the twenty-third, and the man of about fifty's sentence about that was: WRITE IT DOWN AND DO NOT ASK HIM TO READ IT.** **THE ENGINEER OF RECORD'S OWN MARK IS FOUR INCHES AND BRANCHES TWICE AND IS NOT A SECOND MARK AND IS NOT LONGER THAN IT WAS, and the mark being hot on the twenty-first is not the mark, and the headache is not the mark and is not entered as the mark, and the four accounts of that arm are four and nothing said about that arm in this batch is a fifth. THE INJURY IS NOT AN ACCOUNT OF HIS ARM AND IS NOT A FIFTH ACCOUNT OF ANYTHING.**
7. **THE FIELDBOOK, OPENED ONCE IN FIVE VOLUMES, ON A PERSON, AND NOT ON A PAGE.** Day 441, a Saturday, at about the first hour of the afternoon, in a yard at this holding, in about eleven people, **by Coll Renner, licensed, on the roll for the Tarrow district, not on the roll for the district the node stands in, who came at his own cost and said so in a yard and who said four things, the fourth of which is that nobody is to thank him for coming.** The cost was written in the reader of this body's own hand and read back three times before the instrument went near anything, and a plain wire gauge was put against the book and read, and the reading of the test was written down first. **THE BEAD WAS LAID AGAINST THE LEFT FOREARM OF THE MAN OF THE NORTH ROW WITH THE COUGH, about four inches along the inside, in the place a mark runs in a person who has been holding, AND THE SKIN OF IT WAS WET, and it took.** He offered before he was asked and asked for it to be read out afterwards that the reason was that he has got no mark and not that anybody asked him, and nobody thanked him. **The reading was eleven seconds, which the reader of this body cannot account for and has never been able to account for in any reading, and it is in the cost.**

> **Take the water off the middle first.**
> **The two ends will hold while the middle is empty.**
> **If one of the two ends lets go, do not close the middle.**

**THE PANEL GETS NO NAME AND THE THREE LINES ARE NOT SAID BY ANYBODY AFTERWARDS EXCEPT AS A PROCEDURE, and it does not say who holds the middle and the reader of this body did not say and the man of the north row with the cough did not say.** The fen read the fourth line out and then stopped for about four seconds and then read the first line again. The book went back into the oilcloth and the oilcloth into the crate and the crate went up the four-day road on the twenty-third at about the seventh hour at this holding's cost, and the total cost both ways is **six shillings and fourpence**, being two shillings and sixpence a day for four days each way and a crate of one shilling and fourpence, and this holding had four pounds and fivepence in the box and has not been asked for it.
8. **THE USE LOG STANDS AT FIFTEEN LINES AND DID NOT MOVE, AND THE FIELDBOOK CONTACT GOT NO LINE, AND THE REASON IS ON THE PAGE.** Coll Renner's answer, in his own words: NO LINE IS REQUIRED. I have a book and I enter a contact in it in my own hand with the hour on it and the licensed person on it and my roll on it, and I have entered one this afternoon, and it is in my book and not in this one, and the two books are not the same book, and there is nothing in the rule that puts a line in yours, and I am not the person who decides what goes in your book and you are not the person who decides what goes in mine. **THE READER OF THIS BODY'S OWN REASON IS THAT THE FIFTEENTH LINE IS A CONTACT ON A BOARDED FLOOR AND THAT A MAN WHO NEEDS A NEW LINE FOR A NEW KIND OF THING HAS FOUND A NEW INSTRUMENT AND NOT A NEW KIND OF WORK. Ch 240 names eight things that got no line: a schedule, a reading, a launder cut by a village, a not known, a figure read twice by somebody else's hand, a gate count, a hold, a rota in force for thirty-nine mornings, a barrow of leaf mould carried by one woman for forty-eight months, a crate, four days of a road in each direction, a bead laid against a man's arm, a day and a night on a stone, and a covenant of six lines — AND THE FIGURE IN THE LIST IS ELEVEN AND NOT EIGHT, and the earlier count of eight was taken from a paragraph that named eight and not from the list the paragraph named.**
